en: Janaka of Videha sat down.
The connection of this [passage] is as follows: having withdrawn the eight persons, beginning with the body, from their respective locations and having brought them back again into the heart—
Furthermore, having expanded [the breath] fivefold by means of the differentiation of the directions,

and having withdrawn it back into the heart, one should dissolve both the heart and the body into the thread (sūtra) called *samāna*— which consists of the activity of the six paths beginning with *prāṇa* and is the self of the universe— and which is established upon one another.
Having withdrawn the world-soul into the Sūtra,
that person of the Upaniṣads who was designated as "not this, not this" (neti neti) and who transcends the states of being the body, the heart, and the Sūtra,
is pointed out directly both as the witness and by way of his nature as the material cause in the words, "Consciousness, Bliss."

This commencement of the two Brāhmaṇas is for the purpose of providing another means of attainment, namely that the very same [Self] must be attained again by means of the deities of speech and so forth.
The narrative, however, is intended to demonstrate proper conduct.
(Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.1.1)
Janaka of Videha was sitting in state.
Then Yājñavalkya arrived.
He said to him: "Yājñavalkya, for what purpose have you come? Do you seek cattle, or do you seek subtle questions?"
"Both indeed, O Saṃrāj," he said. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.1.1)

Janaka of Videha sat down— that is, he took his seat and provided a place for visitors— intending to receive those who desired an audience with the king. Then, at that moment, Yājñavalkya arrived, having come for the sake of securing his own livelihood and well-being.
Seeing that the king desired to debate, and for the sake of showing him favor, Janaka offered proper worship to Yājñavalkya upon his arrival and said: "O Yājñavalkya, for what purpose have you come?
Have you come again desiring cattle?"

"Or rather, do you wish to hear from me questions concerning atoms, subtle limits, or the determination of subtle entities? "Both, O Emperor—both the cattle and the questions," [he replied]. "Emperor! Emperor! [This is] a mark of one who has performed the Vājapeya sacrifice;
for he who rules a kingdom by command is also called an Emperor.
A sovereign (*samrāj*); his address is "O sovereign," or he is the king of the entire land of Bhārata-varṣa. //4,1.1//
"Let us hear what someone has told you.
"Jitvan Śailini told me: 'Speech, indeed, is Brahman.'"
"Just as one who has a mother, a father, and a teacher might say, so did Śailini declare: 'Speech, indeed, is Brahman.
For what could there be for one who does not speak? [The other] replied, "But you have told me its abode and its support."
"He did not tell me," [the king said].
"That is only one quarter, O Emperor," [Yājñavalkya replied].
"Then do you tell us, Yājñavalkya."
"Speech indeed is its abode, space is its support; one should meditate upon it as wisdom.
"What is the nature of this wisdom, Yājñavalkya?
"Speech itself, O King," he said.
"Indeed, O Emperor, it is through speech that kinship is known:
the Rigveda, the Yajurveda, the Samaveda, the Atharva-Angirasa, history, ancient lore, the sciences, the Upanishads,
verses, aphorisms, explanations, commentaries, what is sacrificed, what is offered, what is eaten, what is drunk, this world and the next."
The world and all beings are made known by speech alone, O Sovereign.
Speech, indeed, O Sovereign, is the supreme Brahman;
speech does not desert him.
All beings flow toward him;
having become a god, he goes to the gods—
he who, knowing this, meditates upon it.
"I shall give you a thousand cows with a bull as large as an elephant," said Janaka of Videha.
Yājñavalkya replied, "My father believed that one should not accept a gift without having first given instruction."
"But what someone has told you—since you have served many teachers, you must have heard from various masters—let us hear that.
The other replied: "My teacher, by name Śilina, the son of Śilina (Śailini), told me: 'Speech indeed is Brahman'; that is, the deity of speech is Brahman. He said:
"He is one who possesses a mother (*mātṛmān*), meaning a son for whom there exists a mother who is his instructor and the giver of proper instruction."
Henceforth, he whose instructor is his father is "one who has a father";
from the time of the initiation (*upanayana*) until the return home (*samāvartana*), he whose instructor is the teacher (*ācārya*) is "one who has a teacher.

Thus, being endowed with these three causes of purity, that virtuous teacher never deviates from authority on his own; whatever he says to the disciple, having mastered it, Śailini spoke thus: "Speech indeed..."
"Brahman," [he said].
"For what would come of not speaking?
For one who is mute, there would be no purpose whatsoever here or in the hereafter."
However, he said to you the abode (*āyatana*) and the support (*pratiṣṭhā*) of that Brahman. "Abode" refers to the body;
"support" is that which serves as the basis throughout all three periods of time.
The other said, "The other [teacher] did not tell me.

The other replied: "If that is so, then this Brahman is one-footed—that is, of this Brahman there is only one foot; this one-footed Brahman, even when meditated upon, does not lead to the fruit because it is empty of the other three feet.
If this is the case, then you, O Yājñavalkya, being a knower, tell us about it."

And he said: "Speech alone is the abode; for the deity Brahman, speech alone is the instrument, the body, while the unevolved [avyākṛta] space is the foundation during the times of origination, persistence, and dissolution.
One should worship this as 'Wisdom' (prajñā). This "Wisdom" is the secret name (upaniṣad) of the fourth quarter of Brahman; considering it to be Wisdom, one should worship this Brahman.
"What is the nature of this Wisdom, Yājñavalkya? Is it Wisdom itself, or is it the cause of Wisdom?"
"Just as the two supports of the abode are distinct from Brahman, is it the same in this case?
"No," he replied. "How then?
"Speech alone, O Emperor," he said; "Speech alone is wisdom," he said—thus he spoke, meaning that wisdom is not something separate [from speech].
But how is it that speech itself is wisdom?
It is said: "O Emperor, by means of speech indeed is a kinsman known; when it is said, 'This is our kinsman,' the kinsman becomes known—such as the Ṛgveda and so forth.
Likewise, the collection of dharmas characterized by sacrifice is 'iṣṭa' (offered), and those characterized by oblation are 'huta' (poured)."

"O Emperor, it is by speech alone that food is made known for the purpose of eating, and drink for the purpose of drinking; this world and the next world, the birth to be attained, and all beings—these are made known by speech alone. Therefore, O Emperor, speech is indeed the supreme Brahman; speech does not desert one who knows the Brahman as described."
All beings here bestow upon him their offerings through gifts of tribute and the like.
Having become a god, after the falling away of this body, he who knows this and meditates upon it goes to and attains even the gods.
For the sake of the completion of his knowledge, [he gives] a thousand cows with a bull as large as an elephant—a bull equal to an elephant is a "hastirṣabha"—and that is the "hastirṣabha" thousand.

"I give," said Janaka of Videha. Yājñavalkya replied: "My father held this view—that one should not take wealth from a disciple without having instructed him and made him accomplished—and this is my own intention as well. (4.1.2)
"Whatever anyone has told you, let us hear that. "Udaṅka Śaulbāyana told me."
"Brahman is indeed breath," said Śaulbāyana. Just as one who has a mother, a father, and a teacher might speak, so did Śaulbāyana say, "Brahman is indeed breath.
For what could there be for one who does not breathe?
"But he did not tell you its abode or its support," [the other] said. "He did not tell me," [the first] replied. "This, O Emperor, is indeed one-footed."
"Tell us that, Yājñavalkya.
"The vital breath (prāṇa) indeed is its abode, space (ākāśa) its support;
one should meditate upon it as 'the dear' (priya)."
"What is the dearness [of the self], Yājñavalkya?
"The vital breath (*prāṇa*) alone, O Emperor," he said.
"Indeed, O Emperor, it is out of love for the vital breath that one causes one who is not entitled to sacrifice to perform a sacrifice."
He accepts what should not be accepted;
even there, there is fear of being struck down in whichever direction he goes, solely for the sake of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), O Emperor.
The vital breath, O Emperor, is indeed the supreme Brahman.
The vital breath does not desert him;
all beings flow toward him.
Having become a god, he goes to the gods.
"To him who, knowing this,
venerates it," said Janaka of Videha, "I shall give a thousand [cows] with an elephant and a bull.
Yājñavalkya replied, "My father thought that one should not accept a gift without having first instructed [the pupil]."
"Whatever one told you—Udaṅka by name, the son of Śulba (Śaulbāyana)—said, 'The vital breath (prāṇa) indeed is Brahman. As before, the deity is Vāyu;
the vital breath itself is the path, space is the foundation, and 'the dear' is its secret name (upaniṣad). One should meditate upon it as such.
But how, again, is it dear?"

Indeed, O Emperor, for the sake of the desire for the vital breath (prāṇa), for the purpose of the vital breath, one causes even those unworthy of sacrifice to perform sacrifices; one accepts gifts even from those from whom they should not be accepted, such as fierce men; and one goes in whatever direction there is apprehension of death—that is, fear of being killed—even toward a direction infested with thieves and the like; and in that direction there is the fear of death. All this occurs because the vital breath is dear.
"It is for the sake of the desire for vital breath alone, O Emperor.
Therefore, vital breath indeed, O Emperor, is the supreme Brahman; vital breath does not desert him. The rest is the same. //4,1.3//
"Whatever anyone has told you, let us hear that. "Barku Vārṣṇa told it to me."
"The eye, indeed, is Brahman"—
thus did Vārṣṇa speak, just as one who possesses a mother, a father, and a teacher might say;
for what could there be for one who does not see?
"But he did not tell you its abode or its foundation. "He did not tell me," [the king replied]. "This, O Emperor, is indeed one-footed."
"Tell us that, Yājñavalkya.
"The eye indeed is its abode, space its support;
one should meditate upon it as Truth."
"What is the truth, Yājñavalkya?
"The eye alone, O Emperor," he said.
"For indeed, O Emperor, they say to one who sees with the eye, 'Have you seen?'"
He said, "I saw it," and that becomes the truth.
O Emperor, the eye is indeed the supreme Brahman;
the eye does not desert him.
All beings flow toward him;
having become a god, he goes to the gods—
he who, knowing this, meditates upon it.
"I shall give you a thousand cows with a bull as large as an elephant," said Janaka of Videha.
Yājñavalkya replied, "My father was of the opinion that one should not accept a gift without having first given instruction."

Regarding what someone told you—Barku by name, the descendant of Vṛṣṇi, a Vārṣṇa—the eye is indeed Brahman; the deity is Āditya, and the secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*) concerning the eye is "Truth" (*satyam*).
For while that which is heard by the ear might be false, that which is seen by the eye cannot be so.
Therefore, O Emperor, when they ask one who has seen, "Did you see the elephant?", if he says, "I saw it," that becomes the truth.
But that which someone else might say, "I heard it," can be erroneous; however, that which is seen with the eye is indeed true, because of its non-erroneous nature. //4.1.4//
"Whatever anyone has told you, let us hear that. "Gardabhīvipīta Bhāradvāja told me."
"The ear, indeed, is Brahman. Bhāradvāja spoke thus, "The ear, indeed, is Brahman," just as one who has a mother, a father, and a teacher might speak;
for what would there be for one who does not hear?
"But he did not tell you its abode or its foundation. "He did not tell me," [the king replied]. "This, O Emperor, is indeed one-footed."
"Tell us that, Yājñavalkya.
"The ear indeed is its abode, space is its foundation; one should meditate upon it as 'the infinite.
What, Yājñavalkya, is its infinity?"
"The quarters themselves, O Emperor," he said.
"Therefore indeed, O Emperor, whatever quarter one goes toward, one never reaches its end,
for the quarters are infinite."
The quarters, O Emperor, are indeed the ear;
the ear, O Emperor, is the supreme Brahman.
The ear does not desert him.
All beings flow toward him;
having become a god, he goes to the gods—
he who, knowing this, worships it thus.
"I shall give you a thousand cows with a bull as large as an elephant," said Janaka of Videha.
Yājñavalkya replied, "My father believed that one should not accept a gift without having first instructed the giver."

"Regarding that which was said to you as 'Gardabhīvipīta' by name—Bhāradvāja by lineage—hearing (*śrotra*) is indeed Brahman. One should meditate upon this with the thought: 'Hearing is Brahman. The deity of the quarters is in hearing; one should meditate on it as Ananta (the Infinite).
What is the infinity of hearing?"

The quarters of space themselves constitute the infinity of the sense of hearing; therefore, O Emperor, whether one goes toward the east, the north, or indeed any direction whatsoever, one never reaches its end.
For this reason, the quarters are infinite.
The quarters, O Emperor, are indeed the sense of hearing.
Therefore, the infinity of the auditory organ is simply the infinity of space. 4.1.5.
"Whatever anyone has told you, let us hear that.
"Satyakāma Jābāla told me: 'The mind, indeed, is Brahman.'"
"Just as one who has a mother, a father, and a teacher should speak, so did Jābāla say: 'The mind, indeed, is Brahman.
For what could there be for one without a mind? [Nārada] replied, "But he did not tell you its abode and its foundation."
"He did not tell me," [the king said].
"That is but one quarter, O Emperor," replied Yājñavalkya.
"Then do you tell us, Yājñavalkya."
"The mind alone is its abode, space is its foundation, and bliss is its essence; one should worship it thus.
"What is this bliss, Yājñavalkya?
"The mind alone, O Emperor," he said. "For by means of the mind, O Emperor, one desires a woman; from her a son resembling himself is born."
That is bliss.
Mind indeed, O Emperor, is the supreme Brahman;
mind does not desert him.
All beings flow toward him;
having become a god, he goes to the gods—
he who, knowing this, meditates upon it.
"I shall give you a thousand [cows] with a bull as the chief," said Janaka of Videha.
Yājñavalkya replied, "My father believed that one should not accept a gift without having first instructed [the donor]."
Satyakāma by name, the son of Jabālā, is Jābāla.
The deity in the mind is the moon;
its secret teaching (upaniṣad) is "Bliss."
Since the mind itself is bliss, therefore, O Emperor, a man who desires a woman is drawn toward her; that is to say, he makes his request.

Consequently, whatever woman he desires and is drawn toward, a son resembling and conforming to her is born; he is the cause of bliss. That mind by which he brings this about is bliss. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.1.7)
"Whatever anyone has told you, let us hear that. "Vidagdha Śākalya told me:
'The heart, indeed, is Brahman.'"
Just as one who has a mother, a father, and a teacher might speak, so did Śākalya say: "The heart, indeed, is Brahman.
For what could there be for one without a heart? But he [Yājñavalkya] said to him: "Tell me its abode and its support."
"He did not tell me," [the king said]. "He told you only one quarter of it, O Emperor," [Yājñavalkya replied]. "Then do tell us, Yājñavalkya."
"The heart is its abode, space is its foundation.
One should worship it as 'Stability' (sthitih). What is this stability, Yājñavalkya?"
"It is the heart indeed, O Emperor," he said.
"The heart, O Emperor, is the abode of all beings;
the heart, O Emperor, is the foundation of all beings."
For indeed, O Emperor, all beings are established in the heart alone.
The heart, O Emperor, is the supreme Brahman;
it does not abandon him.
All beings flow toward him;
having become a god, he goes to the gods—
he who, knowing this, meditates upon it.
"I shall give you a thousand cows with a bull as large as an elephant," said Janaka, the King of Videha.
Yājñavalkya replied, "My father believed that one should not accept a gift without having first given instruction."
"Śākalya was consumed by fire [for his error]. 'The heart, indeed, is Brahman'—the heart, O King, is the abode of all beings.
For we have stated in the Śākalya-Brāhmaṇa that beings, whose nature consists of name, form, and action, have the heart as their support, and that they are established in the heart."
Therefore, O Emperor, all beings indeed become established for the sake of support;
therefore, one should meditate upon the heart as stability, and Prajāpati is the deity in the heart. 4.1.7.
Thus ends the first Brāhmaṇa of the fourth Adhyāya in the Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya.
Now begins the second Brāhmaṇa of the fourth chapter.
Janaka of Videha, descending from his seat of kūrca grass, said: "Homage be to you, Yājñavalkya!"
"Teach me," he said.
He replied, "Just as a king, O Emperor, when about to set out on a long journey would prepare a chariot or a boat, even so have you prepared yourself with these secret doctrines (upaniṣads).
Being thus a distinguished and wealthy man, having studied the Vedas and been instructed in the secret doctrines, where will you go when you are released from here?"
“I do not know that, O Blessed One, where I shall go,” [Yājñavalkya replied].
“Then indeed I shall tell you that, where you shall go. “Let the Blessed One speak,” [said Maitreyī]. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.2.1.

Janaka of Videha—because Yājñavalkya knew all the Brahman-knowledges along with their specific qualifications—abandoned his role as teacher and, rising from his seat known as the *kūrca*, approached him; that is to say, he prostrated himself at his feet and said: "Salutations to you, O Yājñavalkya! Instruct me; that is to say, teach me."

The word *iti* serves to mark the conclusion of the sentence. Yājñavalkya said: "Just as in the world, O Emperor, one who is about to travel a great and long road would prepare a chariot for traveling by land, or a boat for traveling by water—even so, one whose self is composed, meditating upon these Brahmans joined with these Upanishads, will go to the end by means of these very Upanishads."
Your self is not merely conjoined with these [qualities], but is likewise established in the Upaniṣads; thus you are a *vṛndāraka*—meaning venerable, honored, wealthy, and a lord, not poor.

You have studied the Vedas—that is, the Veda has been studied by you—so you are one who has "studied the Vedas" (*adhītaveda*). Furthermore, the Upaniṣads have been explained to you by your teachers, so you are one for whom the Upaniṣads have been taught (*uktopaniṣatka*). Thus, even though you are endowed with all such prosperity, you remain in the midst of fear due to the lack of knowledge of the Supreme Self.
The meaning is that you are indeed deprived of your purpose for as long as you do not know the Supreme Brahman.
Being liberated from this body and so forth, and being concentrated by these [disciplines] which stand in the place of chariots, where—in what—will you go? What reality will you attain?
“O Blessed One, I do not know that object of worship, nor do I know where I shall go.
Now, if you do not know where one who has accomplished his purpose has gone, then I shall indeed tell you where you will go. “Let the Blessed One speak,” [he said].
If you are well-disposed toward me, listen. (4.2.1)
START Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.2.2:
This person who is here in the right eye is indeed named Indha. Although he is Indha, they call him Indra by an indirect name.
For the gods, as it were, love what is out of sight and hate what is manifest.
"Indha" indeed is his name; "Indha" is thus his name.
He who was previously described as "the Brahman that is the eye," the Person within the sun, is this very one who is specifically situated here in the right eye.
And his name is "Satya" (the True).

Because this person possesses the quality of radiance (*dīpti*), he is directly perceived; thus, his name is "Indha" (the Kindler). Yet, although he is Indha, they call him "Indra" cryptically (*parokṣeṇa*).
For the gods, as it were, prefer the cryptic and dislike the manifest; they loathe the utterance of a manifest name.
Thus, you have indeed become identified with Vaiśvānara, the Self. //4.2.2//
Now, this person-form in the left eye is his wife, Virāj. That which is the space within the heart is the meeting place of these two.
Now, their food is this lump of blood that is within the heart;
their covering is this network-like membrane that is within the heart;
and their path for moving about is this channel that rises upward from the heart.
Just as a hair split a thousandfold, so do these channels called *hitā* (the beneficial) lie established within his heart. Through them, this [subtle essence] flows in;
therefore, he becomes, as it were, one who subsists on even more refined food than this corporeal self.

Now, this person-form in the left eye is his wife. She is the Virāj, the food, who is the object of enjoyment for that Indra—the enjoyer—with whom you have identified yourself as the Vaiśvānara Self. Because she is indeed the object of enjoyment, this food and the eater are a single couple in the state of dream.
Who is this?
It is this space within the heart—that is, within the heart, in the middle of the lump of flesh that is the heart.
Now, for these two, the food to be eaten, which is the cause of their subsistence, will be described as follows.
What is that?
It is this lump of blood within the heart—a mass of blood that has assumed the form of a lump.
Food that is eaten undergoes a twofold transformation: that which is coarse goes downward.
Furthermore, that which remains is cooked by the fire and undergoes a twofold transformation:
the middle essence gradually builds up the body, a mass composed of the five elements, starting from blood;
while the subtlest essence is this very mass of blood within the heart of Indra, who exists as the *liṅga*-ātman in union with his consort.

That which they call the *taijasa* (fiery) has entered into the subtle channels within the hearts of Indra and Indrāṇī when they have become united as a couple, and it serves as the cause of their maintenance.
This very point is expressed in the passage beginning with, "Now, this is their food," and so forth.
Furthermore:
Now, this is their invitation (*pravāraṇa*):
when they have eaten and are about to sleep, there is a covering; for the Śruti ordains that which is common in the world.
What, then, is this covering here?

This which is within the heart is like a net (*jālaka*) because it abounds with many openings in the form of numerous channels (*nāḍī*). Now, this is their *sṛti*—the path; it is called *saṃcaraṇī* because one moves along it (*saṃcarati anayā*), being the path for traveling between the states of sleep and waking. What is that path?
This channel which rises upward from the heart, from the region of the non-heart,
its measurement is stated as follows:
just as a hair in the world, when split a thousandfold, becomes extremely subtle, so too is this [channel] of the body subtle.
The veins called *hitā* (beneficial) are so named because they are indeed beneficial; they are established within the lump of flesh in the heart.
Spreading out from the heart, they extend everywhere like the filaments of a *kadamba* flower. Through these extremely subtle veins, this food flows—that is, it goes and permeates.
Thus, this body of the deity, being nourished by this food which serves as its support, remains stable.
Therefore, since this physical body (*piṇḍa*) is nourished by gross food, whereas this subtle body (*liṅga*), which is the body of the deity, subsists being nourished by subtle food;

and even the food that causes the growth of the physical body is indeed "separated" (*pravivikta*) when compared to the gross [waste] such as urine and feces—the food that sustains the subtle body is subtler than even that.
Hence, the physical body has separated food.

Therefore, even more secluded than that secluded food is this [state]; it becomes like the subtle self (liṅgātman) itself, distinct from this body—by "body" (śārīra) is meant that which belongs to the body—and from that bodily self, the Vaiśvānara, it does not become nourished by the gross Taijasa [self]. //4.2.3//
Of him, the eastern direction is his forward vital breaths;
the southern direction is his southern vital breaths.
The western direction is the western vital breaths;
the northern direction is the northern vital breaths;
the upward direction is the upward vital breaths.
The downward direction is the downward vital breaths;
all directions are all the vital breaths.
This very Self is "not this, not this."
It is ungraspable, for it cannot be grasped; it is indestructible, for it cannot be destroyed; it is unattached, for it is not attached.
"He does not tremble, he is not harmed.
O Janaka, you have indeed attained fearlessness," Yājñavalkya said.
Janaka of Videha said: "Let fearlessness come to you, O Yājñavalkya, since you, O Blessed One, have made us know fearlessness.
Homage be to you!
Here are the Videhas, and here am I."
This very one, having become the heart and being sustained by the subtle vital breath (*prāṇa*), becomes the *taijasa* (the luminous self) itself.

For this knower who has gradually attained the *taijasa* state from the *vaiśvānara*, having reached the heart-self from the *vaiśvānara*, and having further reached the vital-breath-self from the heart-self—the eastern direction constitutes his forward-moving vital breaths; likewise, the southern direction constitutes his southern vital breaths.
All directions are all vital breaths (*prāṇas*).
One who knows this thus has approached the vital breath, which is the self of all, as his own self.
Having withdrawn that universal self into the innermost self, he attains the fourth state (*turīya*), the Self, which is the seer’s true nature beyond "not this, not this" (*neti neti*).
The wise man who proceeds by this sequence—that very Self described as "not this, not this" (neti neti) and so forth, ending with "he does not suffer"—has already been explained.
"Truly, O Janaka, you have attained the fearless," which is devoid of the fear caused by birth, death, and so on—Yājñavalkya spoke thus indeed.
This is what was said: "Now, indeed, I shall tell you that where you will go."

Janaka, the King of Videha, said: "May fearlessness indeed come to you as well, O Yājñavalkya, since you, a venerable and worshipful one, have made known—that is, caused us to know—the fearless Brahman to us, by removing the veil of ignorance created by limiting adjuncts.
What else can I give as the fee for this knowledge, other than my very self, which I have bestowed upon you?

Therefore, let there be salutation to you; these Videhas are yours—let them be enjoyed as you wish—and here I am, standing in the state of a servant; please accept me and the kingdom as you desire. This is the meaning. //4.2.4//
Thus ends the second Brāhmaṇa of the fourth Adhyāya in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.
Now begins the third Brāhmaṇa of the fourth Adhyāya.
Yājñavalkya went to Janaka of Videha, thinking,
"I shall have a discussion with him."
Now, when Janaka of Videha and Yājñavalkya were once engaged in a discussion regarding the Agnihotra sacrifice,
Yājñavalkya granted him a boon. He chose the right to ask any question he desired.
He gave it to him;
and the Emperor alone questioned him first.
The connection of the passage, "Yājñavalkya went to Janaka, the King of Videha," is as follows:
The Self consisting of consciousness is Brahman itself—direct, non-mediated, and the innermost of all;
it is the Supreme alone, according to such scriptural texts as, "There is no other seer but He; there is no other hearer but He."

This very Self, having entered here, exists as characterized by speech and other organs; though it was understood in the Madhu-kāṇḍa during the dialogue with Ajātaśatru through the negation of agency and enjoyership in respect to the vital breaths and so forth, it is nevertheless presented again in the question of Uṣasta by means of the characteristics of breathing and so forth.
That which was understood in general through such passages as "He who breathes with the breath," and "The seer of seeing," is understood as having a nature of unimpaired power.

And its transmigratory existence, caused by external limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), is just as the appearance of a serpent, water, silver, or impurity in a rope, a mirage, a mother-of-pearl shell, or the sky is caused solely by the superimposition of something else and not inherent; likewise, the Self— which is without adjuncts, indefinable, designated as "not this, not this" (*neti neti*), immediate and direct, the innermost of all, Brahman, the Imperishable, the Inner Controller, the person praised in the Upaniṣads, and known as consciousness and bliss— has been understood.

That very [self], designated as the "fuel" (*indhana*), which has subtle food, then dissolves into the "liṅga-self" within the heart, which has even more subtle food; from that, the "world-self" characterized by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is dissolved.

Having thus dissolved even the world-self which serves as the adjunct—just as one removes a snake and such from a rope by means of knowledge—one directly realizes the Brahman that is the innermost of all, defined as "not this, not this" (*neti neti*).
Thus, having been granted freedom from fear by Yājñavalkya, Janaka departed according to the scripture in brief.

In this context, while introducing the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth (*turiya*), it was mentioned incidentally that the fuel consists of more refined food, that all the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are [the self], and "He is 'not this, not this'.
Now, through the gateway of waking and dreaming, a detailed comprehension must be achieved by means of extensive reasoning.
Fearlessness is to be attained;
and the true nature of the Self is to be realized by way of dispelling doubts concerning its contrary misconceptions.

It is for this purpose that the following is commenced: [the realization] that it is distinct [from the body], pure, self-luminous, characterized by an essential nature whose powers are never lost, essentially consisting of unsurpassed bliss, and non-dual.
The narrative (ākhyāyikā), however, is for the purpose of illuminating the method for the transmission and reception of knowledge,
and especially for the praise of knowledge,
as it indicates the granting of boons and so forth.
Yājñavalkya went to Janaka of Videha;
while on his way, he thought to himself: "I shall not say anything at all to the king, for my purpose in going is merely for the sake of *yogakṣema* (well-being and security)."

Even though Yājñavalkya had made the resolve, "I shall not speak," he nevertheless explained each and every point that Janaka asked; what, then, was the reason for this reversal of his resolve? To explain this, the narrative is recounted:

previously, it is said, there was a dialogue between Janaka and Yājñavalkya concerning the Agnihotra sacrifice. Having perceived Janaka’s profound understanding regarding the Agnihotra, Yājñavalkya was highly pleased and, it is said, granted a boon to Janaka.
And that Janaka, the progenitor, chose as his boon precisely the question regarding desire; and Yājñavalkya granted him that boon.
By the power of that granting of the boon, [Janaka] prompted him to speak even though he did not wish to explain.
Although Yājñavalkya remained silent, the Emperor Janaka himself questioned him first.
In that very context, there is no mention of the knowledge of Brahman because it is incompatible with ritual action;
and because knowledge is independent.
For the knowledge of Brahman is independent, requiring no other auxiliary means, and is the instrument for achieving the goal of man. (4.3.1)
"Yājñavalkya," [the King asked], "what is the light of this person?
"The sun is his light, O Emperor," he replied.
"By the light of the sun alone, this person sits, moves about, performs his work, and returns.
"It is just so, Yājñavalkya. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.2.
Having addressed him by saying "O Yājñavalkya" in order to draw his attention, [the question is asked]:
"What is the light of this person?"—that is, what is the light of this person by which he performs his activities?
Thus, this ordinary person—who is a composite of body and organs consisting of a head, hands, and so forth—is being questioned as to what his light is.

Does this person perform the functions of light by means of another light external to the collection of its own parts, or rather does it accomplish the work of light through a light that falls within the collection of its own parts? It is with this intention that he asks. And what follows from this—whether the work of light is accomplished by a light distinct [from the body] or by one that is non-distinct?

Listen to the reason for this: if its nature were determined to be such that it accomplishes the functions of light only by means of a distinct light, then even regarding objects where the function of light is not perceived, we would infer that this effect is indeed caused by a distinct light.

However, if it conducts its activities by means of light that is non-distinct from itself, its own self, then even when the light is imperceptible, upon seeing the effects of light, one must infer a light that is non-distinct [from the object].

Now, if there were simply no fixed rule—that is, if light, whether distinct or non-distinct from the person, were the cause of the person's worldly activity, then there would be no certain determination regarding the nature of light; thinking thus, Janaka asks Yājñavalkya, "What is the light of this person?
One might object: "If Janaka possesses such skill in inference, why does he not understand this for himself? Why does he ask at all?"
This is true;

nevertheless, because the specific relations between the mark (*liṅga*) and the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*) are extremely subtle, they are considered difficult to comprehend for many even among the learned, let alone for a single person.
For this very reason, the deliberation of an assembly (*pariṣad*) is required for the determination of subtle matters of dharma.
Furthermore, a specific qualification of the person is required;
[the assembly] must consist of at least ten, or three, or even one. Therefore, although the king possesses skill in inference, it was nevertheless appropriate for Yājñavalkya to question him.
This is because there arises a gradation in the proficiency of men regarding consciousness.
Alternatively, the Śruti itself, following the human intellect, instructs us by presenting the path of inference under the guise of a narrative.

Yājñavalkya also, being cognizant of Janaka’s intention and wishing to teach that the light of the Self is distinct [from the body], accepted for Janaka only those inferential marks that establish its distinctness, such as the well-known light of the sun.
"An emperor," he said.
"How so?
By means of the sun itself—that light which assists the eye and is distinct from the aggregate of its own parts—this ordinary person [perceives]."

The person sits, he lies down, he moves about, he goes forth to a field or to the forest; having gone there, he performs his work and beholds many external lights—this is for the purpose of demonstrating the non-deviation of the mark (liṅga).
"It is even so, Yājñavalkya. 4.3.2.
"When the sun has set, Yājñavalkya, what light does this person have?
"The moon indeed becomes his light."
"By the light of the moon alone, this person sits, moves about, performs actions, and returns.
"Just so, Yājñavalkya. *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 4.3.3.
"Likewise, Yājñavalkya, when the sun has set, what light does this person have? "The moon alone is his light. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.3)
"When the sun has set, Yājñavalkya, and the moon has set, what light does this person have?
"Fire indeed becomes his light."
"By fire alone as his light he sits, moves about, performs his work, and returns. "Just so it is, Yājñavalkya. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.4.
"When the sun has set and the moon has set, fire is the light. (BrhUpBh_4.3.4)
"Yājñavalkya, when the sun has set, when the moon has set, and the fire has gone out, what light does this person have?
"Speech itself becomes his light," he replied.

"By speech alone as his light, this person sits, moves about, performs action, and returns. Therefore, O King, even in a place where one's own hand is not discerned, wherever speech sounds forth, there he leans toward it.
"Just so, Yājñavalkya," [the King replied]. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.5.
When the fire has been extinguished, speech becomes the light; by the word "speech," the sound is intended.
By means of that object, which is sound, the sense organ of hearing is illuminated.
When the sense of hearing is fully illumined, discernment arises in the mind.
By means of that mind, one engages in external activity;

for the Brāhmaṇa says, "For with the mind alone one sees, with the mind one hears. How is it that light comes before speech? Since the luminosity of speech is not well-known, he says: "Therefore indeed, O Emperor, because a person carries out his worldly affairs (vyavaharati) by means of speech as his light, therefore this luminosity of speech is well-established."
The state of being light (*jyotiṣṭva*).
How so? At whatever time, during the rainy season, when there is generally darkness from clouds and all other lights have set, even one's own hand is not clearly discerned by a living being.
Then, at that time, when all physical activity has ceased due to the absence of external light, it is there that the breath (*śvas*) utters speech.

Or it barks, or the donkey brays; he approaches that very place by means of that sound. Through that light, there is a continuous connection between the ear and the mind; through that, speech attains the state of being an effect of light. By means of that speech and that light, he "approaches"—that is, he goes near and becomes present there.
This is the meaning.
And therein one performs and experiences karma.
There, the mention of "light" (*vāgyotiḥ*) is for the purpose of indicating [the other objects] such as odor and so forth;
for when the nose and other [senses] are assisted by odor and the rest, activity, cessation, and so forth occur.
By that, there is also assistance provided by them to the aggregate of the body and its organs.
"It is even so, Yājñavalkya. 4.3.5.
"Yājñavalkya, when the sun has set, when the moon has set, when the fire has gone out, and when speech has been stilled, what light does this person have? "The self alone becomes his light."
"By his own light alone, he sits, moves about, performs actions, and returns. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.6)

When speech has become quieted, and when the external supporting factors— smell and the others as well— have also become quieted, it follows that all activity of this person has ceased. This is what is meant.

When, in the waking state, the external organs such as the eyes and others, being assisted by external lights such as the sun, function, then the empirical activity of this person is clearly perceived.

Therefore, we consider that even when all external lights have set— during the states of dreaming and deep sleep, as well as in the waking state under similar conditions— the accomplishment of the functions of light for this person occurs through a light distinct from the mere aggregate of his own limbs.
Furthermore, the accomplishment of the functions of light is observed in dreams, as well as the seeing of meeting or parting from kinsmen, traveling to other regions, and so forth;
likewise, there is the awakening from deep sleep with the recollection: "I slept happily; I was not aware of anything.
Therefore, there exists some distinct light.
What, then, becomes the light for this person when speech has become quiet?
It is said: "The Self alone becomes his light.

By "Self" is meant that which is distinct from the aggregate of the body, the organs, and its own constituent parts; it is the illuminator of the body and the organs, like the external lights such as the sun, yet unlike them, it is not itself illuminated by anything else—an internal light.
And by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*),
it is established that this [light] is distinct from the body and the instruments of action.

Furthermore, that light which is distinct from the body and the instruments of action, which sustains the aggregate of the body and the instruments, and which is perceived by the external instruments such as the eyes— [is the Self].
It is not seen in that way by the eyes and other senses when the lights such as the sun have ceased;
however, the effect of light is observed. Therefore, it is understood that "he sits, moves about, performs action, and returns, by means of this very light of the Self.
Consequently, it is certain that there is a light situated within.

Furthermore, it is argued that because that light is distinct from the light of the sun and so forth and is non-material (abhautika), it is for that very reason ungraspable by the eyes and other senses—just like the light of the sun and so on. This is not so;
for [the relationship] is with that which belongs to the same class.
It is observed that the benefit of the aggregate of body and organs, which is material, is performed by the light of the sun and so forth, which is itself material.
This is to be inferred according to its specific nature:

even if it were indeed distinct from the body and organs, that which assists them—such as light from the sun and so forth—is to be inferred as belonging to the same genus as the aggregate of the body and organs, because it assists the aggregate of the body and organs, like the light of the sun and so forth.
As for the claim that there is a difference [between the self and light] due to its being internal and imperceptible, that is inconclusive with respect to the lights of the eyes and other senses.

Since the lights such as the eye, which reside within and are not perceived [externally], are indeed material, therefore your claim that the light of the Self is established as something distinct is merely a product of imagination. Furthermore, because the light exists only when the aggregate of the body and its organs exists, it is inferred to possess the properties of that aggregate; and since inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*) is fallible, it lacks authority.
For by the force of general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*), you seek to establish a light distinct from the body and its organs, like that of the sun;
yet perception cannot be sublated by inference.
This very aggregate of the body and its organs is what perceives, hears, thinks, and cognizes through direct experience.
If indeed another light were to assist this [self], as the sun and so forth do, then that other light would be the self, just like the sun and so forth.
However, that which directly performs the act of seeing must itself be the self; it is the aggregate of the body and the instruments [of perception], and nothing else.
For when there is a contradiction with direct perception, inference lacks authority.

If this very aggregate (saṃghāta) is the self that performs the acts of seeing and so forth, why is it that this agency in seeing and other functions occurs for it only at certain times and not at others, even though it remains entirely unimpaired?
This is not a fault, because it is observed;
for indeed, there is nothing that is impossible when it is actually perceived.
Indeed, when a firefly is seen as both luminous and non-luminous, no other cause can be inferred.
And if it were inferable, then by virtue of some commonality with one thing, everything would be inferable everywhere;
and that is undesirable.

Nor is it the case that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of things does not exist; for the heat of fire or the coldness of water do not have other causes. If it is argued [that these depend on] living beings, merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), and so forth, then it would follow that merit, demerit, and the rest must themselves possess an intrinsic nature that depends on further causes.
If it is argued that "let it be so," then there would be the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), and that is undesirable. No;
for in dreams and recollections, one perceives only what has already been seen.
As for what was stated by the proponent of intrinsic nature— that the acts of seeing and so forth belong to the body alone and not to something distinct—
that is not so;
for if the acts of seeing and so forth belonged to the body alone, there would be no perception of that which is seen in a dream.
A blind man, seeing a dream, sees only that which has been seen before, not an unseen form such as those belonging to Śākadvīpa and other lands.
From this, it is established that he who sees a previously seen object in a dream is the very same one who previously saw it while the eye was intact, and not the body.
If the body were the seer, then once that eye by which he saw had been removed, he would not see that same previously seen object in a dream.

Furthermore, there is a well-known worldly convention among those whose eyes have been plucked out—that is, among the blind—such as: "I saw the peak of the Himalayas before; today I saw it in a dream.

Therefore, even when the eyes are not extracted, it is understood that the one who sees in a dream is the very same seer, and not the body. Likewise, since the seer and the rememberer are one in memory, the seer is indeed the rememberer. And when this is so, even with eyes closed, one sees a form previously seen in a dream just as if it were being seen [directly].

Therefore, that which is closed is not the seer; since one perceives the form of what was remembered when the eyes were closed, it is understood that it was the very same [seer] that existed as the seer even when the eyes were open. Furthermore, because there is an absence of the perception of forms and so forth for one who is intact [but dead], if the deity alone were the seer, acts such as seeing would continue even after death.
Therefore, since perception does not occur when the body has departed and occurs when it is present, it is understood that the agent of such actions as seeing is not the deity (the soul).

If it is argued that the eyes and other sense organs themselves are the agents of the actions of seeing and so forth, we say no; for if there were different agents, the synthesis expressed in "I who saw that, I now touch" would be impossible.
If it is argued that the mind [is the seer], no;
because the mind also is an object, like color-form and so forth, its status as a seer and so on is untenable.
Therefore, it is established that [the seer] resides within and is distinct [from the senses], like the sun and other such luminaries.
As for what was stated— that another light, belonging to the same genus as the aggregate of the body and its instruments,
must be inferred because it is assisted by lights such as the sun which belong to that same genus—
that is incorrect.
Since the relationship between benefactor and beneficiary is observed to lack any fixed rule,
how is it that fire is seen to receive assistance for its blazing from fuels such as grass and *ulapa*— which are of the same class (*samānajātīya*) as earthen things?
Yet, one cannot infer on that basis alone that the assistance for the blazing of fire must everywhere be provided by things belonging exclusively to that same class.
For it is observed that even by water, which is of a different class (*bhinnajātīya*), assistance toward combustion is rendered to both lightning-fire and digestive fire;
therefore, in the relationship between the beneficiary and the benefactor, there is no rule that they must be of the same class or of different classes.
Sometimes people of the same class are assisted by people of the same class, and sometimes by those of different classes, such as stationary objects, animals, and so forth.
Therefore, the argument that [the internal light] is not a cause because it is assisted by lights such as the sun, which belong to the same class as the aggregate of the body and its organs,

is refuted. Furthermore, as for your claim that the reason— "because it is invisible like the light of the sun and so forth, as seen in the case of the eyes"— does not establish the existence of another light within nor its distinctness from the organs, due to being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to the eyes and other organs— that is incorrect.
Since the qualification of the reason— "given that it is distinct from the instruments such as the eye"—
is logically established, the claim that light possesses the nature of being a property of the aggregate of effects and instruments is incorrect;
for it contradicts inference.

For it has been stated that light is an entity distinct from the aggregate of the body and the instruments of action, like the sun and other luminaries; thus, this proposition—that light is a property of the aggregate of the body and the instruments—is contradicted by that inference.
Furthermore, the fact that [the state of being conscious] exists only when that [aggregate] exists is unproven, because light is not perceived in a dead body.
If inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato-dṛṣṭam anumānam*) were invalid, it would follow that all worldly activities such as drinking and eating would be abolished;
and that is undesirable.

For in the world, having perceived that drinking and eating result in the cessation of hunger and thirst, one does not observe the undertaking of drinking and eating on the basis of that generality [if such inference were invalid].

For it is observed that people who have already experienced food and drink infer, by means of general correlation, the cessation of hunger and thirst through other instances of food and drink, and proceed toward them for that purpose.

As for the claim that "this very body is the agent of actions such as seeing," that was refuted at the very outset by the argument that the seer is an entity distinct from the body, as evidenced by dreams and memory.
By this same reasoning, the selfhood of any light other than the Self is also rejected.
Furthermore, as for the occasional appearance and non-appearance of light in fireflies and the like,

this is possible because their appearance and non-appearance are caused by the contraction and expansion of their parts, such as their wings. As for what was stated— that the nature of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) must necessarily be accepted as being the bestower of results— [that too is untenable].
Because, if that were accepted, it would result in the abandonment of your own established doctrine (siddhānta).
By this, the fault of infinite regress (anavasthā) is also refuted.
Therefore, there exists a distinct, internal light which is the Self (ātman). //4.3.6//
"Which is the Self?"—"It is this person consisting of consciousness among the vital breaths, the light within the heart.
Being the same [in both states], he moves through both worlds; he meditates, as it were, and he stirs, as it were."
For having become a dream, he transcends this world and the forms of death.

Although its distinctness and so forth are established, nevertheless, due to the delusion caused by observing that [the organs] are assisted by those of the same class, one asks— "Which one?"— out of a lack of discrimination, thinking that it might be one of the very organs or something distinct from them. Such a delusion is possible because the subtlety of logical reasoning is difficult to discern.

Alternatively, even though it has been established that [the self] is distinct from the body, because all the instruments (karaṇa) appear as if they possess consciousness due to the non-perception of the self through discrimination, I therefore ask: "Which one is the self?
Which among the body, senses, vital breaths, and mind is that self which was mentioned by you?

It has been said, "By which light he sets. Alternatively, this Self intended by you, consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), is like all these vital breaths (*prāṇa*) consisting of consciousness; among these vital breaths, which one is it?

Just as when Brahmins have assembled [one might ask], "All of these are brilliant; which among them is a knower of the six Vedāṅgas?", so too, in the previous explanation, the interrogative statement was only "Which is the Self? up to the point of "the person consisting of consciousness, the light within the heart.
For the word "consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*), the entire interrogative statement extends up to "the person consisting of consciousness, the light within the heart; which is he?"

Since it is logical that the phrase "this which consists of consciousness" (*yo 'yaṃ vijñānamayaḥ*) refers to a specific determined object, and that the word "which" (*katamaḥ*) in the question "Which is the Self? (*katama ātmā*) serves to complete the interrogative sentence, it is concluded—without any intervening connection—that the entire passage from "Which is the Self? up to the end of the question constitutes the inquiry, while everything following "this which... is the answer.
The designation "this which" is used because the self is directly perceived.

"Consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*) means predominantly consciousness; it is called "consisting of consciousness" because of the failure to distinguish [the self] from the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the intellect and consciousness.
For it is perceived only in conjunction with the intellect and consciousness, just as Rāhu is perceived when in conjunction with the moon and the sun.
For the intellect (*buddhi*) is the instrument for accomplishing all purposes, like a lamp placed before one in the darkness.
Indeed, it has been said: "With the mind alone one sees; with the mind one hears.

For the entire range of objects is perceived only when distinguished by the light of intellectual consciousness (*vijñāna*), just as things in the dark are perceived when distinguished by the light of a lamp placed before one.
But the other organs are merely gateways for the intellect (buddhi).
Therefore, the term is qualified by that very [intellect] as "consisting of consciousness" (vijñānamaya).

For those who explain it as a modification of the consciousness of the Supreme Self (paramātman), the non-scriptural nature of the word "consisting of consciousness" is established, because in passages such as "consisting of consciousness, consisting of mind" (vijñānamayo manomayaḥ), the word "consisting of consciousness" is seen to have a different meaning.
Furthermore, a word whose meaning is doubtful can be determined either by observing its usage elsewhere with a certain application, or from the remainder of the sentence (vākyaśeṣa),
or by the force of a settled logical principle;
for it is read later on as "sadhīḥ."
Because of the statement "within the heart," it is appropriate that [the self] consists primarily of consciousness.
The locative case in the word "prāṇeṣu" (in the vital breaths) is used to demonstrate distinction, characterized by proximity— just as in the expression "a stone among trees"—
for the question of whether the self is distinct from or non-distinct from the vital breaths is indeed a matter of doubt.
The meaning is that [the Self] is distinct from the vital breaths;
for whatever exists within certain things is necessarily distinct from them,
just as a tree is distinct from stones.
In that case, [if it were] in the heart, there would be a cognition of the nature of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) regarding the vital breaths; therefore, he says: "within the heart" (*hṛdyantaḥ*).
By the word "heart," the lotus-shaped lump of flesh is meant, because the intellect (*buddhi*) resides there; thus, "in the heart" means in the intellect.
The word "within" (*antar*) is for the purpose of demonstrating its distinction from the modifications (*vṛtti*) of the intellect.

The Self is called "light" because its nature is luminosity. For by means of that luminous Self, one sits, moves about, and performs actions; for this aggregate of causes and effects (the body) is like a pot placed in the light of the sun, or like an emerald or other gem cast into milk and other substances for examination, which [reflects] only its own shadow.

Just as milk and other substances produce their own effects, so too does the light of the Self (ātma-jyotis), though it is situated within the heart and is subtler than the heart itself, produce its own shadow by unifying the heart and the aggregate of the body and the organs;
this is because, through a gradual progression of subtlety and grossness, it is the innermost of all.
First, because of its transparency and its proximity, the intellect (*buddhi*) becomes a reflection of the light of the self's consciousness.
For that reason, among those who possess discrimination, the notion of "I" (the conceit of self) arises first with respect to that intellect.
Furthermore, due to its immediate proximity to that, the mind (*manas*) possesses the appearance of consciousness through its contact with the intellect.
Then [it enters] the sense-faculties through the conjunction with the mind;
immediately after that, it enters the body.
Through contact with the sense organs,
the Self, by means of its light which is the very nature of consciousness, illumines the entire aggregate of causes and effects through a continuous succession.

For it is because of this that the unstable notion of self-identification arises in all people regarding the aggregate of causes and effects and their functions, according to their lack of discrimination.
And so it was said by the Blessed One in the Gītā: “Just as the one sun illumines this entire world, so the Knower of the Field illumines the entire field, O Bhārata.”

And there are such passages as: “The splendor that resides in the sun,” and so forth; and in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad: “He is the eternal among the non-eternal, the consciousness among conscious beings”; and: “Everything shines only after Him who shines; by His light all this is illumined”; and the mantra-text: “By whose splendor the sun burns above.”

Therefore, this person (*puruṣa*) is the light within the heart; he is called "person" because, like space, he is all-pervading and full. Furthermore, his self-luminosity is unsurpassed, because he illuminates everything while being himself unilluminated by anything else.
This very person, whose nature is self-luminous, is the one about whom you ask: "Which is the Self?"

It has been stated that when external lights— which assist all the instruments— have set, the inner light within the heart, the Puruṣa who is the Self, assists the instruments by means of the internal organ.

Even when external lights such as the sun, which assist the external instruments, are present, since those lights like the sun exist for the sake of another, and since the aggregate of body and instruments is insentient and thus cannot have its own purpose realized without the assistance of the Self who is the light for its own sake, this aggregate of body and instruments does not [function] in the absence of that assistance.
It serves for worldly transaction;
for indeed, all worldly activity at all times proceeds solely through the favor of the light of the Self,
as is known from another scriptural passage beginning with, "That which is this heart and mind, consciousness and perception."
For all the worldly transactions of living beings are indeed based on self-conceit (*abhimāna*). We have already explained the cause of this self-conceit by means of the illustration of the emerald.

Even though this is so, nevertheless, regarding the waking state, because the light of the Self (*ātmajyotis*) is not within the range of any of the senses, and because it is agitated by the convergence of the activities of the internal and external organs such as the intellect (*buddhi*), [the Self is not perceived].
It is possible to extract and demonstrate that light called the Self, like the stalk from the *muñja* grass; therefore, desiring to demonstrate it through the state of dream, the text begins:
"Being the same, he moves between both worlds.
That person who is himself the light of the Self, being "the same"—that is, similar—[moves].
By what?
By the heart, because it is the subject under discussion and is proximate.
And as for the word "in the heart" (*hṛdi*), the intellect, which is denoted by the word *hṛt*, is both the subject under discussion and proximate.
Therefore, there is non-difference precisely because of that.

What, then, is this non-difference? It is the non-perception of a distinction, as in the case of a horse and a buffalo. The intellect is the object to be illumined (*avabhāsya*), while its own light, which is the illuminator (*avabhāsaka*), is like a lamp.
The non-perception of a distinction between the object to be illumined and the illuminator is well known.
Because of its purity, the light of meditative concentration becomes similar to that which is illuminated.
Just as when illuminating something red, it becomes similar to the red and takes on a red form;
likewise, when illuminating something green, blue, or red, the light becomes identical to those colors.
Thus, it has been stated by means of the illustration of the emerald gem that, while illuminating the intellect, [the Self] illuminates the entire field through the medium of the intellect.
Therefore, it is "identical with all" (sarveṇa samānaḥ) by way of the commonality of the intellect;
and for this very reason, He will later say, "consisting of all" (sarvamaya).
Therefore, because it cannot be shown in its own form as light—being like the stalk of a *muñja* reed extracted from its sheath—it is impossible to demonstrate it directly.

Consequently, the entire world becomes utterly bewildered regarding this self-light, superimposing upon it all activity belonging to name and form, as well as the attributes of light pertaining to name and form; thus, people are deluded, thinking: "Is this Self this, or not this? Is it of such qualities, or not of such qualities? Is it an agent, or a non-agent? Is it pure, or impure?"
Through conceptual constructions such as "bound," "liberated," "stationary," "gone," "come," "existent," or "non-existent," it is therefore equal [to all].

Thus, it migrates sequentially through hundreds of conjunctions of series consisting of the abandonment of one aggregate of the body, senses, and so forth, and the taking up of another, traversing both worlds— that which has been reached and that which is to be reached— namely, this world and the next world.
The similarity of the intellect (*dhī*) alone is the cause for wandering between the two worlds, and not [the self] by itself.
In this regard, it is stated that the similarity caused by the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of name and form (*nāmarūpa*), which is the basis of delusion, is the cause, and not [the self] by itself.
Because, being "common" (*samāna*), it wanders through both worlds in succession, he demonstrates that this is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*). For...

It appears as if meditating, as if performing the activity of meditation, as if thinking; for, by illuminating the intellect—which possesses the activity of meditation—with its own inherent light in the form of consciousness situated within it, it becomes similar to and identical with that intellect.
Thus, just like light, it seems to meditate, and from this arises the delusion of people that "it is thinking."
But in the ultimate sense, it does not meditate;
likewise, it "seems to move," as if it were moving excessively.
Since those very instruments—the intellect and so forth—and the vital airs are moving, it "seems to move" because it is their illuminator and thus appears similar to them.
But that light of the Self does not, in the ultimate sense, possess the nature of motion.

How, then, is this understood? To demonstrate the meaning that the wandering through both worlds and so forth is caused by the very delusion of similarity [to the waking state], the reason is taught: "For that Self, having become a dream... [sa ātmā hi yasmāt svapno bhūtvā].

By whatever cognition it is identical, that cognition becomes whatever it may be, and thus this [Self] appears as if it were that very thing. Therefore, when this intellect enters the state of sleep—that is, when the intellect attains the function of sleeping—then it also attains the state of sleep. When the intellect awakens, then this [Self] also [awakens]; hence he says: "Having become a dream, manifesting the function of sleep of the intellect..."

Having assumed the form of the mental modification of sleep, it transcends—meaning it passes beyond—this world characterized by waking activity, which consists of an aggregate of causes and effects and serves as the locus for worldly and scriptural transactions; having transcended it, it remains illuminating the mental modification consisting of dream by means of its own distinct self-luminosity. Therefore, this [Self] is indeed of the nature of self-luminosity.
That [Self] is pure, devoid of agent, action, instrument, and fruit.

From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), it is merely the similarity of consciousness that serves as the cause for the delusion of worldly conventions, such as the transition between the two worlds. Death consists of forms; death is karma, ignorance, and so forth—it has no other form than these. By its very nature, its forms are nothing other than the body and the senses.
Therefore, one transcends those forms of death which are the substrata of the fruits of action.

But is it not the case that there is no other light of the Self (*ātmajyotis*) that illuminates the intellect (*dhī*) as its equal, since such a light is not perceived either through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) or through inference (*anumāna*), just as one cannot perceive a second intellect existing at that very same time?

As for the claim that there is similarity between the illuminated object and the illuminator because their distinction is not perceived—such as in the case of a jar and light—that may well be so; for in that case, since light is perceived as distinct from the jar, there is a similarity between two things that are joined together despite being different. But it is not so here, for there is no other light that illuminates cognition in the manner that [light illuminates] a jar or similar objects.
We perceive [the light] either through direct perception or through inference.
For it is cognition itself that, as the illuminator of the nature of consciousness, possesses both its own form and the form of the object.
Therefore, neither by means of inference nor by means of direct perception can a light distinct from cognition be established as its illuminator.

As for the illustration you have stated—that there is a similarity between the object of illumination and the illuminator, such as a jar and light, which are distinct yet conjoined—we have merely stated this as a concession; in reality, the jar and so forth are not distinct from their illumination.
In the ultimate sense, the jar and so forth are themselves of the nature of illumination, together with the light.
For indeed, jars and other such things arise from one another;
it is consciousness alone that appears in the form of objects such as jars accompanied by light.
When this is so, there is no external example [to prove the existence of external objects], because everything is merely characterized by consciousness.
Having falsely imagined that very consciousness to possess the impurity of the forms of grasped object and grasping subject, some further imagine it to be pure;
they maintain that consciousness, being liberated from those graspers, remains as a momentary, translucent entity.
Others, however, desire its cessation.

Furthermore, other Mādhyamikas declare that even that consciousness—which is concealed and devoid of the portions of grasped object and grasping subject—is merely empty, like external objects such as jars.

All these conceptualizations are opposed to the path of ultimate good belonging to the Vedic tradition, because they deny the self-luminous light (*ātma-jyotis*) which is distinct from the manifestations of the Buddha’s consciousness.
Regarding this, we shall first address those for whom an external object exists.
A jar or similar object does not possess the quality of illuminating itself.
A jar situated in darkness is never observed to be illuminated by its own self;
rather, it is invariably seen to be illuminated through contact with the light of a lamp or other source, as in the perception, "the jar is illuminated."

Furthermore, even in the case of a jar and light which are in contact, there is indeed a difference between them, because a distinction is observed whenever they are joined or separated, just as in the case of a rope and a jar.
And if there is difference, there must be an illuminator distinct [from the object]; for a thing does not illuminate itself by its own self.
[Objection: But it is observed that a lamp illuminates its own self.
For ordinary people do not employ another light to see a lamp, as they would for a jar or similar object;
therefore, the lamp illuminates itself. No, because there is no difference in its being something to be illuminated.

Although a lamp illuminates other things because it is itself luminous, even so, it does not deviate from being illuminated by a consciousness distinct from itself, just like a jar or similar objects.
And when this is the case, its state of being illuminated by something distinct is necessarily established.
[Objection: But just as a jar, while being illuminated by consciousness, illuminates both itself and the jar; [Reply: No.
Because there is no distinction whether [the illumination] comes from itself or from another;
for just as a jar is illuminated by consciousness, so too the lamp’s being illuminated by consciousness is no different.
As for the claim that a lamp illuminates both itself and the jar, that is incorrect.
Why?
When it does not illuminate itself, what would it be like?
For at that time, no distinction whatsoever is perceived in the lamp, whether from its own side or from another.

For that alone is an object of illumination for which there is a distinction between its state when the illuminator is present and when it is absent; yet, the claim that "the lamp illuminates itself" is utterly false.
Furthermore, the fact that a lamp is perceivable by consciousness is no different from the case of jars and other objects.
Therefore, if consciousness were to grasp the self, the lamp cannot serve as an illustrative example.
Furthermore, the fact that consciousness is apprehended by sentience is no different from external objects.
Since consciousness is apprehended by sentience, when there is doubt as to whether it is apprehended by the apprehended-consciousness itself or by the apprehending-consciousness,
it is proper to postulate the principle observed elsewhere regarding such a doubtful matter, and not something contrary to what has been observed.
And this being the case, just as it is observed that external lamps are objects of apprehension by a distinct apprehender,

so too, since consciousness is an object of apprehension for sentience (caitanya), it is logical to postulate— despite its own luminosity— that it is apprehended by a distinct sentience like a lamp, rather than being apprehended by nothing other than itself.
If it is argued that the self, which is the apprehender of consciousness, must be a light distinct from consciousness, and thus there would be an infinite regress—
no; for, according to reason, the mere fact of being an object of apprehension is stated as the logical mark (*liṅga*) for the existence of a distinct entity as its apprehender.
However, no sign (liṅga) ever exists for its being exclusively a grasper, nor for the existence of another grasper of that [grasper].
Therefore, there is no consequence of an infinite regress (anavasthā).
If it is argued that if consciousness were to have a graspable object distinct from itself, there would be an infinite regress due to the requirement of another instrument (karaṇa), we say: no.
Because there is no such rule;
for this rule does not apply everywhere.

It cannot be established as an absolute certainty that wherever one thing is perceived by means of another thing, there must necessarily be another instrument distinct from the object and the subject.
Because of the observation of diversity.

How so? First, a jar is perceived by means of a self that is distinct from its own self; furthermore, light such as a lamp is an instrument distinct from both the object to be grasped and the grasper.
For the light of a lamp and so forth is not a part of the jar, nor is it a part of the eye.
Even though the lamp is perceptible by the eye just like the jar, the eye does not require any other instrument—standing in the place of light—distinct from the lamp itself.
Therefore, it cannot be established as a rule that wherever there is the state of being perceived by a distinct perceiver, there must necessarily be another instrument.

Therefore, if consciousness were to be grasped by a grasper distinct from itself, an infinite regress could never be established either through the door of the instrument (karaṇa) nor through the door of the grasper (grāhaka).
Consequently, it is proven that there exists a distinct inner light of the self (ātmajyotis) separate from consciousness.
[Objection: But surely there is no external object—such as a jar or a lamp—that is distinct from consciousness.
For whatever is not perceived apart from something else is seen to be merely that [thing].

Just as objects such as jars and cloths apprehended in a dream-consciousness are understood to be nothing but dream-consciousness itself— because they are not perceived apart from the dream-consciousness, just like the jar or lamp in the dream— so too, in the waking state, everything such as jars and lamps is indeed nothing but waking-consciousness alone.

In this regard, that which was stated—that because consciousness appears as something distinct, there exists another light separate from consciousness, just as in the case of a jar and so forth—is false;
for if everything were merely consciousness, there would be no example [to support such a claim]. This is not so, because we accept [the existence of objects] to whatever extent they appear.
But you do not, as an absolute certainty, deny the existence of an external object.
[Objection: "I certainly do not deny it. [Reply: No;

for since there is a distinction between words and their referents—as in the cases of "consciousness," "jar," and "lamp"—one must necessarily admit that there exists an external object distinct from them, at least to the extent that such distinctions are observed.
If an entity distinct from consciousness is not admitted, then since words such as "consciousness," "pot," and "cloth" would have the same referent, they would necessarily become synonyms.

Likewise, if there were identity between the means and the result, it would follow that the treatises which teach the distinction between the goal to be achieved and the means of achievement are useless;
or else, it would imply that their author lacks knowledge.
Furthermore:
because the proponent, the opponent, the argument, and the faults [of the argument] are admitted to exist apart from consciousness (*vijñāna*).
For it is not the case that the self, consciousness alone, or the argument of the proponent and opponent, or its faults, are admitted [to exist], since the opponent and so forth must be refuted.
For it is not accepted that one's own consciousness is to be denied, nor that the self of anyone is [denied] by itself;
and if that were so, there would follow the consequence of the collapse of all worldly transactional activity.
Furthermore, it is not accepted that the proponent and others are apprehended by their own selves alone.
For those [objects] are accepted as being apprehended as distinct [from consciousness].

Therefore, like that, every object apprehended as distinct is [unreal], because it is an object of the waking state, just like the objects presented in the waking state; thus the example is both valid and beneficial.
This is also like [the objects of] another continuum and like [the objects of] another cognition.

Therefore, even by the Vijñānavādin, it is not possible to deny the existence of another light distinct from consciousness. If it is argued that this is incorrect because there is no absence of consciousness in a dream, we say no; for even from the non-existence [of something], the status of being a distinct entity is established.
Whether the object, such as a jar, be non-existence or existence, in either case you yourself have already admitted that the cognition of the jar and so forth is of the nature of existence;
it cannot be set aside because there is no logical principle to overturn it.
By this, the emptiness of everything is refuted.
The Mīmāṃsaka position—that the inner self (pratyagātmā) is ungraspable as "I" with respect to the self—has been refuted.
As for the claim that a jar with light and a jar without light are distinct entities that arise separately, that is incorrect;
for even at another moment, there is recognition (pratyabhijñāna) that "this is that very same jar."
If it is argued that recognition occurs due to similarity, as in the case of hair and nails that have been cut and grown back, we say no; for even in those cases, momentariness is not established,
and because the genus remains one and the same.
Furthermore, regarding hair, nails, and so forth that have grown back after being cut,

the cognition of them as "hair" or "nails"— which arises from their generic nature (*jāti*) and is caused by that— is non-erroneous. For, in the case of visible hair, nails, and so forth that have been cut and regrown, there does not arise a cognition [of them] as being that very same individual instance (*vyakti*).
In the case of someone who perceives objects separated by a long period of time, there arises the cognition "this is that very same thing.
Therefore, the example is not analogous.

For when an object is recognized through direct perception (pratyakṣa) as being "that very same thing," it is not logical to infer its difference; since the inferential mark (liṅga) would be fallacious in the face of contradiction by direct perception.

Furthermore, the cognition of similarity is untenable because cognition is momentary. For the cognition of similarity could only arise when one person who has seen a first object subsequently sees another object.
