However, one who perceives an object does not remain for another moment in order to perceive another object,
because consciousness is momentary and its function is exhausted by the single act of perceiving an object.
For it is through the cognition "this is similar to that" that the notion of similarity arises.
"By that" refers to the recollection of what was seen; "this" is the cognition of the present.

If, having recollected what was seen by "that," one were to persist until the moment of the present as "this," then the doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavāda*) would be abandoned. Alternatively, if the recollective cognition "by that" has already ceased, and the other, distinct, present cognition "this" also ceases, then the cognition of similarity—"this is similar to that"—would be impossible.

Because there is no single entity that perceives multiple [objects], designation is untenable; furthermore, since consciousness is exhausted by the very act of seeing the object to be seen, designations such as "I see this" or "I saw that" are untenable, because for one who has seen, the moment of designation does not persist. If it were to persist, the doctrine of momentariness would be abandoned.

Furthermore, if there were a designation and a cognition of similarity for one who has not seen [the object], then— just like the designation of specific colors and the cognition of their similarity by one blind from birth— all such things, including the composition of the treatises of the Omniscient One, would result in being nothing but a "blind tradition" (*andhaparamparā*). And this is not accepted.

However, the faults of "the acquisition of what was not done" (*akṛtābhyāgama*) and "the loss of what was done" (*kṛtavipraṇāśa*) are even more established in the doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇavāda*).

If it is argued that the cause for the designation of perception is that a single cognition arises—linked like a chain—consisting of both the preceding and succeeding moments, such that one thinks, "this is similar to that," [we reply:
no.

Because the present and the past exist at different times, the cognition of the present is one link of the chain and the past is another; these two cognitions belong to different times. If the cognition of the chain were to touch upon the objects of both those cognitions, then a single consciousness would not pervade two moments. Therefore, [the chain-cognition] is not established as a single entity.
Furthermore, there would be the loss of the doctrine of momentariness;
and because distinctions such as "mine" and so forth would be untenable, there would follow the consequence of the collapse of all conventional discourse.

Moreover, if everything were merely self-cognizing consciousness, and since consciousness is admitted to have a nature consisting solely of the appearance of pure awareness, then in the absence of any other perceiver of that [consciousness], the manifold conceptualizations of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and so on, would be impossible.
Furthermore, consciousness does not possess multiple contradictory aspects like a pomegranate and the like,
because consciousness has the nature of appearing with clarity.
Moreover, if impermanence, suffering, and so forth were aspects of consciousness, then because they would be objects of experience, it would follow that they are distinct from consciousness itself.

Now, if consciousness itself were identical with that which is impermanent, suffering, and so forth, then the conception of its purification through separation from those [qualities] would be untenable;
for purification occurs through the removal of an adhering impurity,
as in the case of mirrors and the like.

In the case of redness and other qualities, their separation from a substance through an association with another substance is not observed; even there, a prior conjunction is inferred because the production of different qualities in flowers, fruits, and so forth is seen to result from the cultivation of seeds.
Therefore, the postulation of the purification of consciousness is untenable.
Therefore, the purification of consciousness is untenable.
Furthermore, that which is imagined as a stain of consciousness—the appearance as object and subject—is also untenable because of the absence of contact with anything else;
for there can be no contact between that which exists and that which does not exist.
Furthermore, when there is no contact with anything else, a property that is observed in something must, by virtue of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), never be separated from it—

just as heat belongs to fire or radiance to the sun. Therefore, the notion that consciousness becomes defiled through association with impermanent things and is subsequently purified is understood to be merely a succession of blind men, devoid of any valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, regarding their conception of the extinction (*nirvāṇa*) of that consciousness as the goal of man (*puruṣārtha*), even there the impossibility of a basis for the fruit [of action] arises.

For when one is pierced by a thorn, the cessation of the pain produced by the piercing is the fruit; however, if the person pierced by the thorn were to die, a basis for that fruit—the cessation of pain—is not possible.
Likewise, since all things have ceased in *nirvāṇa* and there is no basis for the fruit, the conception of a goal of man is entirely futile.

For one who postulates that the object [of activity] belongs to that being called "person" (puruṣa)—whether it be the self (ātman), consciousness (vijñāna), or [something else]—then upon the liberation (nirvāṇa) of that person, for whom would there be an "object of the person" (puruṣārtha)?

However, for one who maintains that there exists a self distinct from consciousness which perceives manifold objects, everything is logically consistent: the seeing of what was seen, the recollection [of the past], the conjunction with and separation from suffering, and so forth; likewise, defilement is caused by conjunction with another, and purification is caused by separation from that.
However, since the position of the proponent of emptiness (śūnyavādin) is contradicted by all means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), no special effort is made here to refute it. //4.3.7//
Now, this person, when being born— that is, when entering a body— is joined with evils;
when departing— that is, when dying— he leaves the evils behind.

Just as here in this one body, having become a dreamer, he transcends the forms of death—the organs and their functions—and shines forth in his own self within the dream state, even so that very person under discussion, while being "unborn," [is said to be] "being born.
How is he said to be "being born"? It means: attaining the body, which is the aggregate of the physical frame and the senses; that is to say, assuming the state of selfhood within the body.
"By evils" means by the effects and instruments which are the substrata of merit and demerit and are associated with evil;
he is "joined," that is, conjoined with them. The word "departing" (utkrāman) is an explanation of "dying," meaning departing upward toward another body.

By repeatedly clinging to those very things and by the constant taking up and discarding of the body and organs—which are the effects and instruments of evil—he wanders about, being equalized by the intellect (*dhiyā samānaḥ*).

Likewise, this person, undergoing the constant taking up and discarding of the body and organs through birth and death pertaining to both this world and the next, wanders until liberation from *saṃsāra*.
Therefore, it is established that this light of the Self is distinct from the evils consisting of the body and organs, due to their conjunction and disjunction.
For when something possesses that very nature, conjunction with or disjunction from those same things is not logical. //4,3.8//
Regarding this very person, there are indeed two stations:
this world and the station of the other world.
The third intermediate state is the station of sleep. Abiding in that intermediate station, one perceives both stations: this world and the station of the next world.
Then, according to the sequence, one becomes situated in the station of the next world.
Having ascended that ascent, he beholds both evils and joys.
When he sleeps there, having taken a measure from this all-encompassing world, having himself struck it down and himself fashioned it, he sleeps by his own radiance, by his own light;
here this person becomes self-luminous. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.9)
Objection: It cannot be that these two worlds, which one traverses in succession through birth and death as if in dreaming and waking, actually exist.
For while dreaming and waking are perceived directly by everyone, the world of this life and the world beyond are not established by any means of valid cognition.
Therefore, it is these very states of dreaming and waking that constitute the world of this life and the world beyond.
It is said: for this person, there are indeed two stations, neither a third nor a fourth.
Which are they?
This present birth already attained, which is a station characterized by body, sense-faculties, objects, and sensations, experienced through direct perception.
The "other-worldly state" (*paralokasthāna*) is simply the other world (*paraloka*);
and that is to be experienced at a time subsequent to the separation from the body and so forth.
[Objection: But since the dream state is also a state of the other world, is it not improper to assert the restriction that there are only two? [Reply: No.
How, then, is it so? It is "intermediate" (saṃdhya). That which exists at the junction between this world and the next is the intermediate; that third state is the station of dream.
Therefore, there is a determination of two distinct states;
for it is not possible to count something as a third state in relation to two villages merely because it exists at the junction between them.
But how, again, is the existence of that other-worldly state understood, in relation to which the dream-state would be considered an intermediate state?
Because, while abiding in that intermediate state of dreaming, he perceives both these states;
which two? This world and the state of the other world.

Therefore, there exist both worlds distinct from the dreaming and waking states, which he, being common to both, traverses by means of his intellect through the continuous succession of birth and death.
But how, while situated in the dream state, does he see the two worlds? What is his support, and by what process does he do so?
It is said: Now, listen as to how he sees.
"Yathākrama" means that by which one proceeds; it signifies the basis, the support, or the foundation. That which is his basis is his "yathākrama."

The meaning is this: when this person is about to proceed to the state of the next world, he possesses a certain sequential order (*ākrama*) characterized by knowledge, action, and prior cognition (*pūrvaprajñā*), which serves as the means for attaining that next world.

Having seized, taken hold of, and relied upon that sequential order—which is oriented toward the state of the next world like a seed that has reached the state of a sprout—he perceives both [kinds of results]. The plural number is used because the fruits of dharma and adharma are manifold; thus, it means he perceives those of both types.

"What evils" refers to the fruits of evil; however, it is not possible for the evils themselves to be directly perceived. Therefore, the meaning is that "evils" refers to the sufferings which are the fruits of evil. And "blisses" refers to the pleasures which are the fruits of dharma.
One perceives both those evils and joys through the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) formed by what was seen in previous births;
and one also perceives, impelled by merit and demerit or through the grace of deities, those minor fruits of merit and demerit pertaining to a future birth that is yet to be attained.
How, then, is it understood that the perception of evils connected with the state of the next world occurs in a dream?
It is said: because here in this life one sees much that was not experienced [in this very birth], and a dream is not indeed a perception of something entirely unprecedented;
for a dream is generally a memory of what was previously seen.
Therefore, both worlds exist as distinct from the states of dreaming and waking.

As for what was said—that when there is an absence of external lights such as the sun, this person, who is a composite of cause and effect, conducts his affairs by means of a distinct self that serves as light—that very thing does not exist;
for how could there be an attainment of the absence of the sun and other lights where this self-luminous [self] is perceived in its isolation?
By which [reason], this aggregate of causes and effects would always be perceived as being inextricably mixed;
therefore, the Self is either equal to the non-existent or indeed non-existent by its own distinct nature as light.
On the other hand, if it were ever perceived as distinct by its own nature as light, devoid of contact with external or internal elements and elemental derivatives, then—

In order to show that everything will happen exactly as stated, he says this: "That Self which has been under discussion—at what time, in what manner, and with what material cause does He sleep when He experiences deep sleep (*prasvapiti*), and how does He attain the intermediate state (*saṃdhyaṃ sthānam*)? This is now explained.

Of this visible world, characterized by the waking state, which is "all-encompassing" (*sarvāvān*)—meaning it encompasses everything—this world consists of the aggregate of causes and effects, joined with objects and sensations.

Its "all-encompassing" nature was explained in the section on the three foods, beginning with the words, "Now, this indeed is the Self," and so forth. Or, it is "all-encompassing" because all the elements (*bhūta*) and elemental derivatives (*bhautika*) exist within it as its constituent parts; thus it is *sarvavān*, encompassing all.

Having taken—meaning having cut off, removed, and grasped—a single portion, a measure, or a part of that all-encompassing [Self], one who is permeated by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of perceived births; that is the meaning.
Having himself, by his own self, struck down—that is, caused the falling away of—the body, having rendered it devoid of consciousness;
for in the waking state, the favoring of the sun and other [deities] within the eyes and other [senses] serves the purpose of the body's worldly activity.

The bodily activity of the self is impelled by the experience of the fruits of its own merit and demerit; the cessation of that experience of the fruits of merit and demerit within this body is caused by the cessation of the self's karma, and thus it is said that "the self destroys itself. Having fashioned—that is, having created—a dream-body composed of latent impressions (vāsanā), as if it were composed of illusion (māyā), even that creation is said to have the self as its agent because it depends upon that [self's] karma.

By its own light—that is, by the light characterized as the mere appropriation [of objects], meaning by the illumination consisting of the activity of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) which comprises all latent impressions (vāsanā);
for it is that [light] which shines there as the object, consisting of all latent impressions. That is what is called "its own light" (svayaṃbhā) in that context.

By means of that very light which has become his object, and by his own luminosity which takes that as its object—possessing a distinct form and an unimpaired nature of vision—he makes that objective world, consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), his own experience and thus dreams.
This state of functioning is what is called "dreaming.
In this state, at this time, this person—the Self (*ātman*)—becomes himself a distinct light.

The light becomes free from contact with external and internal elements and elemental derivatives. Now, an objection is raised: since only this world has been taken up as the substrate, how can it be said that "in its presence, this person here becomes self-luminous"?
This is not a fault.
For that [dream state] is indeed an object [of perception]; and by means of that very object, this person can here be shown to be self-luminous.
It cannot be shown otherwise, for in the absence of any object, it would be as in the state of deep sleep.

But when that [Self], whose nature is the latent impression of being, is perceived as an object, then it is apprehended as being drawn forth as it were from its sheath— manifesting in its own form the light of the self which is vision, undiminished and devoid of all contact, its essential nature distinct from the eyes and other instruments of action.
Therefore, it is established that in this state, this person is self-luminous. //4.3.9//
There are no chariots there, nor yoke-horses for chariots, nor roads;
yet he creates chariots, yoke-horses for chariots, and roads.
There, Ānanda, there are no joys, delights, or raptures;
yet he creates joys, delights, and raptures. There, moreover, there are no pools, lotus ponds, or flowing streams.
Then he creates ponds, lotus-pools, and flowing streams;
for he is the agent.

[Objection: But how is it that here the person (*puruṣa*) is self-luminous (*svayañjyotis*), since all worldly activity characterized by the grasped and the grasper is seen just as in the waking state?
Furthermore, the lights such as the sun, which assist the eyes and other senses, are likewise seen just as in the waking state.
Under these circumstances, how can the specific determination be made that "here this person becomes self-luminous"?
It is said: because of the difference in nature from the perception of a dream.
For in the waking state, the light of the Self is intermingled with the activity of the senses, the intellect, the mind, and external light;
but here in the dream state, due to the absence of the senses and the absence of the light of the sun and so forth that supports them, it becomes distinct and isolated.
Therefore, it is distinct [from waking].
But surely, objects are perceived in dreams exactly as they are in the waking state; so how can it be said that there is a distinction due to the absence of Indra and others?
Listen: in that dream, there are no objects characterized by chariots and the like.
Likewise, there are no chariot-yokes—that is, horses and the like used for yoking to chariots—found there;
nor do there exist paths, which are the tracks for chariots.
Yet he himself creates chariots, chariot-yokes, and paths.

But how does he create again in the absence of the means for chariots and so forth, such as trees? It is said in reply: Has it not been stated that "having taken a measure from this entire world, having himself struck it down, having himself fashioned it"? Thus, it is the modification (*vṛtti*) of his internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) that persists as this world; therefore, it is said that he fashions it himself.
He states that very point: "he creates chariots and so forth.
However, in that state, there exist no instruments (karaṇa), nor lights such as the sun which assist the instruments, nor objects such as chariots illuminated by them;

rather, only their latent impressions (vāsanā) are seen, resting upon a modification of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa-vṛtti) that has arisen, impelled by the motive of past karma for perceiving those objects.
Now, that light which is seen by one whose vision is unimpaired is this very self-light (ātma-jyotis), here alone, as if a sword drawn from its scabbard.
Likewise, there are no joys (ānanda)—specific pleasures—nor delights (muda)—joys caused by the acquisition of sons and so forth—nor exultations (pramuda)—those same joys intensified;
yet, it creates these joys and the rest.
Likewise, there are no groves, ponds, lotus-pools, lakes, streams, or rivers there; rather,
he creates groves and so forth, which consist merely of the nature of mental impressions (vāsanā),
because he is indeed the creator.

We have stated that [the self] is the cause of action by virtue of being the instrumental cause for the arising of mental modifications based on latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Its agency is not direct; for activity cannot occur therein directly due to the absence of means.
Indeed, activity is not possible without a causal factor (*kāraka*).
Furthermore, hands, feet, and other instruments of action do not exist there [in the state of deep sleep].

However, those [instruments] which exist in the waking state perform action by means of the body and organs illumined by the light of the Self (ātma-jyotis), for the purpose of giving rise to the functions of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) which serve as the substratum for the latent impressions (vāsanā) of chariots and so forth;
therefore, it is said that "he indeed is the agent."
Thus it has been said: "By this light as his own, he sits, moves about, and performs action.
Even there, in the highest sense, the self does not possess agency *per se*, apart from its nature as the illuminator of the light of consciousness (*caitanya-jyotis*).

And when the light of the self, which is consciousness, illumines the body and the organs through the medium of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), those body and organs, being thus illumined, become engaged in actions; it is in that context that agency is figuratively attributed to them.

Regarding the self: that which was stated as "it meditates, as it were; it vibrates, as it were" is here restated; for the purpose of providing a reason [for its being the agent], it is said, "he is indeed the agent. (4.3.10)
Regarding this, there are these verses:
"Having struck down the bodily [self] by means of dream-sleep, he, being himself unslumbering, looks down upon those who sleep."
Taking up the seed, he returns again to his place—the golden person, the solitary swan.

Regarding this very matter thus explained, there are these verses (mantras): "By means of sleep— that is, by the state of dreaming— having struck down the bodily self, having rendered it motionless, he himself, being unslumbering due to his inherent nature of possessing undiminished powers of sight and so forth, gazes upon all external and internal objects that have become 'asleep'— meaning they have subsided into their own form as latent impressions— namely, those which were supported by the modifications of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) arising from the forms of waking and dreaming, while his own vision of the Self remains undiminished."
The meaning is that it sees and shines forth.

Having taken up—that is, having grasped—the pure, luminous form consisting of the mere sense-faculties (*indriyamātra*), the golden one—meaning the person whose nature is the light of consciousness, like gold—returns to the waking state for the sake of further action. He is called "the single swan" (*ekahaṃsa*) because he goes alone, as if solitary.
The "Single Swan" (ekahaṃsa) is so called because, while awake, it alone travels through the states of dreaming, this world, the next world, and so forth. //4,3.11//
Guarding with his vital breath (prāṇa) the lower nest, having moved outside the nest as the immortal one,
he— the golden person, the solitary swan— goes wherever he desires as an immortal. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.12)

Likewise, protecting— that is, preserving— the inferior, lowly nest, which is the body because it is a collection of many impurities and is utterly loathsome, by means of the fivefold vital breath (*prāṇa*)— lest there be the delusion that one has died— he himself moves out from that nest.

Although he sees the dream while remaining within the body, nevertheless, because of his lack of connection with it, he is said to be "as if moving outside," like the ether situated therein. Being immortal—himself possessing the nature of immortality—he goes wherever he desires; wherever his desire arises toward objects, there he goes, following that very desire as it has arisen in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Moving through high and low realms within the state of dream, the god creates many forms;
as if rejoicing with women, as if laughing, and even as if beholding terrors.

Furthermore, in the state of dream— that is, during the stage of dreaming— the luminous one (*deva*), being led toward and attaining various high and low forms— high meaning states such as those of gods, and low meaning states such as those of animals— brings about or manifests numerous,
innumerable forms consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Or else, he appears as if rejoicing with women, as if eating, or as if laughing with his companions.
Or even as one who fears terrors—that is, perceiving terrors such as lions, tigers, and so forth—as if seeing them directly. 4,3.13.
"People see his resting place, but no one sees him. Regarding him, they say: "One should not wake him while he is sleeping."
It becomes difficult for him to heal whomsoever he does not attend to;
moreover, they indeed say that this is his waking state,
for whatever he sees while awake, he sees that even when asleep.
"In this state, this person becomes self-luminous.
Therefore, O Blessed One, I give you a thousand [cows];
please speak further for the sake of liberation. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.14)

All people perceive the garden, the pleasure-ground, and the playground fashioned by this [Self] in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—namely, the village, the city, women, food, and so forth—which constitute a playground created by such impressions.
But he does not see them; no one sees him.

"Alas! It is a great misery; oh, the misfortune of the world that it does not perceive itself, even though it has come within the range of vision as something utterly secluded and capable of being seen!"—thus the Śruti shows compassion for the world. The intention is that in the dream state, the Self becomes utterly secluded and self-luminous.

They say that one should not awaken such a person [who is sleeping]. Furthermore, there is common worldly recognition of the fact that in sleep, the self-luminosity [of the Self] exists as something distinct [from the body].
What is this [recognition]?
"One should not suddenly and violently awaken that self while it is sleeping and stretched out"—thus say physicians and other people in the world.

Surely they perceive that [the self], having withdrawn from the waking body through the doors of the senses, exists externally in its isolated state; for this reason they say one should not awaken it while it is stretched out.
Furthermore, they see a fault in this: for when it is being awakened too violently, it does not properly engage those doors of the senses as it is being suddenly roused.

This is what he says: "It becomes difficult for him to heal that [part] which he does not regain. That is, whichever region of the sense-organ from which the semen was taken and departed, that region of the sense-organ this Self does not regain.
Sometimes, through a reversal of order, he causes the sense-faculties to enter.
Consequently, when defects such as blindness or deafness arise, it becomes difficult to treat; that is to say, this body becomes one for which medical treatment is painful.
Therefore, even by common experience, its self-luminosity in dream is understood from the statement:
"Having become a dream, he transcends the forms of death. Thus, in the state of dreaming, the Self is its own light.
Moreover, others indeed say that this state of dreaming is nothing other than the waking state itself.
There is no intermediate place distinct from this world and the next; rather, it is this very world that is the waking state.
If this is so, what follows?
As for what happens when one hears:
since this dream occurs in the very same place as the waking state, at that time this Self has not withdrawn from the body and its organs but is mixed with them;
therefore, the Self is not self-luminous. Consequently, in order to refute its self-luminosity, others say: "This [dream] of his is indeed in the waking state."

And regarding this, they state the reason: "Because whatever objects, such as elephants and so forth, a person perceives while awake in the waking state, those very same things he perceives even when asleep. This is incorrect, because the sense organs have ceased to function.
For when the sense-faculties have ceased, one sees dreams;
therefore, no other light is possible there.
Thus it has been said: "There are no chariots there, nor yoked horses," and so forth.
Therefore, in this state, this person is indeed self-luminous.
That there exists a self which is self-luminous has been demonstrated by the illustration of dreaming;
and it is also stated that "he transcends the forms of death."
Moving sequentially through this world, the next world, and so forth, it is distinct from this world and the next;
likewise, it is distinct from the two nests of waking and dreaming.
And because it moves at will therein, it is eternal—this was established by Yājñavalkya in each successive step.
"Therefore," said Janaka, "I give you a thousand [cows] for the sake of the knowledge and its application. Thus enlightened by you, I say: "To you, the Blessed One, I give a thousand;
moreover, liberation and the inquiry into desire were what I intended.
This [knowledge of the Self] is suitable for that purpose, and because it leads to that, it is indeed a part thereof."
"From here, I shall appoint you to hear the determination of all questions regarding desires for the sake of liberation; speak henceforth so that,
through your grace, I may be completely liberated from saṃsāra."
The gift of a thousand [cows] is for the purpose of determining a portion of the meaning of the term "liberation" (vimokṣa). //4,3.14//

Having rejoiced and wandered about in this state of profound serenity, and having seen both the auspicious and the inauspicious, he hastens back again according to the rule, according to his source, for the sake of dream-sleep itself.
Whatever he sees there, he remains untouched by it.
"For this person is indeed unattached.
"It is just so, Yājñavalkya.
Therefore, I give a thousand [cows] to the Blessed One."
"Therefore, speak further for the sake of liberation."

That which was introduced as "by his own light he sets out" has been established here through direct perception: that in the state of dream, this person becomes self-luminous. As for what was said—that having become a dreamer, he transcends this world and the forms of death—[that too is now explained].
In this regard, the following doubt arises: it is only the forms (*rūpa*) of death that one transcends, not death itself;
for it is directly perceived that in a dream, one who is detached from the body and its organs experiences joy, fear, and so forth.
Therefore, surely he does not transcend death at all.
For the effects of karma—such as joy, fear, and so forth—are observed within death itself.
Moreover, if this [being] were bound by death by its very nature, then liberation would not be possible;
for liberation from one's own nature is not logically tenable.
For no one is liberated from intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
However, if death is not an intrinsic nature, then liberation from it will be possible.
In order to demonstrate how that death is not a self (*ātman*) or a phenomenon (*dharma*), he said: "Speak further for the sake of liberation. Thus [he spoke].
Being questioned by Janaka, Yājñavalkya proceeded with the desire to demonstrate that [Self]: "That indeed is the person under discussion, the self-luminous one.
He is the one who was shown in the state of dreaming. This is called 'the state of perfect serenity' (*saṃprasāda*) because in it one becomes perfectly serene (*samyak prasīdati*).

Having abandoned the turbidity born from the collision of hundreds of activities of the body and senses in the waking state, one becomes somewhat serene in the dream state, being liberated from them."

But here, because one becomes perfectly serene in deep sleep (*suṣupta*), deep sleep is called "perfect serenity" (*saṃprasāda*). For the text will later describe the Self abiding in deep sleep with the words, "For then he has crossed over all sorrows," and "He is the one seer, like water. This very Self, having gradually entered into this state of perfect serenity and remaining in deep sleep—

How is he "serene"? It means that, while still in the state of dreaming and desiring to enter deep sleep, having enjoyed pleasures—having experienced delight by seeing friends, kinsmen, and so forth; having sported in various ways;
and having perceived the exhaustion resulting from such activity—he sees, but does not perform, both merit and the fruit of merit, as well as evil and the fruit of evil.
However, we have already stated that there is no direct perception of merit and demerit;
therefore, [the self] is not bound by merit and demerit. For he who performs meritorious or non-meritorious acts is the one who is bound by them.
For one does not become bound by that through mere sight.
Therefore, having become a dream, he indeed transcends death; it is not that he does not transcend death, but rather that he transcends only the forms of death.
Hence, there is no suspicion that death is the essential nature of the Self.
If death were one's inherent nature, it would occur even in a dream;
yet it does not so occur.
If it were an inherent nature, the action would be constant, and there would be no liberation at all.
But its intrinsic nature does not exist even in a dream, because it is absent there;
therefore, its liberation from death through merit and demerit is possible.
[Objection: Is it not the case that its intrinsic nature exists in the waking state? [Reply: No.
For that [dreaming] is produced by limiting adjuncts such as the intellect (buddhi) and so forth;
and this has been established by the scriptural statement, "By similarity, it thinks, as it were, it moves, as it were.

Therefore, because in the dream state there is an absolute transcendence of the form of death, there is neither the suspicion of its being natural nor the possibility of its not being liberated from that state.
"Having moved there" means having experienced the exertion that is the fruit of moving.
Thereafter, following the experience of the state of serene confidence (*saṃprasāda*), "back again according to the rule" (*pratinyāyam*): "rule" (*nyāya*) refers to the fixed method;
"method" (*āya*) is the path of departure. "Back again" (*prati*) refers to the returning journey, which is the opposite of the previous departure. That is "back according to the rule."
The meaning is that it returns again just as it came.
"To its respective source" means to its respective place;
for one who has entered the state of deep sleep from the state of dreaming returns again to that very same place.
He returns to his source for the sake of dreaming, indeed for the state of dreaming.

[Objection: But one does not perform merit or demerit in a dream; how then is the fruit of those two understood? [Reply: Just as one certainly performs [actions] in the waking state, so too in the dream, because the perception is the same. Therefore, he says: whatever that Self sees there in the dream—whether it be the fruit of merit or demerit—he follows after it, yet he is not bound by it; he is not at all bound by what was seen.
For if what was done in a dream were truly accomplished by him, he would be bound by it;
even after waking from the dream, he would still be possessed of its result.
Yet, in the world, there is no common recognition of being possessed of the results of karma performed in a dream.
For no one considers himself a wrongdoer on account of a sin committed in a dream;
nor does the world, upon hearing of the sin of a dreamer, censure him or avoid him. Therefore, he remains entirely unaffected by it.
And those who report it say, along with the word itself, "I saw elephants today, made into jars, as if running.
Therefore, it has no agency. But how is it that it lacks agency?
The conjunction of a material entity with other material instruments and organs is observed to be the cause of action;
however, no immaterial thing is seen to possess action, and the Self is immaterial; therefore, it is unattached.
And because this Person is unattached, he is not followed by what was seen in the dream state.
For this very reason, agency in action is in no way possible for it.
For agency would exist through the conjunction of the body and the instruments of action; yet that conjunction, which is attachment, does not belong to it, since "this Puruṣa is indeed unattached.
Therefore, it is immortal.
"So it is, Yājñavalkya!

I give you a thousand [cows], O Blessed One; speak further only for the sake of liberation, since the analytical discernment of action—which constitutes one part of the subject matter of liberation—has been correctly shown."
"Therefore, speak further for the sake of liberation. //4.3.15//

Having enjoyed himself and wandered about in this dream state, and having seen both good and evil, he hastens back again according to the rule, back to his original source, namely to the waking state. Whatever he sees there, he remains untouched by it.
"For this person is indeed unattached.
"It is even so, Yājñavalkya.
Therefore, I give a thousand [cows] to the Blessed One."
"Therefore, speak further for the sake of liberation alone."
In that context, the statement "for this person is unattached" (BrhUpBh_4,3.16) provides the reason for his non-agency through non-attachment.
Furthermore, it was stated previously that "by the power of karma, he goes wherever he desires.
Since desire arises from attachment, the reason stated—that "this person is unattached"—is shown to be unestablished.
But this is not so.
How then?
It is said that he is indeed without attachment: "Now, this very person in this dream state... [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.10.1].
Having returned from the state of deep sleep, having enjoyed himself and moved about as he desired in a dream, he sees both merit and evil— all as previously described—
for the sake of waking up, that is, for the state of the waking world.
Therefore, this person is indeed unattached.
If one were to have sexual union in a dream while being a desirer, then, having returned to the waking state, one would be stained by the defects arising from that union. //4.3.16//

Indeed, having enjoyed himself and wandered about in this state of waking, and having seen both good and evil, he hastens back again according to the rule and according to his source, toward the state of dream itself. Just as that [person], upon returning from the dream to the waking state, is not affected by the defects arising from the dream because of his lack of attachment, so it is here.
Thus, one is not smeared by the defects born of attachment to the waking state; indeed, one is not smeared by the waking state. This is what is being said:
"He, indeed, having enjoyed himself and wandered about in this waking state," and so forth, as before.
Whatever he sees there in that waking state, he does not carry with him when he departs from it, for this person is unattached.
Now, how is it determined that [the Self] acts only after seeing? For one performs merit and demerit therein and perceives their fruit;

since agency is established through the state of being both the agent and the illuminator, this aggregate of the body and organs functions illuminated by the light of the Self—as expressed in passages such as "By the light of the Self alone, he goes out. Therefore, its agency is figurative (*upacaryate*), not inherent agency.
And so it has been said: "It meditates, as it were; it moves, as it were.
This [activity] is produced solely by limiting adjuncts such as the intellect (*buddhi*) and is not inherent [to the Self].

However, here, with reference to the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the Self is described as independent of limiting adjuncts: "Having seen both merit and evil, one does not create them. Therefore, there is no suspicion of contradiction between what precedes and what follows.
Because it is free from limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*), from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), it neither acts nor is it stained by the fruit of action.

And thus it was said by the Blessed One: "O son of Kuntī, because it is beginningless and devoid of qualities, this immutable Supreme Self (*paramātman*), even while dwelling in the body, neither acts nor is it stained."
Thus it is said.
Likewise, the gift of a thousand [cows] is mentioned because the seclusion from desire has been demonstrated.
Furthermore, by these two sections—"Now, indeed, he [the self] in this dream"—and "Now, indeed, he [the self] in this waking state"—non-attachment itself is established.

Since one who has gone to the end of sleep, being serene, becomes unattached due to the non-perception of actions such as theft performed at the end of the waking state, therefore, in all three states, this [self] is inherently unattached.
Therefore, he is immortal.
Being distinct from the nature of the three states, he rushes back toward his source for the sake of the "end of sleep," which means for the sake of the serene state (*saṃprasāda*).
This is because we observe that the term "sleep" (*svapna*) is used to denote the waking of vision, and because the qualification by the word "end" (*anta*) is thus appropriate.

And by the phrase "he runs to this end," deep sleep will be shown. Furthermore, if it is said, "Having enjoyed himself and wandered about in the world of dreams, he moves between these two ends— the world of dreams and the world of waking"— then, because of this observation, in the expression "to the world of dreams" (*svapnāntāya*), the term "dream" (*svapna*) refers specifically to the state of dreaming.
Nevertheless, nothing is faulty, for that which was intended to be established is indeed established through its very incongruity.
Because, having seen merit and demerit in the waking state, and having enjoyed and acted, one who has reached the end of a dream does not follow after the defects of the waking state. //4,3.17//
Just as a great fish swims along both banks, the near and the far, even so this person moves along these two ends: the state of dream and the state of waking. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.18)

Thus, this person—the Self—is self-luminous and distinct from the body and the organs; it is distinct from desire and action, which impel them, because this person is indeed unattached (*asaṅga*). This meaning—that it is so because of its unattached nature—has been established by these three sections beginning with, "Now, this [Self], in that state of serene composure... (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.15).

In this regard, how can there be non-attachment for the Self? Because, by means of a sequential movement— passing from the waking state to dream, from dream to deep sleep (saṃprasāda), and from deep sleep back to dream,

and in turn from dream to the waking state, and from the waking state back to the end of dream— in this manner, through such a succession of movements, the distinctness of the three states has been established.

This matter was already introduced previously in the passage, "Having become [a dream], he transcends this world and the forms of death"; having explained that in detail, the text now begins with the words "In that regard... because only the illustration remains to be stated. In that context, regarding the meaning as it has been demonstrated, this illustration is adduced: just as in the world a great fish—that which is both large and a fish—is not carried away by the river current; such is the meaning.
He obstructs the current and moves at his own will between both banks of the river, traveling sequentially from the eastern to the western bank.
Even while traveling, though situated between the two banks, he is not rendered subject to the force of the river's current flowing between them.
In this very same way, this person travels back and forth between these two extremes.
"Which two?
"The state of dreaming and the state of waking.

The purpose of showing this illustration, however, is to demonstrate that the aggregate of the body and the organs—which takes the form of death—is, along with its motivators, desire and action, not a property of the Self; and that the Self is distinct from this [aggregate].
It has been explained in detail. //4,3.18//
Just as in this space a hawk or a falcon, having flown about and become weary, folds its wings and remains poised for rest,
even so does this person hasten toward that end.
There, when one is asleep, one desires no desire at all and sees no dream whatsoever.

And here, by means of the transition through the three states, it has been stated that the Self, which is self-luminous and distinct from the aggregate of the body and the organs, is dissociated from desire and action; thus, the collective meaning stated is that this [Self] does not possess the attributes of transmigratory existence by its own nature, but rather its state of being a transmigrant is caused solely by limiting adjuncts and is superimposed by ignorance.
And therein, the three states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep have been described in a scattered manner, not shown collectively as a single whole.
For in the waking state, through ignorance, one is perceived as being with attachment, subject to death, and accompanied by the aggregate of effects and instruments (the body and senses).
In the dream state, however, one is perceived as being joined with desire and yet free from the form of death.
Furthermore, having returned from deep sleep to the waking state, and from the waking state back to deep sleep, he becomes serene and unattached; thus, his state of non-attachment is also observed.

However, since the fruit being summarized through the unity of the discourse—his nature as eternally liberated, awakened, and pure—is not demonstrated by bringing it all together in one place, this section is commenced to demonstrate that.
For such is his nature in deep sleep, which will be described as: "Now, this is his form, free from desire, free from evil, and fearless."

Since he is about to enter such a distinct state of deep sleep, [the author] asks, "How so? and states that the meaning of this matter becomes manifest through an illustration; thus, an illustration is presented here:
"Just as in this physical space, a hawk or a falcon..."
By the word *suparṇa*, the swift falcon (*śyena*) is meant.

Just as, having sported and flown about in this sky, being weary and exhausted by the activity characterized by various modes of flight, it folds its wings together and settles properly—that in which it rests is the *saṃlaya*, the nest; and it remains for the sake of the nest alone.
It is sustained by itself and is itself alone.
Just as this illustration is, so too does this person run toward that end.
This is an epithet for that which is denoted by the word "end": in which end, when one has fallen asleep, one desires no desire whatsoever.
And thus, one does not see any dream,
nor does one desire anything; by this, every desire is prohibited without distinction between the state of dreaming and the waking state,
because of the use of the term "anything" (*kañcana*) which leaves no remainder.
Likewise, regarding the phrase "not any dream":
even that which is seen in the waking state is considered a dream by the Śruti; therefore, it says, "he sees no dream whatsoever.
And so another Śruti states: "He has three abodes and three dreams."

Just as in the illustration a bird approaches its own nest to remove the exhaustion born of flying about, so too for the bird-like self— which is joined with the fruits of actions arising from the union of the body and the senses during the waking and dreaming states— there arises an exhaustion similar to that of flight; to remove that exhaustion, it seeks its own nest, its abode, which is distinct from all the attributes of transmigratory existence and devoid of the toil of all actions, instruments, and their results.
He enters his own self. //4,3.19 //
Now, these channels of his called *hitā* (the "placed") exist with a fineness like that of a hair split a thousandfold;
they are filled with white, blue, brown, green, and red [fluids].

Now, when it seems as though they are killing him, or conquering him, or an elephant is chasing him away, or he falls as if into a pit—whatever fear he perceives while awake, that he imagines here through ignorance. But when he thinks, "I am like a god, I am like a king; I am indeed all this," [that is his state of knowledge].
That is his supreme world.

BrhUpBh_4.3.20: If this [Self] has as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) the state of being devoid of all attributes of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra-dharma*), and its possession of the attributes of transmigratory existence is caused by external adjuncts (*paropādhi-nimitta*);
and if that cause by which it possesses the attributes of transmigratory existence produced by external adjuncts is ignorance (*avidyā*);
then, is that ignorance intrinsic (*svābhāvikatva*) or adventitious (*āgantukatva*), like desire, action, and so forth?

If liberation is possible because [ignorance] is adventitious, then what is the proof for its adventitiousness? Or how could ignorance not be a property of the self? To determine the true nature of ignorance, which is the seed of all misfortune, the following section is commenced: tā... [The text continues with the verse: "Since it does not exist in the absence of the self, and since it arises when the self is present, therefore ignorance is understood to belong to the self. (1.2) [Commentary: Because it does not exist when the self is absent, and because it arises when the self is present, ignorance is known to be a property of the self. Just as the color blue exists only when a blue substance exists and does not exist when that substance is absent, so too does ignorance exist only when the self exists and does not exist when the self is absent. Therefore, it is established that ignorance is a property of the self. Furthermore, this is not merely a logical inference; rather, it is stated that "it is seen by the wise," meaning that those who possess the eye of wisdom perceive it thus. For example, just as a person with healthy eyes perceives a white conch shell as white, so too do the wise perceive the self as being associated with ignorance. Thus, it is concluded that ignorance is indeed a property of the self. This concludes the first chapter. The second chapter follows. (1.3) [Commentary: Now, the following doubt may arise: "If ignorance is a property of the self, then why is it not perceived? To resolve this, the following is stated: "But it is not perceived because it is subtle, like the heat of water. (1.4) Just as the heat of water is not perceived due to its subtlety, so too is ignorance not perceived because it is subtle. It is not that it does not exist at all. This is because it is the cause of all suffering. If it were non-existent, then there would be no suffering, and consequently, there would be no liberation either. Therefore, it is established that ignorance exists as a property of the self. This concludes the second chapter. The third chapter follows. (1.5) [Commentary: Now, the following doubt may arise: "If ignorance is a property of the self, then why is it not perceived even by the ignorant? To resolve this, the following is stated: "But it is not perceived by the ignorant because they lack the means of knowledge. (1.6) Just as a person born blind cannot perceive colors, so too the ignorant cannot perceive ignorance because they lack the means of valid cognition. It is not that ignorance does not exist for them. This is because they experience the fruits of ignorance, such as birth, old age, and death. Therefore, it is established that ignorance exists even for the ignorant, though it is not perceived by them. This concludes the third chapter. The fourth chapter follows. (1.7) [Commentary: Now, the following doubt may arise: "If ignorance is a property of the self, then why is it not perceived by the yogis? To resolve this, the following is stated: "But it is perceived by the yogis through the power of meditation. (1.8) Just as a person with supernormal vision perceives subtle objects, so too the yogis perceive ignorance through the power of their meditative concentration. It is not that it is not perceived by them. This is because they have destroyed the veil of ignorance. Therefore, it is established that ignorance is perceived by the yogis. This concludes the fourth chapter. The fifth chapter follows. (1.9) [Commentary: Now, the following doubt may arise: "If ignorance is a property of the self, then why is it not perceived by the Buddhas? To resolve this, the following is stated: "But it is not perceived by the Buddhas because they have completely transcended it. (1.10) Just as a fire that has been extinguished is no longer perceived, so too ignorance is not perceived by the Buddhas because they have completely transcended it. It is not that it does not exist for them. This is because they have attained the state of omniscience. Therefore, it is established that ignorance is not perceived by the Buddhas. This concludes the fifth chapter. The sixth chapter follows. (1.11) [Commentary: Now, the following doubt may arise: "If ignorance is a property of the self, then why is it not perceived by the Arhats? To resolve this, the following is stated: "But it is not perceived by the Arhats because they have severed the continuity of rebirth. (1.12) Just as a seed that has been burnt cannot sprout, so too ignorance is not perceived by the Arhats because they have severed the continuity of rebirth. It is not that it does not exist for them. This is because they have attained the state of final liberation. Therefore, it is established that ignorance is not perceived by the Arhats. This concludes the sixth chapter. The seventh chapter follows. (1.13) [Commentary: Now, the following doubt may arise: "If ignorance is a property of the self, then why is it not perceived by the Pratyekabuddhas? To resolve this, the following is stated: "But it is not perceived by the Pratyekabuddhas because they have realized the truth for themselves. (1.14) Just as a person who has awakened from sleep does not see the illusions of a dream, so too ignorance is not perceived by the Pratyekabuddhas because they have realized the truth for themselves. It is not that it does not exist for them. This is because they have attained the state of solitary enlightenment. Therefore, it is established that ignorance is not perceived by the Pratyekabuddhas. This concludes the seventh chapter. The eighth chapter follows. (1.15) [Commentary: Now, the following doubt may arise: "If ignorance is a property of the self, then why is it not perceived by the Bodhisattvas? To resolve this, the following is stated: "But it is not perceived by the Bodhisattvas because they have compassion for all beings. (1.16) Just as a mother does not abandon her child even if she is afflicted by illness, so too the Bodhisattvas do not perceive ignorance as an obstacle because of their great compassion for all sentient beings. It is not that it does not exist for them. This is because they have vowed to liberate all beings. Therefore, it is established that ignorance is not perceived by the Bodhisattvas. This concludes the eighth chapter. The ninth chapter follows. (1.17) [Commentary: Now, the following doubt may arise: "If ignorance is a property of the self, then why is it not perceived by the Śrāvakas? To resolve this, the following is stated: "But it is not perceived by the Śrāvakas because they are focused on their own peace. (1.18) Just as a person who is preoccupied with their own safety does not notice the dangers around them, so too the Śrāvakas do not perceive ignorance because they are focused solely on their own liberation. It is not that it does not exist for them. This is because they have attained the state of Arhatship. Therefore, it is established that ignorance is not perceived by the Śrāvakas. This concludes the ninth chapter. The tenth chapter follows. (1.19) [Commentary: Now, the following doubt may arise: "If ignorance is a property of the self, then why is it not perceived by ordinary people? To resolve this, the following is stated: "But it is not perceived by ordinary people because they are deluded by it. (1.20) Just as a person who is intoxicated by wine does not perceive the reality of the world, so too ordinary people do not perceive ignorance because they are deluded by it. It is not that it does not exist for them. This is because they experience the results of their actions. Therefore, it is established that ignorance is not perceived by ordinary people. This concludes the tenth chapter. The eleventh chapter follows. To resolve this, the following is stated: "But it is not perceived by the gods because they are distracted by pleasure. (1.22) Just as a person who is distracted by worldly pleasures does not perceive the transience of life, so too the gods do not perceive ignorance because they are distracted by celestial pleasures. It is not that it does not exist for them. This is because they eventually fall from their divine state. Therefore, it is established that ignorance is not perceived by the gods. This concludes the eleventh chapter. The twelfth chapter follows. (1.23) [Commentary: Now, the following doubt may arise: "If ignorance is a property of the self, then why is it not perceived by the Asuras? To resolve this, the following is stated: "But it is not perceived by the Asuras because they are consumed by envy. (1.24) Just as a person who is consumed by jealousy does not perceive the faults of others, so too the Asuras do not perceive ignorance because they are consumed by envy toward the gods. It is not that it does not exist for them. This is because they suffer from constant conflict. Therefore
Or rather, these channels called *hitā* belonging to this person characterized by head, hands, and so forth, exist with a minuteness—that is, a fineness—equal to that of a hair split a thousandfold.
They are filled with white fluid, blue, brown, green, and red; the meaning is that they are filled with these specific varieties of fluid, such as whiteness and the rest.
And here, the specific qualities of the tastes (rasa) become manifold and diverse due to the various combinations and imbalances of wind (vāta), bile (pitta), and phlegm (śleṣman).

Within these very subtle channels (nāḍī)—which are as minute as a thousandth part of the tip of a hair, filled with white and other fluids, and extending throughout the entire body—the seventeen-fold subtle body (liṅga) resides.
All latent impressions (vāsanā), produced by the experience of the various phenomena of saṃsāra, are dependent upon that [subtle body].

That subtle body (*talliṅga*), which is the substratum of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), is transparent due to its subtlety like a crystal gem; yet, by virtue of contact with the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of the essences (*rasa*) circulating through the channels (*nāḍī*), and impelled by merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), it manifests specific modifications (*vṛtti-viśeṣa*).
Through latent impressions, it appears in the forms of women, chariots, elephants, and so forth.

Now, this being the case, when at some time a false cognition called ignorance (*avidyā*) arises—caused by latent impressions—in the form "some enemies or other thieves have come and are killing me," that is what is being described.
"It seems as if it were striking down this dreamer.
Likewise, "the elephant seems to chase him" means it obscures him, puts him to flight, or makes him run away.
"He falls as if into a pit" means he perceives himself as falling into something like a dilapidated well or similar depression.

For such a false impression arises for him, based on a modification of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa-vṛtti) illuminated by extremely base demerit (adharma), and based on a modification whose very nature is suffering, because its nature is indeed suffering. To say more: that very same fear characterized by elephants and so forth which exists in the waking state is here, in this dream, considered to be of the form of fear even without the actual presence of elephants and the like, solely through the false emergence of the impressions of ignorance (avidyā-vāsanā).

Furthermore, it is now stated as to what is the object and what is the characteristic of that ignorance which is being diminished and that knowledge which is being increased: "Now, when one becomes like a god"—when knowledge concerning deities has arisen during the waking state, then by means of that arisen latent impression (vāsanā), one considers oneself to be like a god.

This is also said regarding the dream state: "like a god, like a king seated upon his throne, consecrated"—one who is permeated by the latent impression of royalty considers oneself to be the king even in a dream.

Thus, when knowledge—which has arisen from ignorance that is being utterly destroyed—becomes universal in its scope regarding the Self, even in a dream, one who is steeped in that [knowledge] thinks, "I am indeed all this.
That state of being the Self of all is the supreme world of this Self; it is the supreme state of the Self, which is innate.
But that which is perceived as something other than the state of being the Self of all, even by as much as the tip of a hair, is the thought "I am not [all]."

Those non-self-existent worlds that are presented by ignorance (*avidyā*) in its various states—those inferior worlds ending with the stationary (*sthāvara*)—are the objects of conventional worldly discourse (*saṃvyavahāra*).
In comparison to those worlds, this entire state of being the Self of all (*sarvātmabhāva*), which is without interior or exterior, is his supreme world (*paramo lokaḥ*).
Therefore, when ignorance is removed and knowledge (*vidyā*) has reached its culmination, the state of being the Self of all is liberation (*mokṣa*).

Just as self-luminosity is perceived directly in the dream state—as expressed in the words, "where they seem to kill him, or they seem to conquer him"—these two are the effects of knowledge and ignorance: the state of being the Self of all and the state of having a limited self. Through pure knowledge, one becomes the Self of all.
And through ignorance, one becomes non-omniscient;
one becomes differentiated from something or other. From whatever one is differentiated, with that one is in conflict.
Because of being contradictory, it is destroyed, conquered, and shattered.

And this occurs because of its distinctness when it does not have all things as its object. But how could that which is a totality be distinct, such that it would be contradictory? In the absence of contradiction, by what would it be destroyed, conquered, or shattered?
Therefore, this existence of ignorance is stated as follows:
it causes one to grasp that which is the self of all as being not the self of all; it presents as present an object other than the self that does not exist.
One renders oneself non-omnipresent;
from that, desire for that object arises;
because of being divided by that desire, one undertakes action.
From that, the fruit [arises].
This has already been stated, and will also be stated later: "For where there is duality as it were, there one sees another," and so forth.
This true nature of ignorance has been demonstrated along with its auxiliary causes;
and the entire effect of knowledge, which is the state of selfhood, has been shown by way of the opposite of ignorance.
Furthermore, that ignorance is not an inherent attribute of the Self, because as knowledge increases, it itself diminishes.

When true knowledge has reached its culmination and the state of being the Self of all has been fully established, [ignorance] ceases entirely, just as the cognition of a snake in a rope ceases upon the certain determination of the rope.
And this has been stated: "But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should one see? and so forth.
Therefore, ignorance is not an attribute of the Self;
for the destruction of that which is inherent in its own nature can never occur, just as heat and light cannot be destroyed from the sun.
Consequently, liberation is possible for it [the Self]. 4.3.20.
Now,
this form of his is indeed the Atichandas, free from evil and fearless.
It is like a man embraced by a beloved wife, who knows nothing without nor within.
In the very same way, this person, closely embraced by the conscious Self (prājña-ātman), knows nothing at all, either external or internal.
Now, this is his state in which desires are fulfilled, in which the Self is the desire, which is free from desire, and which is beyond sorrow.

Now, that state of being the Self of all—which is liberation, the fruit of knowledge, devoid of action, its factors, and its fruits—is pointed out through direct perception: that state where ignorance, desire, and action do not exist, which was introduced in the passage, "Where, asleep, one desires no desire and sees no dream.
This very form of his, which is the state of being the Self of all, has been described as "his highest world. That is "free from desires" (*aticchanda*), meaning it is beyond all desire.
Because it is beyond form (*rūpa*).
*Chanda* means desire; that form from which desire has transcended is "beyond-desire" (*aticchanda*) form.
That other word "sānta-chandas" denotes the meters such as Gāyatrī and so forth; this one, however, signifies desire,
and therefore it ends in a vowel.
Nevertheless, the reading *aticchandāḥ* should be understood as a feature of the specific recitation (*svādhyāya*).
Furthermore, in common usage, the word *chanda* is employed in the sense of desire, as in "one's own will" (*svacchanda*) or "another's will" (*paracchanda*);
therefore, it should be interpreted as *aticchandam*.
In this sense, "this form is devoid of desire";
likewise, by the word *pāpman* (evil), both merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) are meant, because it has been stated: "he is joined with evils" and "he casts off evils."
"Free from evil" means devoid of merit and demerit (dharma and adharma). Furthermore, it is "fearless," for fear is indeed the effect of ignorance, as it has been said:
"Through ignorance one imagines fear."
This is a negation of the cause by means of its effect;
"fearless form" means that which is devoid of ignorance.
This very state, the fruit of knowledge, is the nature of being the Self of all.
This very form—free from evil and devoid of fear by virtue of this desirelessness—is devoid of all the attributes of transmigratory existence;
therefore, it is this form that is fearless.
And this was already introduced previously at the conclusion of the immediately preceding section on Brahman, according to the scriptural tradition: "O Janaka, you have indeed attained the fearless."
In this context, however, it has been elaborated through reasoning in order to strengthen the conviction regarding the meaning of the revealed scriptures:
this Self is by its very nature the light of consciousness; it illumines everything by means of its own light of consciousness. Whatever it perceives therein—
It is said that it "delights," "moves," and "knows."
And it is established by logic that the essential nature of the Self is eternally the light of consciousness.
If this Self exists undestroyed, abiding in its own very form, why does it not [recognize] itself as "I am"? Or [why does it not recognize] the Self?
Or does he not know that "these beings are outside," as one does not know it during the waking and dreaming states?
To this, it is replied:
Listen now to the cause of ignorance: oneness alone is the cause of ignorance.
How is that so? It is said:
for the intended meaning becomes evident through an illustration. Thus he says: "In that regard, just as in the world, with respect to one who is dear and beloved..."

Being completely embraced by a woman who desires him, he, being desirous, knows nothing whatsoever external to himself— that is, no object other than himself— and nor does he know anything internal, such as "I am this," or "I am happy," or "I am miserable."
But when not embraced, that distinct entity knows everything, both the external and the internal; however, after the time of being embraced, due to the attainment of oneness, it no longer knows.

In this very way, just as in this illustration, the *puruṣa*—the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*)—is distinct from contact with the elements and their subtle constituents (*bhūtamātra*), like a lump of salt.
Like the reflection of the moon and other objects in water and so forth, he who has entered here into the body and the senses is this Puruṣa;
he is by means of his own essential nature, which is supreme reality and his own innate light.
Completely embraced, perfectly enveloped, become one, and without interval, being the self of all,
he perceives no external object whatsoever, nor even anything internal within himself, such as "I am this, I am happy, or I am miserable."
Regarding what you asked— namely, "If its nature is the light of consciousness, why does it not know here?"—
the reason I have stated for that is its unity,
just as in the case of a man and a woman who are closely embracing one another.
In this context, it is stated that the diversity of objects is the cause of specific cognition;
and it is further stated that ignorance (*avidyā*) is that which presents as a separate entity another thing from the causal self.
When one becomes detached from that ignorance, then everything for him becomes nothing but oneness.

And therefore, when the distinction between the factors of action—such as the knower, the object of knowledge, and so forth—is absent, how could the emergence of specific cognition or desire be possible within the self-luminous light of the Self, which abides in its own nature?

Since this oneness of all things is indeed its very form, therefore this form of the Self—which is self-luminous by nature—is "one whose desires are attained" (*āptakāma*), because these [desires] have subsided;
thus, it is called "one whose desires are attained."
For desire is divided by way of difference from this [Self], and thus it results in the non-attainment of one's desires.
Just as in the waking state, the form of Devadatta and others is perceived as distinct, this [state] is not so divided from anything; therefore, it is the attainment of all desires.
Is it that it is not divided from some other separate entity, or is that very entity the Self itself? To this he says: "There is nothing other than the Self."
How so?

Because it is "one whose desires are the Self" (ātmakāma); that is, in that state, the Self alone is the desires, which, though appearing as if divided elsewhere and being desired as something other [than the Self], are in reality the Self itself. This is because, in the states of waking and dreaming, there exists ignorance (*avidyā*), which is the cause for the presentation of the Self as something else; whereas here, due to the absence of that ignorance, it is "one whose desires are the Self."

Thus, because there is an absence of any object of desire, this form is "without longing" (akāma); it is "the end of grief" (śokāntara), meaning "cutting off grief" (śākacchidra) or "devoid of grief" (śokaśūnya), or alternatively, "the middle of grief" (śokamadhyama).
In every respect, this form is "without grief" (aśoka), which means it is free from sorrow. //4,3.21//
In this state, the father becomes no longer a father, the mother no longer a mother; worlds become no longer worlds, gods no longer gods, and the Vedas no longer Vedas.

Here, the thief becomes no longer a thief, the killer of an embryo no longer a killer of an embryo, the outcaste no longer an outcaste, the son of a degraded woman no longer such, the mendicant no longer a mendicant, and the ascetic no longer an ascetic.
Not followed by merit, not followed by evil;
for then he becomes one who has crossed over all the sorrows of the heart.

It has been stated that the subject under discussion—the Self which is self-luminous—is entirely free from ignorance, desire, and action; for the Self is unattached by nature, and those [factors] are merely adventitious.

In this regard, the following doubt arises: even though its essential nature is consciousness, it does not cognize due to being in a state of oneness, just as a man and a woman do not cognize when they are in close embrace. Thus it was said.
In this context, the following was stated incidentally: that self-luminosity (*svayañjyotiṣṭva*) of this Self, like desire, action, and so forth, is not its inherent nature.
When the doubt arises that this is because it is not perceived in the state of serene clarity (*saṃprasāda*), [the text] provides the analogy of a man and a woman to refute that;
it shows that while self-luminosity indeed exists, it is not apprehended in deep sleep due to the cause of unification (*ekībhāva*), but it is not adventitious like desire, action, and the rest.
Having stated this as a digression, he returns to the subject at hand.
And here, this is the subject under discussion: that very form of the Self which is perceived directly in deep sleep, being entirely free from ignorance, desire, and action.

This has been described exactly as it is—namely, that this form transcends all connections—because in this state of deep sleep, this form is "beyond all desires," "free from evil," and "fearless. Therefore, in this [state]...

The father is the progenitor. That status of being a father toward his son, which arises from the act of procreation, is caused by karma; and because he is disconnected from that karma at this time, the father also becomes a non-father, since he is liberated from the karma that is the cause of the father-son relationship.

Likewise, it is understood by implication that even a son becomes as if sonless in relation to his father; for he has transcended that very action which is the cause of the relationship between the two, as it has been stated: "He whose evil has been destroyed."
Likewise, the worlds that were to be conquered through action have been conquered; because of the absence of connection to those actions, those worlds are now "non-worlds" (alokāḥ).
Similarly, the gods who were constituent parts of ritual action—because of the transcendence of connection to those actions—they are now "non-gods" (adevāḥ).

Likewise, the Vedas, characterized as mantras which express the relationship between the goal and the means and thus constitute constituent parts of ritual action by virtue of their denotative function [are likewise transcended].

The Vedas already studied and those yet to be studied are connected to a person solely by means of ritual action; therefore, upon the transcendence of that action, at this time even the Vedas become non-Vedas.
It is not only because he has transcended the connection with auspicious actions, but rather because he is no longer bound even by extremely terrible inauspicious actions.

He states this same point as follows: "In this context, the 'thief' (stena) is understood to be one who steals the gold of a Brāhmaṇa, because he is mentioned in the same grammatical construction as the killer of an embryo (bhrūṇahan). By that terrible deed, he becomes liberated at this time—that deed by which this thief is called a perpetrator of a mortal sin (mahāpātakin)."
Likewise, the killer of a fetus is not liberated from his state merely by his present action;
rather, he is liberated even from that which is innate—the very cause for attaining an extremely low birth.
One born from a Śūdra father and a Brāhmaṇī mother is indeed a Caṇḍāla, and it is precisely this Caṇḍāla who is meant here.
Because he is not bound by the karma that is the cause of his birth, he does not become a *caṇḍāla*.
A *paulkasa* is one who is a *pulkasa*; specifically, a *pulkasa* is one born of a *śūdra* father and a *kṣatriya* mother. He, too, ceases to be a *pulkasa*.
Likewise, it is said that he becomes unconnected with the actions characterized by the stages of life (*āśrama*).

A wandering mendicant (*parivrāj*) is called a *śramaṇa* because he is one whose actions constitute his defining characteristic; since he is liberated from those, he is "no longer a *śramaṇa*" (*aśramaṇa*). Similarly, a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) is "no longer an ascetic" (*atāpasa*). Both terms are used for the purpose of indicating all the castes (*varṇa*), stages of life (*āśrama*), and so forth.

What need is there for much? It is followed by neither that which has been pursued nor that which has not been pursued; it is unconnected. This refers to merit consisting of action prescribed by the scriptures, as well as to evil characterized by the non-performance of what is enjoined and the performance of what is forbidden.
The neuter gender is used because the word *rūpa* (form) is intended;
for the phrase "the fearless form" (*abhayaṃ rūpam*) continues to apply.

Furthermore, what is the reason for this lack of connection? That cause is stated: because at that time he has thus "crossed over" or transcended all sorrows (*śoka*). Here, "sorrows" refers to desires (*kāma*); for the longing for a desired object becomes sorrow when one is separated from that object. Indeed, a person who dwells on the qualities of a desired object—whether it be unattained or already lost—is tormented by thought; therefore, sorrow, delight, and desire are synonyms.

Because one who has transcended all desires indeed becomes such here; for it is said that "one who has transcended desire does not desire anything at all. Thus, occurring in this context, this word *śoka* must necessarily be a synonym for *kāma*.
And *kāma* is the cause of karma.
For it will be said: “As is his desire, so is his resolve; as is his resolve, so is the action he performs.
Therefore, because he has transcended all desires, it is appropriate that he is described as "not followed by merit" and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "the heart of the heart": the "heart" refers to the mass of flesh shaped like a lotus, and the internal organ, the intellect (*buddhi*) situated therein, is called the "heart."
Because they reside therein, it is like [the sound of] a bed or a cry;
for the sorrows of the heart are actually sorrows of the intellect (*buddhi*), since it has been stated: "Desire, resolve, doubt—all this is merely the mind."
And it will say: “The desires that reside in his heart.
Indeed, this statement—both “residing in the heart” and “the sorrows of the heart”—is intended to dispel the delusion that [desires] have the self as their locus.
Furthermore, at this time, he transcends the forms of death, for it has been said that he has passed beyond the connection with the heart-organ.
It is a more logical statement to say that because [the Self] is beyond connection with the heart-organ (hṛdayakaraṇa), it is beyond connection with the desires residing therein;
