for those disputants who claim that desires and latent impressions (vāsanās) resting in the heart approach and adhere to the Self— which is connected to the heart— and even when separated from the heart, they remain in the Self, like the fragrance of flowers in oil contained within a vessel.
[Otherwise,] such statements as "Their desire, their resolve, and the forms of their heart are in the heart" and "the sorrows of the heart" would be rendered meaningless.
If it is argued that this is because they are produced by the organ of the heart (*hṛdaya-karaṇa*), we say no;
for there is the specific qualification "resting in the heart" (*hṛdi śritāḥ*).
For if the heart were merely an instrument, the statement "resting in the heart" would not be appropriate, nor would the statement "for in the heart alone are forms established.
Furthermore, since the Self is intended to be clarified, it is proper that the statement regarding its resting in the heart be taken in its literal sense;
this is because the scriptural passage, "It meditates as it were, it moves as it were," cannot have any other meaning.

If it is argued that because of the qualification "those desires which reside in his heart," there must also be desires residing in the self, we say no; for this is with reference to those not yet residing [there]. Here, the qualification "which are in the heart" does not depend on another locus; rather, it is a qualification made with reference to those desires which are currently not residing in the heart. As for those [desires] that have not yet arisen, those that will arise in the future, and those that have already passed away but ceased through their antidote—these are certainly not considered to be residing in the heart, even though they are possible [to exist].
Therefore, it is appropriate to apply a qualification with respect to them:
"all those who are firmly rooted and present in the object are liberated.
If it is argued that even so, the qualification is redundant, we say: no.

Among those [desires], because of their predominance and because they are objects to be abandoned, otherwise an unscriptural and undesirable assumption would result: namely, that desires have the self as their locus (*ātmāśrayatva*).

If it is argued that the locus of desires is indeed scripturally established, because the statement "he does not desire any desire at all" is a prohibition of what has already been attained [by worldly experience], we say no.

"Having become a dreamer endowed with intelligence," [it is said] because of the dependence on another, because of the resulting attainment of having desire as its support, and because of the statement regarding non-attachment.
For indeed, the statement regarding non-attachment is not tenable if there is dependence on desire;
and we have already stated that attachment is desire.

If it is argued that, according to the scriptural text "one who desires the Self," he possesses a desire directed toward the Self, we say no; for that text means that there is no desire for anything distinct [from the Self].
If it is further argued that the Self's being the substratum of desire and so forth is established by the logic of the systems of the Vaiśeṣikas and others, [we reply as follows:]
The logical arguments of the Vaiśeṣika and other systems need not be taken into account because they contradict specific scriptural statements such as "it does not abide in the heart";
for when there is a contradiction with scripture, those arguments are admitted to be mere fallacies,
and furthermore, they subvert the self-luminosity [of the Self].

Furthermore, since desires and the like in a dream have as their object the pure seer alone, the self-luminosity of the Self is established; and if that were subverted, the well-established [nature] would be contradicted.
Moreover, if they were inherent in the Self, their being objects of vision would be untenable, just like a specific quality residing in the eye.
For the object of vision is necessarily distinct from the seer; thus, the self-luminosity of the seer is established.
That [position] would be subverted if one were to postulate that [the Self] is the substratum of desire and so forth; furthermore, it would contradict the meaning of the entire scripture.
If one were to postulate even a single aspect of the Supreme [Self] as the substratum of desire and so forth, the entire body of scriptural teachings would be rendered inconsistent.
And we have explained this in detail in the fourth [chapter].

For with great effort, the proponents of other systems must refute those selves who are imagined to have desire and so forth as their basis, in order to establish the meaning of the teaching regarding oneness with the Supreme Self; yet, if such an imagination were carried out again, the very purpose of the teaching would be subverted.

The Vaiśeṣikas and Naiyāyikas, who postulate that the self possesses qualities subject to its own will, are not to be respected because they contradict the meaning of the Upaniṣadic scriptures. 4.3.22.
Indeed, when one does not see that [Self], it is because, though seeing,
one does not see it; for there is no loss of the seer’s power of seeing, because of its imperishability.
But there is no second thing, other than that and distinct from it, which he might see.

It has been stated that because of the unity [of the two], as in the case of a man and a woman, one does not see; and it has also been stated that he is "self-luminous" (*svayañjyotiḥ*). This self-luminosity consists in having consciousness as one's essential nature (*caitanyātmasvabhāvatā*).
For if the self were of the nature of consciousness, like the heat of fire and so forth, how could it abandon its own nature even while remaining one;
and if it does not abandon it, why does it not perceive here in deep sleep?
It is a contradiction to say that consciousness is the very nature of the self and yet it does not know.
Neither of these two [statements] is contradictory; both are indeed logically consistent.
How so? That which one does not see while in deep sleep—that very thing one sees there; seeing indeed, one does not see.
Regarding that which you think one does not see while in deep sleep, you should not grasp it in that way.
Why?
Because one indeed sees there;
for we know that in deep sleep one does not see even the breath, since neither the eye nor the mind is active as an instrument of seeing.
For when the faculties of seeing, hearing, and so forth are active, there arises the conventional expression "he sees" or "he hears. Yet we do not perceive the instruments themselves as seeing;
therefore, this [self] does not see at all.
Indeed not;
rather, one becomes [an enlightened one] while seeing itself.
How so?
For there is no loss—that is, no destruction—of that vision which belongs to the seer who is the agent of seeing;
it does not exist [as such].
For it is like the heat of fire.
Is this not a contradiction that is being asserted—that the vision of the seer is not destroyed, yet it is impossible to say so?
Would it not follow from the statement "it is not destroyed" that it is indestructible? No;
for [the scripture] is merely indicative.
For the destruction of that which is produced, being established by logical necessity, cannot be prevented even by a hundred statements;
this is because a statement is merely indicative (jñāpaka).
Indeed, destruction is established by logical necessity.
Even with a hundred statements, that which has been produced cannot be prevented [from occurring],
because a statement merely makes known an object as it is attained.
This is not a fault.
Because perception is possible in the same way as the sun and other luminaries illuminate.
Just as the sun and others, being of the very nature of eternal light, illuminate by means of their own inherent and eternal light;
for it is not said that those whose essence is non-luminous illuminate by producing light.
Rather, it is by its very nature as eternal luminosity;
likewise, this self is called a "seer" because of its vision, which is eternal and whose nature is never lost.
In that case, however, the status of being a seer is merely figurative.

It is precisely thus that its status as the primary seer is established. For if the self’s nature as a seer were observed to be otherwise [i.e., produced], then this quality of being a seer would be secondary;
however, there is no other mode of seeing for the self than this. Thus, it is only in this way that its primary status as a seer is logically consistent, and not otherwise.

Just as the luminosity of the sun and other such bodies is by their very nature eternal and unproduced, and that alone constitutes their primary luminosity because no other form of luminosity is possible for them.
Therefore, the vision of the seer is not destroyed; thus, there is not even a scent of contradiction.

If it is argued that the use of a word ending in the suffix *tṛc* is observed only in reference to an agent of a non-eternal action—as in "the cutter," "the breaker," or "the goer"—and that the same applies here to the word "seer" (*draṣṭṛ*), we say no, because [the word] is also seen used in the sense of "one who illuminates."

If it is argued that [the self] may exist in the case of illuminators because they cannot otherwise be explained, but not in the case of the self, we say no; for scripture declares that "vision is never lost.
If it is argued that this is not so because we observe the experience of "I see" and "I do not see," we say no.
Because it depends on the specific functioning of the instruments [of perception],
and because the vision of the self is seen to be undiminished even in dreams by those whose eyes have been plucked out;
therefore, the vision of the self is indeed of an undiminished nature.
In deep sleep, one continues to see by means of that very vision which is undeluded and whose nature is self-luminous;
how then can it be said that "one does not see"? It is replied: [as follows].
But that does not exist. What is it? A second thing existing as an object. What remains?

Then, whatever the seer might have seen as divided by way of "otherness from other," whatever he might have perceived— that internal organ, the eye, and the form which were the causes for perceiving those specific distinctions— had been presented as distinct due to ignorance; at this time, they become one,
because of the embrace of the Self with the Supreme.
For an observer who is limited, the instruments exist as distinct entities for the purpose of perceiving specific objects;
but this [Self], being completely embraced in its own totality by its own supreme conscious Self— just as a man is embraced by his beloved—
does not have instruments and objects established as separate from it.
In the absence of that [self], there is no perception of particularity;
for that [perception] is produced by instruments and so forth, not produced by the self,
yet it appears as if produced by the self.
Therefore, this delusion regarding the self is produced by that [ignorance], and the vision of the self is thereby obscured. //4.3.23//
Indeed, when one does not smell that [object], it is because, though smelling, one does not smell it;
for there is no loss of the smeller's power of smelling, because of its imperishability.
But there is no second thing, other than and distinct from that, which one could smell.
Indeed, that which one does not taste, one does not taste because one is indeed tasting;
for there is no cessation of the act of tasting on the part of the taster, because of his imperishability.
Yet, there is nothing second to him, nothing else distinct from him, that he might taste.
Indeed, that which one does not speak while speaking, one does not speak;
for there is no loss of the speaker's capacity to speak, because it is imperishable.
But there is no second thing existing apart from him, distinct from him, which he might speak.
Indeed, that which he does not hear, he does not hear even while hearing;
for there is no loss of the hearing power of the hearer, because it is imperishable.
But there is no second thing existing apart from him, distinct from him, which he might hear.
Indeed, that which one does not think, even while thinking, one does not think;
for there is no loss of the thinker’s power of thought, because it is indestructible.
But there is no second thing, other than that and distinct from it, which one might think.
Indeed, that which one does not touch while touching it,
for there is no destruction of the toucher’s power of touching because of its imperishability;
yet there is no second thing existing apart from it, distinct from it, which it might touch.
That which he does not perceive, he indeed perceives even while not perceiving;
for there is no loss of the perceiver’s power of perception, because it is indestructible.
But there is no second thing, other than and distinct from him, that he might perceive. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.30)
The rest is the same. Indeed, when he does not smell that, indeed, when he does not taste that—
Indeed, that which he does not speak there,
that which he does not hear there,
and that which he thinks there— [all that is Brahman].
"Indeed, that which it does not touch;

indeed, that which it does not perceive"—this separate mention [of *manas*] is because, although *manana* (the function of the mind) and *vijñāna* (cognition) possess the eye and other organs as their auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), they nonetheless possess an operation upon objects of the past, future, and present independently of the eyes and so forth. Thus, they are mentioned separately.

Furthermore, is there a difference in properties among vision and the other faculties—just as heat, illumination, and combustion are distinct properties of fire—or is it that the diversity of properties belongs to a single, undivided property, caused by external limiting conditions (*upādhi*)?
On this point, some explain:

the unity and plurality of the self-substance (*ātmavastu*) exist by its very nature, just as in the case of a cow, where its unity as the substance "cow" and its plurality [as individual cows] are both inferable.

Because non-deviation is observed everywhere, one might think that just as with those [faculties], the self likewise possesses a mutual plurality among seeing and the other functions, while having unity with the self; however, this is not so, because the passage is intended for another purpose.
For this statement beginning with "That which indeed... does not have the aim of demonstrating the distinctions between the dharmas such as seeing and the rest.
What then?

If the light of the self is consciousness, why does it not know in deep sleep? Since this doubt arises—that surely, therefore, the light of the self is not consciousness—the following passage beginning with "That which indeed... is commenced to refute it;
for that natural light of the self as consciousness, which was observed during the waking and dreaming states through various limiting adjuncts such as the eyes and so forth—

Deep sleep, which has entered into the conventional usage of designations such as "seeing" and so forth, is said to exist merely by restating its state as it is found; for, when the activity of the distinctions of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) has ceased, it is not manifested and thus its nature is unperceived, yet it appears as if divided by those very adjuncts.
In that state, the conceptualization of distinct attributes such as "seeing" arises from a lack of understanding regarding the intended meaning.
Because it is a single solid mass of the flavor of consciousness, like a solid block of salt;
because it would contradict such scriptural passages as "Consciousness and bliss," "Truth, knowledge," and "Brahman is consciousness";
and because of the application of these very words [to Brahman].

Furthermore, worldly linguistic usage— such as "one cognizes form with the eye," "one cognizes sound with the ear," and "one cognizes the taste of food with the tongue"— everywhere shows that those things denoted by words such as "vision" (dṛṣṭi) and so forth are indeed expressible by the word "consciousness" (vijñāna).
And linguistic usage is a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa).
And because this is supported by an illustrative example:

for just as in the world, a crystal—which possesses a transparent nature—assumes the forms of green, blue, red, and so forth, solely due to its conjunction with various limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as those objects;

likewise, through its conjunction with the various limiting adjuncts of the eyes and other organs, the differentiation of powers such as seeing and so forth is perceived in the light of the Self (ātman-jyotis), whose very nature is a mass of consciousness (prajñāna-ghana).

Because the mass of consciousness (prajñānaghana) possesses a nature of transparency like that of a clear crystal, and because it is self-luminous, a distinction of powers is perceived therein. Just as the light of the sun, when joined with various objects of illumination, appears indistinguishable from the distinctions of green, blue, yellow, red, and so forth, yet remains devoid of those forms; so too is this case.
And likewise, the eyes and other senses, which illuminate the entire world, take on its form;
as it has been said: "By this light of his own, he sets," and so forth.
Furthermore, it is not possible to conceive of a multiplicity of natures within that which is partless.
Because there is an absence of examples;

furthermore, whatever differentiation of properties such as omnipresence is imagined for space, and the possession of various qualities such as odor and taste for atoms and so forth, that too, when examined, is caused solely by external conditions (*paropādhi*).
To begin with, so-called "all-pervasiveness" is not an inherent property of space.

Rather, the conventional designation of "all-pervasive" is based on its existence everywhere in its own form by virtue of depending upon all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); space itself, however, is neither going nor not-going anywhere inherently.
For "going" is defined as the cause of conjunction with another location for that which is situated in one location.
Furthermore, that action does not occur in the absence of differentiation;
likewise, there are no distinct properties in space,
nor are there any in atoms and so forth.

That which is called an atom (*paramāṇu*) is the most subtle constituent part of dense earth consisting of odor; it is essentially of the nature of odor alone, and it is impossible to imagine that it possesses foul odor.

If it is argued that it might possess taste and other qualities, this is not so, because even those would be caused by contact with water and the other elements. Therefore, there is no illustrative example for a partless entity possessing multiple attributes.

Thus, by this [argument], the postulation of distinct modifications of the various powers such as vision and so forth, corresponding to the distinct categories of the eye, visible form, and so on, is applied to the Supreme Self. //4.3.24–30//
For where there is, as it were, something other [than the Self], there one might see another, one might smell another, one might taste another,
one might speak to another, one might hear another, one might think of another, one might touch another, or one might perceive another.
One should understand this. *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 4.3.31.
It has been stated that, as in the states of waking and dreaming, whatever one perceives does not exist as a second thing distinct from oneself;
therefore, in deep sleep, one does not perceive any particularity. Now, if this indeed is his very nature, what is the cause for his perception of particulars through the abandonment of that nature?
Now, if it is argued that specific cognition itself is its very nature, why does it not cognize the particularity?
It is said: listen.
In whatever state—whether in the waking state or in a dream—something else, as if it were another object distinct from the Self, is presented by ignorance (avidyā).

In that state, because of that [delusion] presented by ignorance, one imagines oneself as if distinct from another; thus, while there is no real self distinct from the object, and no object distinct from the self, one might see or perceive another as distinct.
And this has been demonstrated in the case of a dream, where it is said, "as if they were killing, as if they were conquering," through direct perception.
Likewise, one might smell, taste, speak, hear, think, touch, or cognize another [object]. (4.3.31)
He becomes one with water, the sole seer, without a second. This, O Emperor, is the world of Brahman.
Thus did Yājñavalkya instruct him:
"This is his supreme goal;
this is his supreme attainment."
This is his highest world;
this is his supreme bliss.
All other beings subsist on a mere fraction of this very bliss.

But where that ignorance which presents other objects is stilled in deep sleep, there is no object distinct [from the Self] differentiated by ignorance; therefore, who could see whom, or smell, or know?

Thus, embraced by his own wise Self whose nature is self-luminous, he is unified, serene, with all desires fulfilled, desiring only the Self, become as pure as water, like water itself, being one because of the absence of a second.

For, due to the absence of a second thing, there is no ignorance. This is the immortal, the fearless; this is the world of Brahman—Brahman itself is the world, hence "the world of Brahman. At this time, when the distinctions of the limiting adjuncts of the body and organs have ceased, he exists in his own self-luminosity, with all connections stilled.
"O Emperor," thus indeed did Yājñavalkya instruct Janaka; "You have been praised, O Yājñavalkya"—this is the statement of the Śruti.
And how did he instruct him? [He said:
"This is the supreme goal of this one consisting of consciousness."

Those other states of existence, characterized by the assumption of a body, which extend from Brahmā down to a blade of grass and are imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*), are therefore inferior because they fall within the domain of ignorance.

This state, however, is the supreme and most excellent among all states such as godhood—which are accomplished through ritual action and knowledge—and it is the totality of the Self wherein one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and cognizes nothing else; this alone is the supreme attainment among all attainments.
This is the supreme among manifestations because it is innate; for all other prosperities are indeed produced.
Likewise, this is his supreme world;
those other worlds which depend upon the fruits of karma are inferior to this one.
But this [Self] is not measured by any action, because it is innate; this is its supreme world. Likewise, this is its supreme bliss.
Compared to those other varieties of bliss produced by the connection between the sense objects and the senses, this is its supreme bliss, because of its eternity.

"Whatever is plenitude (bhūman), that is bliss," according to another scriptural passage. In that state where one sees nothing else and knows nothing else—compared to which this is his supreme bliss, because of its eternity; "whatever is plenitude, that is bliss," according to another scriptural passage.

Where one sees something else, understands something else—that is the limited, mortal, secondary, and insubstantial realm. But this [state] is the opposite of that. This is his supreme bliss. Other beings subsist on a mere fraction, a tiny portion, of this very bliss—a portion presented by ignorance, to be experienced at the time of contact between the sense organs and their objects.

What are those [objects] which, having their own nature differentiated from that very bliss through ignorance, are imagined as being other than Brahman, and upon which living beings depend by means of the contact between the sense objects and the senses, thereby becoming manifest? 4.3.32.

Now, that person among men who is successful and prosperous, who is the lord of others, and who is most abundantly endowed with all human enjoyments— that is the supreme bliss of men. Now, a hundredfold the bliss of men is equal to one bliss of the ancestors who have won the world.
Now, a hundredfold the joys of the ancestors who have conquered the worlds constitute one joy of the world of the Gandharvas.
Now, a hundredfold the joys of the world of the Gandharvas constitute one joy of the ritual deities (*karmadeva*), those who attain godhood through their ritual actions.
Now, a hundredfold the joys of the ritual deities constitute one joy of the birth-deities (*ājānadeva*).

And the bliss of one who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), free from evil (*avṛjin*), and not overcome by desire—this is equal to the hundredfold bliss of the gods by birth (*ājānadeva*). This is one measure of the bliss in the world of Prajāpati; and it is the same for one who is learned in the Vedas, free from evil, and not overcome by desire.
Now, whatever hundredfold joys there are in the world of Prajāpati, that is but one joy in the world of Brahman—
of one who is learned in the Vedas, free from blemish, and untouched by desire. And this indeed is the supreme joy.
"This, O Emperor, is the world of Brahman," said Yājñavalkya.
"Therefore, I give a thousand [cows] to your lordship."
"Tell me further for the sake of liberation.
At this, Yājñavalkya became afraid, thinking: "This wise king has cornered me on all sides. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.33)

Desiring to lead one to the Supreme Bliss— the possessor of the parts— by means of its constituent portions of bliss (*ānanda-mātrā*), which are subsisted upon by all beings from Brahmā down to humans, [the text] says, as if [pointing out] a salt mountain by means of fragments of rock-salt:
"He who among men is *rāddhaḥ*— meaning one who is perfected, complete, and possessed of all his limbs."

He becomes prosperous, endowed with all the requisites for enjoyment. Furthermore, he is the sovereign and independent lord of others of his own kind—not a mere regional ruler (māṇḍalika), but one over all human beings.
This is stated to exclude divine requisites for enjoyment; rather, among those who are already endowed with whatever human requisites for enjoyment exist, he is preeminent.
He who is accomplished is most accomplished; that is the supreme bliss of human beings.

In this regard, because bliss is taught as non-different from the blissful one, it is not a separate entity. It has been stated by the passage beginning with "where there is, as it were, something else," that this measure of supreme bliss has issued forth in the form of the object and the subject.
Therefore, this designation as "supreme bliss" (paramānanda) is appropriate as a description of non-duality.
A king such as Yudhiṣṭhira and others serves as the illustrative example here.

Beginning with human bliss as the first term, it leads upward through a sequence of hundredfold increases until it reaches supreme bliss, wherein all differentiation ceases; that [state] it causes one to realize.
Here, this Ānanda increases by a hundredfold progression until it reaches its ultimate limit;

where the differentiation of calculation ceases due to the absence of seeing, hearing, and reflecting upon anything else—it is with the intention of describing that Supreme Bliss (paramānanda) that he says:
"Now, whatever constitutes a hundred such varieties of Ānanda among humans, that is one [unit] of the ancestors (pitṛs)."
Their qualification is "those who have conquered the world" (*jitaloka*).

Having gratified the ancestors through meritorious acts such as faith (*śraddhā*) and so forth, those for whom the world has been won by that very act are the "conquerors of the world," the ancestors; for those ancestors, one unit of bliss occurs whose measure is a hundredfold the human bliss.
That [bliss], multiplied a hundredfold, becomes one bliss in the world of the Gandharvas;
and that, multiplied a hundredfold, is one bliss of the *karmadevas*.
Those who attain the state of divinity through the performance of Vedic rituals such as the *agnihotra* are the *karmadevas*.
In the same way, there is one bliss for the Ājānadevas.
Those gods who are born by their very origin (*utpatti*) are the Ājānadevas.
And he who is a *śrotriya*—one who has studied the Vedas—and is an *avaḍajina*, meaning one devoid of *vṛjina* (evil or sin), that is to say, one who acts according to what has been taught.

One who is not struck by desire and is free from thirst—the *ājānadeva* (born as a god)—is one for whom all sense-objects have been transcended. For such a person, the word "and" (*ca*) implies that the bliss is equal to that of the *ājānadevas*. Furthermore, when that measure of bliss is multiplied a hundredfold, it constitutes a single unit of bliss in the world of Prajāpati, which resides within the body of Virāj.
Likewise, one who possesses that knowledge, is a *śrotriya* (learned in the Vedas), has studied the Veda, and is free from crookedness, and so forth, as described previously.
"One bliss in the world of Brahmā, within the self of Hiraṇyagarbha, has a magnitude increased a hundredfold compared to that"—
and so on, as before.
Beyond this, calculation ceases.
This is the supreme bliss to which [the self] is joined;
and compared to this supreme bliss, the joys of the world of Brahmā and other realms are but mere droplets, like drops in the ocean.

Thus, the joys that increase a hundredfold at each successive stage reach a state of unity therein. This very thing, which is directly perceived by one learned in the Vedas, is this supreme bliss characterized by utter serenity; for in that state, one sees nothing else.
One hears nothing else;
moreover, because it is abundance (bhūman), it is immortal.
Others are the opposite of that.
And here, although being learned in the Vedas (*śrotriyatva*) and being free from evil (*avṛjinatva*) are equal [in all cases],
the distinction caused by being unaffected by desire (*akāmahatatva*) is the cause for the hundredfold increase in bliss.

In this context, these means— being learned in the Vedas, being free from evil, and being unaffected by desire— are stated as the requirements for the attainment of each respective bliss, just as the *agnihotra* and other rituals are required for the gods to attain their godhood.

In that context, the two qualities characterized by being learned in the Vedas (*śrotriyatva*) and being free from crookedness (*avṛjinatva*) are common even to the lower stages; therefore, they are not accepted as the means for attaining the higher bliss.

However, it is understood that freedom from being overcome by desire (*akāmahatatva*)—given that it arises through varying degrees of dispassion—is the means for attaining the bliss of each successive stage.
This very supreme bliss has been realized as a matter of direct perception by the learned seeker who is free from thirst.

And so says Vedavyāsa: “Whatever sensual pleasure there is in the world, and whatever great divine pleasure there is—these are not worth even a sixteenth part of the bliss that comes from the destruction of craving.”
"Thus," said Yājñavalkya, "this, O Emperor, is the world of Brahman. "Instructed by you in this way, I give you a thousand cows," [the King replied].
"Speak further for the sake of liberation alone"—this has already been explained.
In this passage, "for liberation," Yājñavalkya was afraid;
the Śruti states the cause of Yājñavalkya’s fear:

it was not because of a lack of capacity for speech or due to ignorance that he was afraid, but rather because the wise king had hemmed him in—had surrounded and obstructed him—from all [possible] conclusions to his questions.

The meaning is that he has acted [in this way]. The cause of my fear is this: because of his intelligence, he repeatedly questions me by taking up only portions of the "questions on desire" (kāmapraśna) which I have determined to be in the form of questions for the sake of liberation. All of this is my own [cause for fear].
He seeks to acquire consciousness under the pretext of a question concerning desire. //4,3.33//

Having enjoyed himself and wandered about in that state of dream, and having seen both good and evil, he hastens back again according to the rule, according to his source, toward the state of waking. Herein, the Self consisting of consciousness, who is self-luminous, has been demonstrated in the state of dream.
Through the movement between the end of sleep and the end of waking, the soul's distinction from the body and its organs is demonstrated;
likewise, its separation from desire and action due to its state of non-attachment is shown by the analogy of the great fish.
Furthermore, the effect of ignorance is demonstrated by the passage beginning with "even while dreaming," and so forth.
By implication, the true nature of ignorance has been refuted as consisting in the superimposition of what is not its own attribute and as being a non-self-attribute.
Likewise, the effect of knowledge has been demonstrated as the state of being the Self of all; for even while dreaming, one thinks "I am everything," and that is his highest world.

And therein, this state of being the Self of all is his very nature; thus it is made known that in deep sleep, his form—which transcends all connection with the attributes of transmigratory existence such as ignorance, desire, and action—is directly perceived.
This Self is self-luminous; this is supreme bliss.
This is the object of knowledge.
It is that supreme state of serene composure and the ultimate limit of happiness—thus it has been explained by the concluding portion of the text.
And all of this—the entirety of the subject matter concerning liberation—is illustrative of the subject matter of liberation and of bondage.

These two, liberation and bondage, have been explained along with their causes and their conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) as the effects of knowledge and ignorance; since all of that is merely illustrative, you must now speak regarding liberation and bondage as they pertain to the actual subject matter of desire, serving as the corresponding points of illustration.

When Janaka questioned him further, saying, "Speak, therefore, concerning liberation beyond this," it was stated therein that the single Self, being self-luminous, moves through the states of dreaming and waking without attachment, like a great fish. And just as that [Self], discarding and assuming forms consisting of death— the effects and instruments— moves through the states of dreaming and waking like a great fish, so too does it move through birth and death by means of those very same [forms].
He is joined with and separated from forms of death;
he wanders through both worlds—thus "wandering" is indicated by way of an illustration for the wandering between the states of waking and dreaming.

Therefore, since that wandering here must be described in detail along with its causes, this [section] is commenced for that purpose. And therein, this Self is made to enter from the state of waking into the state of dream.
Therefore, the state of deep sleep (*saṃprasāda*) is included within the realm of liberation (*mokṣa*).

Having been displaced from that, the conventional experience of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra-vyavahāra*) must be demonstrated at the end of the waking state; this is the connection [of the subsequent passage] with it.

Indeed, he who was serene through the sequence of waking and dreaming, having remained in that serenity and then slightly fallen from it, enters again into the waking state alone—having enjoyed and moved about at the end of the dream, and so forth, as previously described.

Just as a well-balanced cart proceeds with a creaking sound, even so this bodily self, mounted by the conscious self (prājña-ātman), proceeds with a creaking sound when he becomes one who breathes upward. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.35.
From this point onward, his transmigratory existence is described.
Just as this self has come from the state of dream to the state of waking, so too will he pass from this body to another body; with this in mind, the text provides an illustration here:

"In that regard, just as in the world a cart (*anaḥ*) is well-secured—meaning very firmly fastened—and is fully equipped with its household utensils, such as mortars, pestles, winnowing baskets, and cooking pots, as well as with food and other supplies."
The meaning is that it is overcome by the burden of the [karmic] accumulations (*saṃbhāra*).
Thus, being overcome by the burden, it emits a sound while moving along, just as it would when controlled by a cart-driver;
in this very way, the aforementioned simile applies to this body, which is "bodily" (*śārīra*) because it exists within the physical frame.
Who is this?
It is the self (ātman) which has the subtle body (liṅga) as its limiting adjunct;

it is that which, through birth and death—characterized respectively by association with and separation from evil—wanders between this world and the next, as well as between the states of dreaming and waking.

Following his departure, the departure of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and the other faculties occurs; he is mounted upon, presided over, and illuminated by the supreme Self, which is the wise one whose nature is self-luminous.
And so it has been said: "By this very light as his own, he sits and moves about";
likewise, "he goes forth emitting [sounds]."

In that state, when the subtle body (*liṅga*), which consists primarily of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and is illuminated by the light of the conscious Self (*caitanyātma-jyotis*), moves, the Self, having that as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), also appears to move.
Thus says another Śruti passage beginning with “In whom [do I rest]? and ending with “as if meditating.
For this very reason it is said: “mounted upon the wise Self (*prājña ātman*)."
Otherwise, being unified with the intellect (*prājña*), how could it move while emitting sounds like a cart?

Therefore, the self, conditioned by the subtle body (*liṅga-upādhi*), being afflicted by the sensation of pain as its vital points (*marman*) are being cut away, moves—that is, goes—while uttering sound. At what time does this occur?
It is said: when this happens.
The word "etad" (this) is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*).

"Breathing upwards" (*ūrdhvocchvāsī*) means that state in which his upward breathing occurs. Even though this is already being observed, it is restated for the sake of generating dispassion (*vairāgya*): "Alas, this saṃsāra is indeed so painful that at the time of departure [from the body]..."

When the vital points (*marmans*) are being cut, there occurs a loss of mindfulness for a person afflicted by painful sensations, and an incapacity to engage in the practice that accomplishes the goals of human life because the mind has been brought under the control of others.

Therefore, the Scripture (*śruti*), out of compassion, says: "One should remain vigilant in the performance of duties that accomplish the goals of human life precisely as long as this state has not arrived. (4.3.35)
When this [body] reaches its state of extreme attenuation— whether through old age or by some affliction— and it attains that attenuation,
then it is like a mango, a fig, or a wood-apple fruit being released from its stalk.
In the very same way, this person, having been completely released from these limbs, hastens back again according to the rule and according to the source, for the sake of vital breath alone.

Regarding this, it is explained as follows: at what time, for what cause, in what manner, or for what purpose does this upward breathing of his occur? This very natural body, consisting of a mass with a head, hands, and so forth, at which time (*yatra*)—meaning at which time—it goes to (*nyeti*), that is, attains (*nigacchati*), this state of minuteness (*aṇimānam*), the condition of being minute (*aṇorbhāvam*), meaning smallness or leanness.

For what reason? Either because of old age, he himself becomes worn out like a fruit ripened by time and undergoes emaciation; or because of affliction—*upatapan* meaning fever and other diseases—he is afflicted by them. Being tormented by disease, due to a disturbed digestive fire (*viṣamāgni*), he does not digest the food he has eaten; consequently, the physical mass (*piṇḍa*), not being nourished by the essence of food (*annarasa*), falls into a state of emaciation. This is what is meant by "or because of affliction."
He undergoes attenuation.
When he has reached extreme emaciation due to the causes of old age and so forth, he becomes one whose breath flows upward.
When his breath flows upward, then, like a cart heavily laden with a load, he departs while emitting [a sound].

These misfortunes—the occurrence of old age, affliction by disease and the like, and the onset of emaciation—are inevitable for one who possesses a body; thus, this is stated for the sake of generating detachment (*vairāgya*). When he departs, casting it off, how does he release the body? To illustrate this, an analogy is given: "In that regard, whether it be a mango fruit, or an udumbara fruit, or a pippala fruit.
The employment of various and diverse examples is intended to demonstrate that death has no fixed cause.
For the signs of death are indeed indefinite and innumerable;
this too is solely for the sake of dispassion.
Since he possesses many signs of death, he is therefore always in the jaws of death.

That by which one is bound together with the stalk is the binding cause, namely the sap; or, that in which one is bound is called the "binding," namely the stalk itself. From that sap or from that stalk as the binding, one is liberated. In this very same way, this person—the subtle body (liṅga-ātman), whose limiting adjunct is the subtle body—is completely and utterly liberated from these limbs, that is, from the members of the body such as the eyes and so forth, which have various causes such as wind and the like.

It is not as when going into deep sleep, where one is protected by the vital breath (*prāṇa*); rather, having withdrawn [the senses] along with the wind (*vāyu*), it proceeds again according to its course. Because of the word "again," it implies that previously this self has also gone repeatedly from body to another body, just as one goes again from the state of dreaming to the waking state; thus, "again according to its course" means returning.
The meaning is "according to how it came.
It rushes toward each respective womb (*yoni*)—that is, toward each individual womb—in accordance with the power of its past actions (*karman*), sacred learning (*śruta*), and so forth.
For what purpose?
The meaning is "for the sake of the vital breath itself" and "for the sake of the arrangement of the vital breaths.
Since it is only when possessed of the vital breath that one goes, the qualification "for the sake of the vital breath" would otherwise be redundant;
for movement from one body to another is indeed for the sake of the arrangement of the vital breaths.
For indeed, the accomplishment of his purpose regarding the experience of the fruits of karma does not occur by the mere existence of the vital breaths;
therefore, it is appropriate to include the qualification "for the distribution of the vital breaths" in order to achieve that specific purpose. 4.3.36.

Just as when a king is approaching, fierce wardens, charioteers, and village headmen prepare for him with food, drinks, and lodgings, saying, "He is coming! He is arriving!"—even so, all beings prepare for one who knows this, saying, "Brahman is coming! Brahman is arriving!"*BrhUp_4,3.37*
In that state, as he departs having abandoned this body, there is no capacity in him to take up another body,
because of his separation from the body and the senses.
Nor are there any others, standing in the place of servants, who— like subjects for a king— prepare another body and wait for him.
Now, this being so, how does he take up another body?

It is said: for this entire world has been taken up as a means for experiencing the fruits of one's own karma, and he, having set out for the experience of the fruits of his own karma, desires to pass from this body to another body; therefore, the entire world is impelled by his own karma.
Having rendered the means of experience unfit for the enjoyment of the fruits of those actions, it simply awaits [the time of birth],
according to the Vedic revelation: "A person is born into a world already made," just as one desiring to pass from sleep into the waking state.

To explain how this is so, a world-renowned analogy is stated: In that regard, when a king who has been consecrated to the kingdom is approaching his own realm, the *ugras*—a specific class of people—or the *pratyenasaḥ*, those of cruel deeds appointed to punish transgressors (*pratyenaḥ*), that is, those engaged in punishing thieves and the like, as well as the *sūtas* and *grāmaṇyas*, the leaders of villages; they [all go out to meet him].
Having already learned of the king's arrival, they prepare with various kinds of food—eatables and chewables—as well as drinks such as wine, and dwellings such as palaces;
and with these things already completed, they wait expectantly, saying, "The king is coming! He is arriving!
Just as it is in this illustration, so too is it for one who knows thus—that is, for the transmigrating being who understands the fruit of action.
For the fruit of action (*karmaphala*) is the subject at hand, and that very thing is referred to by the word "thus" (*evaṃ*).

All beings—the makers of bodies and the sustainers of the instruments (the senses), such as the sun and so forth—are impelled by those actions and await [the soul] with the very means for experiencing the fruits of the actions already performed.
The meaning is that they wait, thinking, "This Brahman, who is both the enjoyer and the agent, is coming to us," and "Thus he is approaching. //4.3.37//
Just as when a king is about to depart on a journey, his fierce executioners, his charioteers, and the village headmen assemble around him,
even so at the time of death all the vital breaths (prāṇas) assemble around this self (ātman).
At which point he becomes one whose breath moves only upward.
Who are those that go along with him as he desires to depart?
And do those who do go there proceed impelled by his actions, or do they go of their own accord by the force of his karma, being the very elements that construct the body for the next world?
To this, the following illustration is given: "Just as when a king desires to set out on a journey (prayiyāsantam), fierce [soldiers]..."

Just as the minor officials, the charioteers, and the village headmen come together toward him with a unified purpose, coming toward him in a state of oneness even without being commanded by the king— merely through their knowledge of his desire to depart— so too, at the time of the end, at the time of death, all the vital breaths, beginning with speech, come together toward this self, the enjoyer.
It has been explained that "therein one becomes breathless after that. //4.3.38//
Thus ends the third Brāhmaṇa of the fourth Adhyāya in the Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya.
When this self, having fallen into weakness, as it were, enters into a state of confusion,
then these vital breaths gather around it.
Gathering these elements of light, he descends into the heart itself.
When this person within the eye turns away,
then one becomes unaware of forms.
In this context of the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* (4.4.1), where the description of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) has been introduced,
it was stated: "When this person is completely liberated from these limbs."

It is stated that the liberation from that [bondage], at what time and by what means, must be described in detail along with the process of transmigration: this very self (*ātman*) under discussion, at whatever time, having entered into or reached weakness—the state of being weak—it is maintained that the weakness of the body is itself the weakness of the self; thus it is said, "having entered into weakness."
For it does not, by its own nature, undergo a state of weakness because it is formless (*amūrta*).
Likewise, delusion (*saṃmoha*)—delusion being a state of confusion, which is the absence of discernment—it enters as if into a state of confusion; that is, it attains it.
Yet, for it, there exists neither delusion nor non-delusion by its own nature.
Because its essential nature is the light of eternal consciousness,
it is by that very fact said to "go as if into delusion.
For at the time of departure, worldly people perceive a state of agitation in the self, caused by the withdrawal of the instruments (the senses).
And thus people say, "He is utterly deluded; he is completely bewildered.
Alternatively, the word *iva* (as if) should be applied to both cases:
"he goes as it were into weakness; he goes as it were into delusion."
Because there is no difference in both cases regarding the fact that they are caused by external adjuncts (*upādhi*),
and because of the mention of a common agent;
for at this time, when these vital breaths (*prāṇa*), such as speech and the rest, completely merge into this self (*ātman*), then there occurs the dissolution of the limbs of this embodied self.
How, then, is there liberation, or in what manner does he approach the Self?

It is said: that Self takes up these "measures of light" (*tejomātrāḥ*)—the measures of light mean the components of light; the sense is that the instruments such as the eyes are so called because they illuminate form and other objects.
Taking these up means taking them up correctly, without any residue, and facing toward [the Self].
"Taking up and withdrawing"— this qualification is made in relation to that dream;
however, in a dream there is no thorough grasping (*samādāna*) without leaving a trace,
but there is merely taking up (*ādāna*).

From such scriptural passages as, "Speech is taken away, the eye is taken away," "Having taken a measure of this all-encompassing world," and "Having taken the pure [essence]," [the soul] follows after—
that is, approaches— the heart which is shaped like a lotus.
The meaning is that its consciousness becomes manifest within the heart.
When the distractions of the intellect and so forth are withdrawn, there is indeed no movement of it from its own nature, nor any modification such as the withdrawal of distraction and so on;
for it has been said, "It meditates, as it were; it moves, as it were."
For all modifications are superimposed upon that [Self] only by means of limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the intellect (buddhi).

When, then, does it attain its state of pure light? It is said: when this person in the eye—the Cākṣuṣa Puruṣa, who is a portion of the Sun—is impelled by the karma of the enjoyer and remains performing the service of the eye for as long as the body is maintained.
At the time of death, however, the eye abandons its support and attains its own self, which is the sun.
This has been stated: "When this person has died, speech merges into fire, breath into wind, and the eye into the sun," and so forth.
Later, at the time of taking up a new body, they will again take refuge [in those elements].
Likewise, it occurs for one who is about to sleep and for one who is waking up.
This refers to the person who consists of sight; at what time—that is, at which moment—he turns away, meaning he turns his face completely away from objects.

Then, at this time, he becomes unaware of forms; the dying person no longer perceives form. At that time, this self begins to gather the subtle elements of light belonging to the eye and the other senses, just as it does during the time of sleep. 4.4.1.
"He becomes unified; he does not see," they say.
"He becomes unified; he does not smell," they say.
"It becomes unified and does not taste," they say.
"It becomes unified and does not speak," they say.
"It becomes unified and does not hear," they say.
"They say he becomes one and does not think; they say he becomes one and does not touch;
they say he becomes one and does not cognize."
The tip of this very heart flashes forth;
by that flash of light, this self departs,
either through the eye, or through the crown of the head, or through other parts of the body.
As he departs, the vital breath (prāṇa) departs after him;
as the vital breath departs, all the vital functions (prāṇas) depart after it.
He becomes endowed with consciousness.
He enters into consciousness itself;
knowledge, action, and his prior experience follow after him.
The collection of organs becomes unified with its own subtle body (liṅga-ātman).
At that very time, those standing nearby say, "He does not see.
Likewise, upon the withdrawal of the deity of the sense of smell, the organ of smell becomes unified with the subtle body; then they say, "He does not smell."
The rest is the same.
Regarding the tongue, they say that because Soma or Varuṇa is the deity there, one does not taste, with reference to their withdrawal;
likewise, they say one does not speak, does not hear, does not think, does not touch, and does not discern.
Then, the withdrawal of the deities and the unification of the organs within the heart is perceived.

When the organs have been withdrawn into the heart, that which is the internal space within it is described as follows: "Of this very heart under discussion—that is, of the cavity of the heart—the tip," meaning the opening of the channel, the exit-door, "shines forth" at the time of sleep, as in the waking state, by its own light produced from the grasping of the subtle elements of light, and by its own splendor, that is, by the Self alone.

By that light of the Self, by that radiance of the heart's tip, this Self—consisting of consciousness and having the subtle body (liṅga) as its limiting adjunct—goes forth; it departs. Thus, in the Atharvaṇa: "Upon whose departure shall I depart? Upon whose staying shall I stay? He created the vital breath (prāṇa).
And therein, the light of the Self’s consciousness is always most manifest.
For it is through the medium of those limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) that all worldly transactions—characterized by birth, death, going, coming, and so forth—occur in the Self.

Indeed, the twelvefold instrument consisting of the intellect (*buddhi*) and the rest is of that nature; it is the "thread" (*sūtra*), it is the life-force, and it is the inner self of both the moving and the stationary world.
By means of that light—the illumination at the tip of the heart—as he departs, by which path does he go out?
It is said: either from the eye, if there were knowledge or action that serves as the cause for attaining the world of the sun;
or from the crown of the head, if it serves as the cause for attaining the world of Brahmā.
Or from other parts of the body, from the various limbs, according to one's karma and according to what has been heard—
that conscious self (vijñānātman) as it departs, having set out for the next world, with its intention directed toward the next world;
after it, the vital breath (prāṇa), which occupies the position of a sovereign minister like that of a king, departs.
And as that vital breath departs, all the other vital breaths, such as speech and the rest, depart after it.
This description follows the order of importance for the sake of explanation; however, a sequential departure like a caravan is not intended here.

At that time, this self becomes endowed with consciousness—it possesses specific consciousness like in a dream—due to the power of karma and not by its own independence. For if it were endowed with consciousness through its own independence, everyone would have accomplished their purpose.
But that [state] is not actually attained [at that time].
Therefore Vyāsa said: "Always permeated by the being of That.

However, at this time, the entire world becomes possessed of consciousness (*savijñāna*) through the specific cognition consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) residing in a particular modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛttiviśeṣa*), which is manifested by [past] action (*karman*).
And one enters and goes toward that destination as if endowed with consciousness; the meaning is that it is illuminated precisely by specific consciousness.

Therefore, at that time, those who have faith, who seek the next world, and who are heedful, should practice the dharmas of yoga, cultivate analytical discernment, and employ distinguished merit for the sake of autonomy.
The purpose of all the scriptures should be diligently applied to the cessation of misconduct;
for at that time [of death], nothing can be accomplished,
since one who is being led away by karma lacks independence.
It has been said: "One becomes virtuous by virtuous action and sinful by sinful action.
Indeed, it is for the purpose of prescribing the means to pacify this evil that all the Upaniṣads of all the Vedas have come forth;
for there is no other means for the ultimate pacification of this evil than the practice of the means prescribed therein.

Therefore, the meaning of this section is that one must apply effort precisely toward the means prescribed in the Upanishads. It was stated that [the traveler] goes forth after discarding the load of the cart's equipment; what, then, is the provision for his journey toward the next world—which stands in the place of the cart-driver’s equipment—and what is it that he consumes upon reaching the next world, as well as that which initiates the body and so forth? [The answer follows: "The food eaten by the one who has departed, and the merit and demerit performed by him while dwelling here—these two indeed become his provisions for the journey. (KaU 1.4.14) The meaning of this verse is as follows: "The food eaten" refers to the food consumed by the one who has departed from this world. Furthermore, "the merit and demerit performed by him while dwelling here"—that is, while living in this world—these two alone become his "provisions for the journey," serving the purpose of sustaining him on the way to the next world. This is because there is no other provision for the journey, and because these two are the causes for attaining the results of karma. The word "only" (eva) is used to exclude other things. The phrase "become his provisions for the journey" means they serve the purpose of sustaining him on the path to the next world. The word "indeed" (hi) indicates that this is well-known. Now, one might ask: "Is it not the case that the food eaten here becomes the cause for the production of the body and so forth in the next world? To this we reply: No, that is not so. For the food eaten here is digested and transformed into excrement and the like, and does not reach the next world. However, the subtle essence (*sūkṣma-bhāga*) of that food, which is the cause of the body and so forth, does indeed go to the next world. And that subtle essence is nothing other than the merit and demerit performed by him while dwelling here. Therefore, it is established that those two alone are the provisions for the journey. Thus, one should strive with diligence in this very means prescribed in the Upanishads. This is the meaning of the section. Regarding the statement that he goes forth after discarding the load of the cart's equipment, one may ask: What is the provision for his journey toward the next world that corresponds to the cart-driver's equipment, and what is it that he consumes after having gone to the next world, as well as that which initiates the body and so forth?
