It is said: as that self (ātman) departs for the next world, knowledge and action—knowledge being of various kinds, whether enjoined, prohibited, or neither enjoined nor prohibited;
and likewise action, whether enjoined, prohibited, or neither enjoined nor prohibited—both accompany it, they fully accompany it.

They both touch and follow after [the body]. "Prior cognition" (*pūrvaprajñā*) means cognition whose object was previously experienced; that is to say, it is the latent impression (*vāsanā*) from the experience of the results of past actions.
And that latent impression becomes a factor (*aṅga*) both at the commencement of a previous action and in the ripening (*vipāka*) of that action.
Therefore, that [cognition] also touches and follows after [the body].
For without that latent impression (*vāsanā*), it is impossible to perform an action or experience its fruit;
indeed, the senses do not possess proficiency regarding an object that has not been practiced.
However, for the senses that have been set in motion by the latent impressions of prior experiences, proficiency arises here even without immediate practice.

Furthermore, it is observed that some individuals possess skill from birth itself in certain activities characterized by arts such as painting, even without practice in this life; yet they may lack skill in others, even those involving extreme ease.
Likewise, for some, no engagement in action or enjoyment of its fruit is possible without prior wisdom (*pūrvaprajñā*).
Therefore, these three—knowledge (*vidyā*), action (*karman*), and prior wisdom (*pūrvaprajñā*)—are like the equipment of a caravan driver, serving as provisions for the journey to the next world.

Since knowledge (*vidyā*) and merit (*puṇya*) are the means for the attainment of another body and for the experience [of its fruits], therefore one should accumulate only auspicious knowledge, action, and so forth, so that the enjoyment and experience of a desired body may come to pass;
this is the meaning of the section. //4.4.2//
Just as a caterpillar, having reached the end of a blade of grass, takes hold of another support and draws itself toward it,
even so this Self, having cast off this body and caused ignorance to depart, takes hold of another support and draws itself toward it.

BrhUpBh_4,4.3: Thus, one who is impelled by the momentum of knowledge and the rest, when departing from the body to enter another, leaves the previous body and enters the new body like a bird flying from one tree to another;
or else, he is led to the place of birth resulting from karma by means of an intermediate, subtle body (*ativāhika-śarīra*).
Furthermore, does the functioning of the all-pervading organs occur while remaining in this very [present] body, or do they become contracted for one who has left the body?
The instruments [of action] of the deceased, having pervaded everywhere like the light of a lamp from a broken jar, undergo contraction upon the commencement of another body. Furthermore,
does the mind alone proceed toward the location where the next body is to begin, as in the Vaiśeṣika system, or is it merely a conceptual construction, as in the Vedānta system?
It is said: "All these indeed are equal, all are infinite"—from this Vedic scripture, the instruments (karaṇas) are of the nature of the All.

Furthermore, because they depend upon the vital breath (prāṇa), which is itself of the nature of the All, their limitation into the internal (ādhyātmika) and external (ādhibhautika) realms is caused by the karma, knowledge, and mental impressions (bhāvanā) of living beings.

Therefore, by virtue of that [limitation], although the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are inherently infinite, their activity contracts and expands according to the body they initiate—conforming precisely to the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the agent’s knowledge.
Thus it has been said: “He is equal to a flea, equal to a mosquito, equal to an elephant, equal to these three worlds, and equal to this entire universe.
And likewise, this statement is consistent with that: [“...”]
“He who worships these as infinite,” and so forth;
and also, “In whatever way they worship Him.
In that regard, the latent impression (*vāsanā*)—known as prior cognition (*pūrvaprajñā*), dependent upon knowledge and action, and continuous like a leech—is present, just as in the state of dream.

Action (karma) initiates another body from the current body; specifically, in the matter of how the heart initiates another body and the new body releases the previous abode, this illustration is provided: *tat*—in that regard, concerning the transition to another body—*idaṃ nidarśanam*—this is the example.
*Yathā*—in whatever manner—the *tṛṇajalāyukā*, or grass-leech, having gone to and reached the end, the conclusion, of a blade of grass, [seizes] another...
"Stepping on another blade of grass" means that having stepped upon—that is, having approached and ascended—that stepping-place, he withdraws his own prior limb into the position of the final limb.
In this very manner, this self under discussion—the transmigrating soul—having struck down this body previously assumed, like one desiring to enter a dream;

having cast it off, having caused ignorance to prevail, and having rendered it unconscious, withdraws itself and takes up another stepping-place, just as a caterpillar does with another blade of grass.
Having assumed another body, it withdraws its own measure [of self] by means of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

Therein it initiates a personal existence (*ātmabhāva*), just as one initiates another body in a dream; for the newly initiated body of the dream-body—whether moving or stationary—is the locus where another body is begun.
And therein, by the power of karma, the instruments (*karaṇa*) come together, having attained their functional activity.
And the external body, which corresponds to grass and clay, is commenced;
and therein, with reference to the arrangement of the organs, the deities such as Fire and others are gathered for the sake of assisting speech and the other faculties.
This is the procedure for the commencement of another body. //4.4.3//
Just as a weaver takes a small amount of thread and weaves it out into another form that is newer and more beautiful,
even so this Self, having struck down this body and caused ignorance to depart, fashions for itself another form that is newer and more beautiful.
Whether it be the rite of the ancestors (pitrya), the Gandharvas (gāndharva), the gods (daiva), Prajāpati (prājāpatya), Brahmā (brāhma), or that of other beings.

In this regard, concerning the commencement of another body, does he begin that other body by repeatedly destroying only the material already acquired, or does he take up entirely new material again and again? To this it is replied by means of an illustration: "In this matter, just as a peśaskārī"—one who works with *peśas*, which is gold; a *peśaskārī* is a goldsmith—having taken a portion (*mātrām*) of the gold, having cut it off and grasped it, fashions (*tanute*), that is, constructs, another form, newer than the previous one, more beautiful than the beautiful.

"In the same way, this self," and so forth, as before. Those very five elements beginning with earth and ending with space— which were explained in the fourth [chapter] in the passage "Verily, there are two forms of Brahman"— which serve as the materials for the body, are repeatedly crushed and crushed.
"Another and yet another" means a newer and more auspicious body, or a specific form and configuration, beneficial for the ancestors— that is, suitable for enjoyment in the world of the ancestors—
or "gandharva," suitable for the enjoyment of the Gandharvas,
and likewise "daiva," [suitable] for the gods.

It belongs to Prajāpati as "Prajāpatya," or it belongs to Brahmā as "Brāhma"; it is connected with the idea that [the soul] creates another body belonging to others, according to their karma or according to what has been heard, or belonging to other beings. //4.4.4//

Now, this self is indeed Brahman— consisting of consciousness, consisting of mind, consisting of breath, consisting of sight, consisting of hearing, consisting of earth, consisting of water, consisting of air,
consisting of space, consisting of fire, consisting of what is not fire, consisting of desire, consisting of what is not desire, consisting of anger, and consisting of what is not anger.
It consists of dharma, it consists of adharma, and it consists of everything;
that is to say, "it consists of this" and "it consists of that.
As one acts and as one conducts oneself, so does one become.
One who performs good deeds becomes good;
one who performs evil deeds becomes evil.
One becomes meritorious through meritorious action and evil through evil action.
Now, moreover, they say:
"This person consists of desire alone.
As is his desire, so is his resolve.
Whatever resolve one has, that action one performs;
whatever action one performs, that one attains. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.5)
Those limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of this Self which are designated as its "bonds"—

those entities by which it is conceived as being "composed of that" when joined with them— are here pointed out collectively in one place: "Now, this very Self who thus wanders in saṃsāra is indeed Brahman, the Supreme, who is beyond hunger and the rest."
"Consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*) means being perceived by the intellect as being composed of that;
"which one is the self? it was said, "this which consists of consciousness among the vital breaths.

"Consisting of consciousness" means being predominantly consciousness, because its nature as having that as its characteristic is clearly discerned in the statements, "it meditates, as it were," and "it moves, as it were."
Likewise, it is "mind-made" (*manomaya*) because of its proximity to the mind;

likewise, it is "vital-breath-made" (*prāṇamaya*) because it consists of the vital breath which has five functions, by means of which consciousness appears as if it were moving. Likewise, it is "eye-made" (*cakṣurmaya*) at the time of seeing forms.
Thus, at the time of hearing a sound, it consists of the ear;
likewise, when the activity of each respective sense organ arises, it becomes composed of that very organ.

Thus, through the gateway of the intellect and the vital breath, being composed of the instruments such as the eye and so forth, it becomes composed of the elements such as earth and the rest that initiate the body.

In that regard, when a body composed of earth is initiated, one becomes composed of earth; likewise, when a body composed of water is initiated in the worlds of Varuṇa and others, one becomes composed of water;
and likewise, when a body composed of air is initiated, one becomes composed of air.
Likewise, when the body of ether is commenced, it becomes composed of ether;
in this same way, these divine bodies are made of fire.
When they are being commenced, one becomes composed of them—that is, composed of fire.

Therefore, compared to those bodies which are distinct from this—namely the bodies of animals and so forth, as well as the bodies of denizens of hell and pretas, which are not composed of light—the self is "composed of light.

Thus, while consisting of the aggregate of the body and its instruments, the self, perceiving another object to be attained, develops contrary notions such as "this has been attained by me" and "that is to be attained by me";
through the desire for that, it becomes "composed of desire."
When one perceives the fault in that desire, the mind—its longing for that object having been stilled—becomes clear, stainless, and peaceful;
being absorbed in that, it is no longer composed of desire.
Thus, when that desire is suppressed by something else, that desire transforms into anger, and becoming absorbed in that, it becomes composed of anger.
When that anger is turned back by some means, then the mind, being serene and undisturbed, is called "free from anger," and one becomes "composed of that" (tanmaya) through it.
Thus, having become composed of desire and anger, or of the absence of desire and the absence of anger, one becomes composed of dharma and composed of adharma.
For indeed, the activity of dharma and so forth is not possible without desire, anger, and the like.
"Whatever action one performs, that is the movement of desire," according to the traditional teaching (*smṛti*).
Having become composed of dharma and composed of adharma, it becomes composed of everything.
Whatever entire effect of merit and demerit has been determined, all that is the fruit of merit and demerit; by attaining that, one becomes composed of it.

What need is there for much? This is established for him: that he is "composed of this" (*idammaya*) because he is perceived through the objects being grasped as "this"; therefore, he is "composed of that" (*adamaya*).
The word "that" (*ada*) refers to the imperceptible by means of the perceptible effect.
For there are indeed infinite particularities of mental cultivation within the internal organ;
they cannot be specified individually.

At each respective moment, they are understood through their effects: "This is present in his heart," or "He acts because of this. Thus, that which is imperceptible and situated within is designated by way of its manifest effect, as being composed of that very [mental state], for the sake of conventional discourse.
"Regarding the phrase 'what one now consists of':
in brief, according to how one acts and according to how one conducts oneself, such is this person—'as he acts and as he conducts himself, so does he become.
The distinction is that 'acting' (*karaṇa*) refers to a fixed action understood through injunctions, prohibitions, and so forth, while 'conducting oneself' (*caraṇa*) refers to what is not fixed."
"One who performs good deeds becomes good" is a qualification of "according to what one does," and "one who performs evil deeds becomes evil" is a qualification of "according to how one acts.

Fearing that "being made of that" (tanmayatva) might mean merely the habitual tendency (*tācchīlya*)—due to the use of the suffix denoting habit—and not simply the mere performance of those actions, he says: "One becomes virtuous by virtuous action and evil by evil action.
Thus, being made of that occurs through the mere performance of virtuous or evil actions; it does not depend upon habitual tendency.
However, regarding the sense of habitual disposition (*tācchīlya*), the distinction is that there is an excellence of identification with that [object].

In this regard, the performance of meritorious acts preceded by desire, anger, and so forth, is the cause of "consisting of everything" (*sarvamayatva*); it is the cause of *saṃsāra* and of the transition from one body to another body.
For it is impelled by this that one takes up various other successive bodies.
Therefore, merit and demerit are the cause of saṃsāra;
for injunctions and prohibitions have these two as their objects,
and it is in this regard that the scripture achieves its purpose.
Furthermore, others who are indeed skilled in the matter of bondage and liberation say: "It is true that merit and demerit preceded by desire and so forth are the cause for the assumption of a body;

nevertheless, it is a person impelled by desire who accumulates meritorious and non-meritorious actions. But upon the abandonment of desire, even though action exists, it does not bring about the accumulation of merit or demerit."
Even when merit and demerit have been accumulated, if they are devoid of desire (*kāma*), they do not initiate results.
Therefore, desire alone is the root of saṃsāra.
Thus it is said in the Ātharvaṇa: "He who, thinking [on them], desires desires, is born again and again through those very desires."

Therefore, this person consists of desire alone; even though there are other constituent elements, he determines with certainty that "he consists of desire alone," because the state of consisting of anything else is not the cause.
Since he consists of desire, whatever kind of desire he has, he becomes "as he desires" (*yathākāmaḥ*), and he becomes "of such a resolve" (*tatkṛtuḥ*).
That desire, manifested by a mere slight longing for a particular object, when unimpeded and becoming clear, attains the state of being a resolve (*kratutvam*).
*Kratu* is neither mere resolve nor certainty; rather, it is that immediately following which action proceeds.

Whatever one's *kratu* is—that is, whatever kind of intention (*kāma*) one has regarding what is to be done—and whatever the form of that *kratu* of his is, such is this [action]. "Whatever *kratu* one has, that very action one performs":
whatever object the *kratu* has, for the sake of accomplishing that fruit, one performs—that is, brings about—the action that is appropriate for it.
Whatever action one performs, that one attains;
one attains its fruit.
Therefore, in this state of being composed of everything and in the condition of transmigratory existence, desire is the cause. //4.4.5//
Regarding this, there is this verse:
"Clinging to that very thing, he goes forth together with his karma, wherever his subtle body (liṅga) and mind are attached."
"Having reached the end of that karma, whatever he does here,
from that world he returns again to this world for the sake of action"—
thus [is it] for one who still desires.
Now, he who does not desire—who is without desire, free from desire, whose desire is attained, whose desire is the Self—his vital breaths do not depart.
Being Brahman, he merges into Brahman.
Regarding that matter, there is this verse, which is also a mantra:
"He goes to that very [state]; he goes to that very [state]," meaning he becomes attached—having developed a longing for it. How does he go?
Together with the action—that is, together with that very action which he performed while being attached to the fruits of action—he goes; he goes to that fruit.
What is that "liṅga"? It is the mind (manas). Because the subtle body (liṅga) has the mind as its primary constituent, the mind is called the "liṅga."

Alternatively, that by which one is characterized (*liṅgyate*), understood, or perceives is the *liṅga*; that is the mind. Wherever that mind is attached—meaning firmly fixed with arisen desire—in this transmigrating being, he indeed performed the action corresponding to that desire.
Therefore, it is solely through the power of attachment of that mind that he attains the fruit of that action.
Therefore, this is established: desire is the root of saṃsāra.
Consequently, for one whose desire has been eradicated, even existing karmas become sterile in their fruition for the knower of Brahman.
As the Śruti declares: "For one whose desires are fulfilled and who has perfected the self, all desires dissolve right here."

Moreover, having reached the end of his action—that is, having reached and experienced the conclusion, the exhaustion of the fruit of that action—he returns from that world to this world for the sake of action; for this world is dominated by action, hence the phrase "for the sake of action. Again, for the purpose of performing action, he performs action once more, and under the influence of attachment to the fruits thereof, he goes again to that other world; such is the cycle.
Thus, indeed, one who desires in this way transmigrates. Since he transmigrates only because he desires in this manner, therefore, one who is free from desire does not transmigrate anywhere;
for it has been stated that movement belongs only to one who is attached to results.

For since action is impossible for one who is without desire, he who does not desire is indeed liberated. But how does one become one who does not desire? He who is without desire (akāma) is one who does not desire (akāmayamāna). How is it said that he is "without desire"? He from whom desires have departed is "one whose desires have gone out" (niṣkāma).
How do desires depart?

One for whom desires are attained is "one whose desires are attained" (*āptakāma*). How are desires attained? By means of the desire for the Self (*ātmakāmatva*); for such a person, there is no other object to be desired that exists as a separate entity.

The Self alone is without interior or exterior, an entire mass of consciousness, a single essence; it is neither above, nor across, nor below. There is no other object distinct from the Self that can be desired. For one for whom everything has become the Self alone—by what means could he see whom? By what could he hear, think, or cognize? Knowing thus, whom could he desire? For only an object known as something "other" becomes an object of desire.
And for this knower of Brahman, there exists no other desire, since his desires are fulfilled.
He who, through the desire for the Self alone, has all his desires fulfilled, is one who is free from desire, devoid of desire, and being without desire, he is liberated.
For indeed, for him to whom the Self alone is everything, there remains nothing that is not-self to be desired.

Furthermore, it is contradictory that there should be another non-self to be desired while everything has become the Self alone. For one who perceives the Self as all, since there is no object to be desired, ritual action is impossible.
As for those who postulate ritual action even for knowers of Brahman for the sake of avoiding transgression, for them, everything indeed exists.
Because that which is to be abandoned—transgression—is intended as something other than the Self;

and we call him a knower of Brahman by whom the Self, which transcends hunger and so forth, is known to be eternally connected with transgression [in its unawakened state]. He perceives the Self as eternally transcending hunger and so forth.
Furthermore, for one who does not perceive anything else as either to be abandoned or to be acquired, action simply cannot be connected to him.
However, for one who is ignorant of Brahman, there is no contradiction in the fact that action exists for the purpose of avoiding transgression (*pratyavāya*).
Therefore, due to the absence of desire, one who is free from desire is not born again; he is indeed liberated.

For him who thus has no desires, since there is an absence of action, there is an absence of a cause for departure; therefore, the vital breaths—speech and the others—do not depart, nor do they ascend out of the body.
And that wise man, having attained all desires through the desire for the Self (*ātmakāmatā*), becomes Brahman even here.

For this form has been shown as an illustration of Brahman, the Self of all, in the passage: "Now, this is his form in which all desires are attained, which is the desire for the Self, and which is desireless."
For this very point, which serves as an illustration, is summarized by the passage beginning with "Then, one who does not desire" (*athākāmayamānaḥ*).

How is such a person liberated? It is said: for him who perceives the Self—which is like the state of deep sleep, devoid of distinctions, non-dual, and whose nature is the light of consciousness that has not been lost—the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) do not depart, because for that one who is free from desire, there exists no state of action and thus no cause for going.
Speech and the other organs do not depart;
rather, the knower, even while appearing here as if possessed of a body, is Brahman itself and, being Brahman, he attains Brahman.

Since he possesses no desires that could serve as the cause for delimiting him from Brahmanhood, he attains Brahman while still here, being Brahman already, and not at a time subsequent to the fall of the body.

For the knower who has died does not undergo a transition into another state of existence; rather, it is said that he "attains Brahman" merely by the absence of reconnection with another body, while his state remains otherwise than that of a living person.
For if there were a transition into another state of existence, the very purpose intended by all the Upaniṣads—namely, the oneness of the Self—would be subverted.
Furthermore, liberation would result from the cause of karma and not from the condition of knowledge;
and that is undesirable, as it would entail the impermanence of liberation.
For an object produced by action is never seen to be permanent.

Furthermore, liberation is accepted as eternal, based on the wording of the mantra: "This is the eternal majesty. Nor is it possible to conceive of anything other than the innate nature as being eternal.

If heat is the inherent nature of fire, it cannot be said to be experienced as a result of human activity; for neither the heat nor the light of fire is experienced subsequent to the activity of the fire-manipulator. To claim that something is both inherent in nature and dependent on human activity is a contradiction.

The state of being characterized by combustion and movement is manifested through the two qualities of heat and luminosity; this is not so in relation to fire itself. Rather, for someone else who perceives it differently, heat and luminosity are properties of fire that appear disconnected due to an intervening obstruction.

Upon the removal of that obstruction, they are manifested through perception in relation to the fire, and based on that, the error arises that these two properties of heat and luminosity have come into existence preceded by the fire.
If even heat and light were not inherent properties,
we would cite that which is the inherent property of fire;
nor can it be said that there are no inherent properties whatsoever for entities.
Furthermore, liberation as the cessation of bondage cannot be established as a non-existent entity like the breaking of shackles;
for it is accepted that the individual self is one with the Supreme Self, according to the Vedic scripture: "One only, without a second.
Nor is there any other bound being for whom liberation could consist in the cessation of bondage, as in the case of the removal of shackles.
We have already explained in detail that nothing exists apart from the Supreme Self;

therefore, we have also stated that the conventional usage of the term "liberation" (mokṣa) refers merely to the cessation of ignorance, just as the cessation of the [illusory] snake occurs when the ignorance regarding the snake in a rope or similar object ceases.
As for those who claim that in liberation another consciousness and another bliss become manifest, they must be asked to define the meaning of the word "manifestation."
If, first of all, the meaning of the word "manifestation" (abhivyakti) is merely the worldly apprehension of an object's pervasion [of the senses], then it must be stated:
is that which is manifested already existent or non-existent?

If it is existent, then for whichever liberated person that [liberation] is manifested, it must be essentially identical to his own self; thus, because there would be no possibility of an intervention by apprehension and because it would be eternally manifested, it follows that it is manifested for the liberated one.
A statement of distinction is purposeful.

If, however, it were manifested only at certain times due to the intervention of perception and is not of the nature of the self, then it would follow that its manifestation must depend on something else;
and thus it would require the means for its manifestation.
However, if [the manifestation] shares the same locus as the perception, then since the postulation of an obstruction is untenable, it would follow that there must be manifestation at all times;
and thus, there would be no dependence on the means for manifestation.
Furthermore, if it shares the same locus as the perception, because the postulation of an obstruction is untenable, there must either be constant manifestation or constant non-manifestation.
There is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for postulating an intermediate state.
Furthermore, it is impossible for dharmas that share a common substratum and are of the nature of a single self (*ātman*) to stand in a mutual relationship of object and subject.

Moreover, the state of being a transmigrating being (*saṃsāritva*) prior to the manifestation of consciousness and pleasure, and the state of liberation (*muktatva*) subsequent to their manifestation, would imply that this [self] is something other than the Supreme Self whose nature is eternally manifest knowledge; this is because they are absolutely distinct, just as coldness is from heat.
Furthermore, if one were to conceive of a difference between the supreme Self and the individual self, the Vedic conclusion would be abandoned.
If it is argued that since liberation is now as devoid of distinctions as it ever was, the exertion for its sake is untenable and the scripture becomes useless, we say: no;
this is not so, because the purpose is the removal of the delusion of ignorance (*avidyā*).
For in reality, there is no distinction between being liberated and not liberated,
because the self is of an eternally unchanging nature;
rather, ignorance regarding it is removed by the wisdom produced through the instruction of the scriptures.
Prior to the attainment of that instruction, and for the sake of that [attainment], effort is indeed appropriate.
If it be argued that for one possessed of ignorance, there would be a distinction in the Self based on whether ignorance has been removed or not,

we have already stated that this is no fault, because we admit that [the Self] is the object of the conceptualization of ignorance— just as the rope, the mirage, mother-of-pearl, and space are respectively the objects of the notions of water, silver, dirt, and so forth.

If it is argued that there might be a distinction in the Self between being an agent and not being an agent due to ignorance—just as there is a distinction in vision caused by the excess or lack of cataracts—we say no.
This is because the agency of ignorance in the Self is denied by the texts stating, "It meditates, as it were; it vibrates, as it were.
Furthermore, the delusion of ignorance is produced by the convergence of numerous activities.
And because it would follow that [the self] is itself ignorance.
Furthermore, one for whom the delusion of ignorance is perceived as distinct [from the self], like a jar or other objects, does not possess that delusion of ignorance.
If it is argued that [the self] must indeed possess the delusion of ignorance because of the experience of the cognition "I do not know; I am deluded," we say no.
Because that [cognition] too apprehends a distinction;
for one who apprehends something as distinct from another is not said to be mistaken regarding that thing.
Moreover, it is a contradiction to claim that there is an apprehension of a distinction regarding that very object while simultaneously being mistaken about it.

You say that "I am deluded" is seen; thus, the ignorance of the one who perceives it, as well as the state of being deluded, becomes the object of that perception and falls into the status of an object (*karman*). How, then, could that which has become an object be the ignorance and the state of delusion which qualify the perceiving subject? Furthermore, if those two are qualifiers of the perception, how could they be objects? They would be pervaded by the perception.
For an action is pervaded by the agent and the act;
moreover, that which is pervaded is one thing and the pervader is another—it is not pervaded by itself.
Tell me, this being so, how could ignorance and the specific quality of seeing be established?

Furthermore, one who perceives the object of perception— ignorance and the vision of non-discrimination— as an attribute of the Self does not grasp it as a property of the perceiver, just as one does not grasp emaciation or leprosy as properties of the body when they occur in the body.

If it is argued that everyone in the world grasps pleasure, pain, desire, effort, and so forth [as belonging to the Self], even so, the distinctness of the world from the grasper would have to be admitted.
If you say, "I do not know what you have said because I am indeed deluded," let him be ignorant and deluded; however, we recognize as wise and undeluded one who perceives things in this manner.
Thus it was said by Vyāsa:
"The Knower of the Field illumines the entire field, beginning with desire.
This has been stated hundreds of times, as in: "The Supreme Lord, abiding equally in all beings, does not perish when they perish," and so forth.

Therefore, there is no distinction within the Self created by bondage, liberation, or knowledge, because it is admitted that the Self is always of a uniform and single essence. Those, however, who otherwise conceptualize the reality of the Self and treat the scriptures on bondage, liberation, and so forth as mere explanatory eulogies (arthavāda), are capable of seeing the footprints of birds in the sky or grasping the sky with their fists.
It is possible to wrap [the world] like a hide;

we, however, being unable to do that, understand from the very beginning that we are indeed Brahman—the reality of the Self which is non-dual, unchanging, unborn, undecaying, immortal, deathless, and fearless—this being the meaning determined by all the Vedāntas.
Thus do we realize.

Therefore, the statement "he goes even to Brahman" is merely figurative; it refers only to the cessation of the continuity of the body, in consideration of the fruit of knowledge, like the extinguishing of a lamp. 4.4.6.
Regarding this, there is this verse:
"When all the desires that dwell in his heart are released..."
"Then the mortal becomes immortal; here he attains Brahman. Just as the slough of a snake might lie dead and cast off upon an anthill, even so does this body lie.
"Then this bodiless, immortal life-breath is indeed Brahman, it is indeed light.
Therefore, I give a thousand [cows] to the Blessed One," said Janaka of Videha.
In Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad Bhāṣya 4.4.7, the analogy of passing from the state of dreaming to the state of waking has been illustrated by its counterpart, transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*).
Furthermore, the causes of transmigratory existence—namely, knowledge (*vidyā*), action (*karman*), and prior cognition (*pūrvaprajñā*)—have been described.
Moreover, those limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of the body and the organs, enveloped by which the Self experiences the condition of being a transmigrator, have also been stated.
Having established the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) are the direct motivators for those [actions], it was determined that desire alone is the cause;

and just as this matter was determined by the Brāhmaṇa passage, so too has it been determined by the mantra. Having thus stated bondage and the cause of bondage, the section is concluded with the words, “Thus, not desiring” (*iti na kāmayamāna*).

Then, beginning with “But when he does not desire,” liberation—characterized as the state of being the Self of all (*sarvātmabhāva*)—is described as the illustrative counterpart (*dārṣṭāntika*) to the state observed in deep sleep.

Furthermore, that state of having one's desires fulfilled (*āptakāmatva*) which was described as the cause of liberation through the desire for the Self (*ātmakāmatā*), is—by implication—nothing other than the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). This is because, without the knowledge of the non-Self, the fulfillment of desires cannot occur simply by desiring the Self; thus, it is stated by implication that the knowledge of Brahman alone is the cause of liberation.
Therefore, although it has been said that "desire is the root," it follows by implication that ignorance (*avidyā*) is the cause of bondage, being the opposite of the cause of liberation.

Here too, liberation and the means to liberation have been stated by the Brāhmaṇa. To further strengthen that very point, a mantra expressed by the word "śloka" is cited: "In this regard, concerning that very same matter, there is this verse-mantra. When—at which time—all desires, which are various forms of thirst, are completely released.

For the knower of Brahman who desires the Self, those well-known objects of pursuit in this world and the next— characterized by the desire for sons, wealth, and worlds— which had resided and taken refuge in the heart, that is, the intellect of this well-known person, fall away entirely along with their roots.
Then, at that time, the mortal, though subject to death, becomes immortal through the separation from desire along with its roots.
The meaning is that even while remaining in this very body, one attains Brahman—that is, one reaches the state of Brahman, which is liberation.
Therefore, liberation does not depend upon going to another place or the like.
Consequently, for the knower, the vital breaths do not depart; remaining as they are, they are merged into their own cause, the Person (Puruṣa).
It has been stated that "only the name remains.

But how is it that when the vital breaths have ceased and the body has dissolved into its own cause, the liberated knower— who exists right here as the Self of all— does not again assume, as before, the state of being an embodied being characterized by transmigratory existence?

To this it is replied: In this regard, the illustration is as follows. In the world, there is a snake (*ahi*); its slough (*nirmoka*) is the snake’s skin. That snake’s slough might lie dead, cast off, and abandoned by the snake in its own body, in such places as an anthill—the meaning being a mound that serves as a refuge for snakes—and remain coiled there. In exactly the same way, according to this illustration, this body lies like something dead, having been abandoned by the liberated one who occupies the place of the snake, through his no-longer-identifying-with-itself state.

Now, the other, who stands in the place of the snake, being liberated and having become immortal, remains in that very same place just as before, yet he is indeed bodiless; he does not possess a body as he did previously.
For previously, through the identification with a body impelled by desire and karma, he was embodied and mortal.
Now, due to separation from that, he is bodiless, and for that very reason, he is immortal.
It is called *prāṇa* because it breathes (*prāṇiti*).

For this will be stated in the forthcoming verse: "The breath of the breath" (*prāṇasya prāṇam*), and also in another Vedic scripture: "For the mind, my dear, is fastened to the breath" (*prāṇabandhanaṃ hi somya manaḥ*).
And because of the force of the context and the sentence, the Supreme Self alone is denoted here by the word "prāṇa";
it is Brahman alone, the Supreme Self alone.

What, then, is that? It is light itself—consciousness, the luminosity—by which the world, illumined by the light of the Self, proceeds undisturbed, having consciousness as its eye and being endowed with the light of discernment.

That question regarding desire which was for the sake of liberation, granted as a boon by Yājñavalkya to Janaka— characterized by the nature of bondage and liberation along with its underlying cause and serving as an illustrative example— that very matter has been determined in detail by the Śruti through the narrative form of the dialogue between Janaka and Yājñavalkya.
Thus, the means for liberation from saṃsāra has been declared for all living beings.
Now, the Śruti itself says that Janaka spoke thus for the purpose of paying the fee for knowledge (*vidyā-niṣkriyārtha*).
How so? "Thus liberated by you, O Blessed One, I give a thousand [cows] to you for the purpose of paying the fee for knowledge"—this is indeed what Janaka of Videha said.

Here, one might ask: since the matter of liberation has been fully determined, why does he not offer the kingdom of Videha and his very self, but instead gives only a thousand [cows], as if it were a partial payment? What is the intention behind this?

On this point, some explain it as follows: Janaka, being a connoisseur of the science of the self (*adhyātmavidyā*), although he had already heard the matter, wished to hear it again through the mantras;
therefore, he did not report everything at once.
Thinking, "Having heard what I desire from Yājñavalkya, I shall report it again at the end," he acted thus.

If one were to think, "If I reveal everything right here, he will cease his desire for hearing [more]," or out of fear that "he will not recite the verses," and thus offer a thousand [cows] as a sign of his intent to listen—
all of this is incorrect; for just as with a person, it is impossible for the Veda, which is the authoritative means of knowledge, to employ a pretext.
And because there remains a further purpose to be accomplished:

even though the subject matter of liberation has been stated, there remains a further purpose to be explained, namely the renunciation known as *saṃnyāsa*, which is a means for the knowledge of the Self and is supplementary to that knowledge; all forms of seeking must be abandoned.
Therefore, the assumption that [the Lord] merely wished to hear a single verse is dishonest.
For the postulation of a meaning not previously stated is a resort for those with no other way;
yet that is improper when another way exists.
Furthermore, we have already stated that this is not merely a matter of praise.
If this is so, one might object that it should be stated that [renunciation] is for liberation alone from the point of truth onwards.

This is not a fault; for it is held that renunciation is not an indispensable requirement [at that stage], just as self-knowledge is not, or like rites of performance (*pratipatti-karman*) in certain cases—according to the traditional teaching (*smṛti*): "One should cast off the body by means of renunciation."

Even in the case of one who has attained the state of a virtuous person (*sādhutva*), there is no need for the question "Is it only for liberation from here onwards? because [the practice] is intended for the maturation of the knowledge of the Self, which is the means to liberation. //4,4.7//
Regarding this, there are these verses:
"The path is subtle, far-reaching, and ancient; it has been touched by me alone, and discovered by me alone."
By that path, the wise who know Brahman go from here upwards to the heavenly world, liberated.
These verses serve as an extensive exposition on the meaning already stated in the Mantra and Brāhmaṇa—that liberation belongs to the knower of Brahman who desires the Self.

The path is "minute" (*aṇu*) because it is subtle and difficult to discern; it is "extended" (*vitata*) because it is wide or, according to another reading, "vitara" because it is a cause for very clear crossing. It is the way of knowledge that accomplishes liberation; it is "ancient" (*purāṇa*), meaning long-standing, because it has been revealed by the eternal Śruti.

The meaning is: "May [this path] not be touched by me"—that is, may it not be attained by me as something belonging to a later time, like the paths of false views arising from the intellect of logicians (*tārkika*).

For when something is obtained by someone, it is as if that person touches it and becomes connected with it; therefore, this path to liberation characterized by the knowledge of Brahman is said to be "not touched" by me because it has been obtained by me.
Not only was it obtained by me, but it has been realized (*anuvitta*) by me alone.
"Subsequent realization" (*anuvedana*) refers to the attainment of the finality and completion of the fruit in dependence upon the maturation of knowledge;
it is like the state of satiety that concludes the act of eating.
The distinction, however, is that previously there was merely the connection with the acquisition of knowledge.
Is it not the case that this seer of the mantra alone attained the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), while no one else attained it, such that he concludes, "I have understood it"?
This is not a fault;
for this passage is intended as a praise of the knowledge of Brahman, meaning that its fruit is unsurpassed and realized by the self as a witness.

Thus, the knowledge of the Self—which brings about the conceit of having accomplished one's purpose and is witnessed by the conviction of the Self—praises the knowledge of Brahman by implying: "What else could there be beyond this?
It does not mean that another knower of Brahman fails to attain its fruit;
for the scripture states in a general sense: "Whosoever among the gods... and so forth.

He says that very thing: "By that path of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), the wise—the meaning is that others who possess discernment (*prajñā*) and are knowers of Brahman as well—attain, they go to, the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman, which is liberation (*mokṣa*). Although the word *svargaloka* (heavenly world) generally denotes a celestial realm, here, due to the context, it signifies liberation.
After the falling away of this body, while still living, they become liberated. (4.4.8)
Regarding that, they say it is white, blue, tawny, green, and red.
This is the path discovered by Brahmā; by it goes the knower of Brahman, the doer of merit, and the man of radiant splendor.
Regarding that path which is the means to liberation, there is a disagreement among those seeking liberation.
How so?
Regarding that [path], some seekers of liberation say it is white—pure and stainless; others say it is blue, others yellow, and others green or red, according to their own perceptions.

However, the wealthy [do not understand] these channels, such as Suṣumnā and the rest, which are filled with the essences of phlegm and so forth, because it has been stated that they are "white, blue, tawny," and so on; rather,
they consider the sun itself to be the path to liberation,
based on such scriptural passages from the Upaniṣads as, "This is white, this is blue."
Because it is impossible for colors such as white to exist in the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).
However, in every respect, these [colors] such as white are other than the path of the knowledge of Brahman under discussion.
[Objection: But is not the "white" [path] the pure path of the two stages?
Because they are pursued along with words such as "blue" or "pure," which denote colors—
those paths to liberation that yogins call "white" and so forth are not actually paths to liberation, for they belong to the realm of *saṃsāra*;
this is because they are connected to the departure [of consciousness] from bodily locations, such as "from the eye," "from the head," or "from other parts of the body."
For they lead to the attainment of the worlds beginning with that of Brahmā.

Therefore, this alone is the path to liberation: since the attainment of all desires through the state of self-desire is impossible, the collection of the effects and instruments—the eyes and so forth—dissolves right here like the extinguishing of a lamp; this is the path of knowledge.
The path has been traversed by a Brāhmaṇa—that is, by one who has renounced all desires—by means of the very nature of Brahman, the Supreme Self.

By that path of the knowledge of Brahman, another knower of Brahman also goes. It is said how such a knower of Brahman goes: having first been a doer of meritorious deeds, and then again having abandoned desires for sons and other things, having united his self with the splendor of the Supreme Self, he becomes one who is perfected in That and whose nature is that splendor.
The meaning is "right here.
Such a knower of Brahman goes by that path;
we have already stated that this does not include those who perform a combination of merit and other works, because of the contradiction.
Salutation to that Self of liberation, the light of non-rebirth, which peaceful renunciants reach when both merit and demerit have ceased.
And because of such Smṛti texts;
because of the instruction to renounce merit and demerit in passages such as, "Renounce both dharma and adharma";
and [because of the description of the state] as "free from desire, free from undertaking, free from salutation, and beyond praise."
The gods know him as a Brahmin who is undecaying and whose karma has been exhausted.
“Such is not the wealth of a brahmin as this: singleness, equanimity, and truthfulness;
virtuous conduct, steadfastness, laying aside the rod, uprightness, and the gradual withdrawal from all ritual actions.”
This is also established by such Smṛti passages as these.

Furthermore, the author will teach here as well: "This is the eternal greatness of a brāhmaṇa; he does not increase by action, nor does he become less. Having thus stated the reason for the absence of any purpose for action, he enjoins the cessation of all activity with the words, "Therefore, one who knows this is peaceful, self-controlled," and so forth.
Therefore, the status of being a "doer of merit" (puṇyakṛt) is exactly as previously explained.
Alternatively, the statement "he who comes by means of the knowledge of Brahman is a doer of merit and is of the nature of light" (puṇyakṛtaijasaḥ) is a praise of the knower of Brahman.

For in the world, great fortune is well-known to reside in both the doer of merit and the luminous yogin; therefore, the knower of Brahman is praised because his great fortune is renowned in the world. 4.4.9.
Into blind darkness enter those who worship ignorance;
into even greater darkness, as it were, enter those who delight in knowledge.
They enter—that is, they attain—the blinding darkness consisting of non-seeing, which governs the cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*). Who?
Those who worship ignorance—which is other than knowledge and characterized by the relationship of means and ends—meaning they follow after ritual action (*karman*).
From that [darkness], moreover, they enter as it were into a much greater darkness. Who?

But those who are devoted to—that is, take delight in—the threefold knowledge (trayī-vidyā) alone, which consists of the means for ritual action and presents the objects of ignorance as its subject matter; that is to say, those who disregard the meaning of the Upaniṣads, holding the view that the Veda is solely concerned with injunctions and prohibitions and nothing else. //4.4.10//
"Joyless indeed are those worlds, shrouded in blind darkness; to them go after death those people who are ignorant and lack understanding. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.11)
If it is asked what fault there is if they enter that darkness characterized by non-perception, it is said:

those worlds are called "joyless," "without bliss," and "unhappy. They are covered—that is, pervaded—by that blind darkness characterized by non-perception; they are the domain of that darkness of ignorance.
Having departed—that is, having died—they go toward, they approach them. Who? [Those who perform rituals for the sake of rewards.]
"Those who are ignorant. Is it by mere ignorance in general? No; it is said: "the unawakened" (*abudhaḥ*).
This is a form derived from the verbal root *budh*, meaning "to understand," with the suffix *kvip* added.
The meaning is that they are devoid of self-realization; "people" refers to those under discussion, or rather, those characterized by the nature of being born. //4.4.11//
If a person were to know the Self, thinking "I am this," desiring what and for the sake of whose desire would he suffer along with the body? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.12)

If one should know oneself—his own supreme form, the knower of the thoughts of all living beings, residing in the heart, and transcending attributes such as hunger and so forth—then perhaps one among thousands might do so.
By the word "if," [the text] shows the rarity of the knowledge of the Self.
How is this supreme Self—the witness of the cognitions of all living beings, who is described by "not this, not this" and so on—to be known, since there is nothing other than Him?

"I am the seer, the hearer, the thinker, the knower, equal, abiding in all beings, and by nature eternally pure, enlightened, and free"—thus [thinks] the Puruṣa, the Puruṣa. Desiring what? What other thing, distinct from his own essential nature, could he desire as a result? Or for whose sake—meaning for the purpose of what other self distinct from himself?
For there is no fruit to be desired for that Self,
nor is there anyone other than the Self for whose sake one might desire anything, because the Self has become everything.
Therefore, desiring what, and for whose sake, would one suffer the body’s exhaustion or ruin?
One would experience sorrow following the suffering caused by the limiting adjuncts of the body;
one would be tormented by the heat of the body.

For one who perceives no self, yet desires other things distinct from that [body], and who exerts himself thinking, "May this be mine," "This belongs to my son," or "This belongs to my wife," becomes entrenched in the continuous cycle of repeated birth and death.
The body suffers pain following upon disease, but for one who perceives the Self as everything, that [suffering] is impossible; this is what he says. //4.4.12//

He whose Self has been discovered and awakened—having entered this perplexing, deep mystery—he is the maker of all, for he is the creator of everything; his is the world, and he alone is that world. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.13)
Furthermore, that Brahmin for whom the Self has been "known" (*anuvitta*)—that is, perceived, awakened to, and directly realized—how so?

It is when the Self has been understood as one's own innermost identity (*pratyagātmatva*) in the form: "I am the Supreme Brahman. This occurs when one has entered into this dense and treacherous thicket of doubt—a mass of manifold calamities and difficulties, a rugged place opposed by hundreds of thousands of obstacles to discriminative knowledge—for him, that Brahmin, the Self has been truly known.
The meaning is "by means of awakening.
He is the maker of all, the creator of the universe.
How is he the maker of all? [This is explained as follows:]

Anticipating the doubt as to what the name "Viśvakṛt" (the Maker of All) signifies, he says: for he is indeed the maker of everything; it is not merely a name, nor is he a "maker of all" only when impelled by another.
Rather, his world is the entire universe.
Is it said that the world is one thing and he is another? No; he is that very world itself.
By the word "world" (loka), the Self is meant;
the meaning is that its entire self belongs to all, and it is the self of all.

This very Self, which has been realized by the Brahmin through awakening as the innermost Self (pratyagātman)—this Self that had entered into the dense thicket of the peril of misfortune—is not a transmigrating being (saṃsārī), but is indeed the Supreme (para).

Because He is the creator of the universe and the Self of all, and all is His Self; one should contemplate: "I am indeed the one, without a second, the Supreme alone. This is the meaning of the verse. //4.4.13//

While still here, we know that [Brahman]; for if we did not know it, there would be a great destruction. Those who know it become immortal; others go only to suffering. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.14)

Furthermore, even here in this world, which is crowded with various objects of desire, you, who are truly virtuous, though deluded by the long sleep of ignorance, somehow—just as it were—know and realize the reality of Brahman as the Self.
The intention is: "This very Brahman under discussion—how wonderful! We have achieved our life's purpose.

If we had not known this Brahman which we now know, then [the term] *vedī* would mean "one who possesses knowledge" (*veda*); that is, one who has knowledge (*veda*) is a *vedī*, and being a knower (*vedī*), he is indeed a *vedi*. One who does not possess such knowledge is an *avedī*.
Therefore, I would have been ignorant.

If I were ignorant, what would be the fault? It would be a great, infinite destruction characterized by birth, death, and so forth—utter ruin. The meaning is: "Oh, we are liberated from this great destruction, in that we have known the non-dual Brahman."

And just as we, having known Brahman, have been completely liberated from this place of destruction, so too those who know that [Brahman] become immortal; whereas those who do not know Brahman at all—meaning others than the knowers of Brahman, namely the non-knowers of Brahman—enter into, that is, undergo, nothing but suffering characterized by birth, death, and so forth; the meaning is that for the ignorant, there is never any turning back from that.
For they indeed take up suffering itself as their self. //4,4.14//
When he perceives this Self, the God, directly— the Lord of what has been and what is to be— then he does not shrink away from anything. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.15)

But when, having somehow obtained as a teacher some supremely compassionate person and having received instruction from him, one subsequently sees—that is, realizes through direct perception—one's own Self as the God who is luminous or the giver of the fruits of the actions of all living beings according to their respective karma, the manifest Lord and Master; ... [the text continues] ...he becomes free from fear. For there is no fear of anything other than a second entity. But when he perceives everything as the Self, how could he have fear? Moreover, a second entity is the cause of fear. And when there is no second, what could he fear? Furthermore, he becomes immortal. For death is the departure from one's own nature (svabhāva) to another state. But for one who has realized his own nature, where could there be a departure? Therefore, he becomes immortal. Thus it is said: "He who knows thus becomes Brahman. This means that he attains the state of Brahman. Just as a person who has reached the presence of the king is called "one who has become the king," so too this knower, having attained the state of Brahman, is designated as "become Brahman. This is the meaning. And because of this very fact, he attains all desires. Since Brahman is the Self of all, and since all desires are contained within the Self, they are attained by one who has realized the Self. This is the meaning.
