This is the meaning. And because of this very fact, he attains all quarters. Since Brahman is the Self of all, and since all quarters are contained within the Self, they are attained by one who has realized the Self. This is the meaning. And because of this very fact, he attains all thoughts. Since Brahman is the Self of all, and since all thoughts are contained within the Self, they are attained by one who has realized the Self. This is the meaning. And because of this very fact, he attains all desires. Since Brahman is the Self of all, and since all desires are contained within the Self, they are attained by one who has realized the Self. This is the meaning. And because of this very fact, he attains all blisses. Since Brahman is the Self of all, and since all blisses are contained within the Self, they are attained by one who has realized the Self. This is the meaning. And because of this very fact, he attains all joys. Since Brahman is the Self of all, and since all joys are contained within the Self, they are attained by one who has realized the Self. This is the meaning. And because of this very fact, he attains all delights. Since Brahman is the Self of all, and since all delights are contained within the Self, they are
This refers to the three times—past, present, and future.
From that god Īśāna, he does not especially shrink back; rather, he desires to protect himself.
For every person in this world, perceiving duality, desires protection from the Lord.
But this one who perceives unity does not fear anything from any source;
therefore, he does not feel aversion at that time.
When he directly beholds Īśāna as his very self, he then does not disparage anything whatsoever.
For he sees everything as the Self; seeing thus, whom could he blame? 4.4.15
Because the year revolves around that [sun] by means of the days, therefore the gods worship that light of lights as life, as immortality. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.16)

Furthermore, because [the light] is "prior to" (arvāk) the Lord—meaning it has as its object something other than Him—the year, which is the self of time and the delimiting factor of everything born, exists only as prior to that [Lord], by means of its own parts, namely days and nights; that is the meaning. Since it is the light of lights—that is, the illuminator even of the lights such as the sun—it is called "life" (āyus); therefore, those who meditate upon it become long-lived.
Therefore, the meaning is that one who desires long life should meditate upon Brahman as possessing the quality of longevity. //4.4.16//
"In whom the five groups of five and the ether are established— him alone I consider the Self, knowing him as the immortal Brahman. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.17)

Furthermore, in which Brahman there are five groups of five— namely, the Gandharvas and so forth, or the Gandharvas, Pitṛs, Devas, Asuras, and Rakṣases, or the four castes with the Niṣādas as the fifth— and in which the unevolved space (avyākṛta-ākāśa) exists,
wherein this thread (sūtra) is woven lengthwise and crosswise; [in that Brahman, the Self is to be known].

O Gārgī, that in which this very space is established—indeed, what is called "space"—that very Self, the immortal Brahman, I consider myself to be; I do not know myself as being anything other than that.
Rather, being a knower of Brahman, I am immortal; though I was mortal through mere ignorance, with the departure of that [ignorance], I, as a knower, am indeed immortal. 4.4.17.
Those who know the breath of the breath, the eye of the eye, the ear of the ear, and the mind of the mind— they have perceived the ancient, supreme Brahman. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.18)

Furthermore, for it is by that light of the conscious Self (caitanyātma-jyotis), having become one's own self, that the vital breath (prāṇa) breathes; therefore, He is the "breath of the breath" (prāṇasya prāṇa).
Likewise, He is the "eye of the eye" and the "ear of the ear.

For it is through the presiding power of Brahman that the eyes and other organs possess the capacity for seeing and so forth; by themselves, they are like pieces of wood or clods of earth, being devoid of the light of the conscious Self.

Those who know that even the mind has a "mind" (the inner controller), and who know the inward Self—which is inferred from the activities of the eyes and other senses—to be non-objective, they have truly perceived, with certainty, the ancient, primordial Brahman existing from the beginning.
For it is said in the Atharva Veda: "That which those who know the Self perceive. (4.4.18)
It is to be perceived by the mind alone; there is not the slightest diversity here. He goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were diversity. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.19)
The means for that vision of Brahman is now stated: it should be perceived by the mind alone, which has been refined by the knowledge of ultimate reality and preceded by the instruction of a teacher.
And regarding that Brahman, the object of vision, there is not the slightest diversity here;
for where diversity does not exist, one superimposes diversity through ignorance.
He goes from death to death— that is, from one mortal end to another— from whom?
From him who sees here as if there were diversity.
The meaning is that, apart from the superimposition of ignorance, there is no duality in the ultimate sense. //4.4.19//
It should be viewed as one alone; this is immeasurable and eternal. Stainless, beyond space, unborn, the Self is great and eternal. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.20)
Since this is so, therefore it should be viewed in this very single manner— as a mass of consciousness, of a single flavor, and as continuous like space—
because this Brahman is immeasurable,
owing to its being one with everything.

For one thing is measured by another; this, however, is one alone, and therefore it is immeasurable. "Firm" (dhruva) means eternal (nitya), immovable (kūṭastha), and unchanging—this is the meaning. Now, is this not a contradiction to say that it is "immeasurable" and yet "known"? To be "known" means to be measured by the means of valid cognition (pramāṇas).
The meaning is that "immeasurable" is the negation of that [measurability].
This is not a fault,
because its purpose is to negate that which is other than a real entity— that is, that which is not a cognizable object of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) consisting of scripture (āgama).

Just as other entities are made objects of knowledge by means of valid cognitions (*pramāṇa*) independent of scripture, so this reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*) cannot be made an object by any other means of valid cognition.

Since everything would be non-manifest (*amata*) [to it], the scripture itself makes it known precisely by negating the activity of the knower, the means of knowledge, and so forth—through such statements as "Who could see whom, and what could one know?"—and not by accepting the linguistic properties of sentences characterized by denotation (*abhidhāna*) and the denoted (*abhidheya*).
Therefore, it is not established by scripture either, in the manner of [the establishment of] heaven or Mount Meru.
For that [cognition] is essentially identical with the one who causes it to be understood,
because the act of causing understanding has as its object that which is to be understood;
for this occurs only when there is a distinction [between the subject and the object].
And in that case, knowledge consists precisely in the cessation of the state of non-self;
it is not that the state of self must be directly produced therein, because the state of self already exists.
For the state of self is eternal, yet it appears as if it were not its own object to everyone.
Therefore, apart from the cessation of the appearance of that which is not its object, no positive state of selfhood (*ātmabhāva*) is enjoined in it.
When the manifestation of other natures ceases, that inherent self-nature which exists in itself alone remains; thus it is said that "the Self is known.
Furthermore, being inherently unmeasurable, it is said that it is not made an object by any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
That it is not an object of knowledge by itself and is not made an object by another means of valid cognition—both of these are entirely without contradiction.
"Dustless" (*viraja*) means free from dust; "dust" (*rajas*) refers to the impurities of merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), and so forth, and he is devoid of that.
"Supreme" (*para*) means the highest, distinct, subtle, or pervasive, even more so than the unmanifested space known as *avyākṛta*.

It is "unborn" (*aja*), because birth is prohibited; by that, the subsequent modifications of being (*bhāvavikāra*) are also prohibited, since they all have birth as their beginning. The Self (*ātman*) is "great" (*mahān*) in terms of dimension, being greater than everything else.
It is eternal and indestructible. //4,4.20//
"Having understood that very [Self], the wise Brahmin should cultivate discernment;
he should not ponder over many words, for that is a weariness of speech. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.21)

A wise Brahmin, having recognized this very Self as such through instruction and scripture, should apply his intellect—which concerns the subject matter taught by the scriptures and teachers and which brings the inquiry to completion.
The meaning is that he should thus perform the means for the application of such intellect: renunciation, tranquility, self-control, cessation, endurance, and concentration.
One should not meditate upon nor contemplate many—that is, numerous—sounds.

Since multiplicity is here prohibited, only a few words that establish the nature of the Self alone are permitted. As it is said in the *Atharvaṇa*: "Meditate on the Self as 'Om' alone; cast off other words.
For the contemplation of many sounds is, indeed, a "wasting away of speech"—that is to say, it specifically causes exhaustion and fatigue. (4.4.21)
This indeed is that great unborn Self (ātman), who consists of consciousness among the vital breaths;
he lies within that space which is inside the heart.
The controller of all,
the lord of all,
the sovereign of all.
He does not become greater by good action, nor indeed smaller by bad action;
he is the Lord of all.
He is the lord of beings; he is the protector of beings;
he is the bridge, the support, so that these worlds may not be confounded.
Brahmins seek to know him through the study of the Vedas, by sacrifice, by charity, by austerity, and by fasting.
Only by knowing him does one become a sage;
it is seeking him alone as their world that those who have renounced the world go forth.

Bondage and liberation, along with their causes, have been declared by means of the Mantras and the Brāhmaṇas, and furthermore, the nature of liberation has been explained in detail through the verses.
Since it must be stated how the entire Veda is applicable to this subject of the Self, this section is commenced for that purpose.

And that [which was stated] in this chapter has been restated here together with its purpose, for the sake of showing that the entire Veda—excluding the collection of optional rites (kāmyarāśi)—is useful precisely in this context; thus, the restatement of the aforementioned meaning begins with "He, verily, this one... The word "sa" (he) serves to refer back to what has already been mentioned.

Who is this that is mentioned and referred to? He points him out [in response]: "He who consists of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*). To prevent the understanding of the immediately preceding sentence from being applied here, he says "he who is this. To the question "Which one is this?", it is said: "He who consists of consciousness among the vital breaths" (*prāṇeṣu*).
The connection with the subsequent statement is for the purpose of removing doubt;
for it was stated previously, at the beginning of Janaka’s question, "What is the Self? [with the reply] "He who consists of cognition among the vital breaths," and so forth.
What is meant is this: the Self-luminous Self is that which has been established by the passage beginning with "He who consists of cognition among the vital breaths."

This very one, having been liberated by means of establishing that desire, action, and ignorance are not the attributes of the Self, and having been brought to the state of the Supreme Self, is indeed the Supreme and none other; thus he is called "this is directly the Great Unborn Self.
This one who consists of consciousness among the vital breaths is exactly as explained in its meaning.

That which is this space within the heart—in the middle of the lotus of the heart—is the Supreme Self alone, free from limiting adjuncts, whose own nature is consciousness; He resides in that very nature, the Supreme Self known as space.
This has been explained as the fourth [state], as the answer to the question, "Where was he then?"
And he is the controller of all, including Brahmā, Indra, and the rest;
for everyone indeed remains under his control. And it has been said: "By the command of this Imperishable One."
He is not merely a controller; he is the lord and ruler of all, including Brahmā, Indra, and others.

Lest one think that his lordship over them is merely due to birth—just as a prince might exercise authority even over servants who are physically stronger—he says "the sovereign of all," meaning he is the presiding protector and independent master.
He is not dependent on ministers and other servants as a prince is;
these three [qualities] constitute the nature of cause and effect for mastery and so forth.
Since he is the sovereign lord of all, he is therefore the ruler (*īśāna*) of all.
For it is well known that he who protects by presiding over something is indeed established in that very thing.

And because he is the lord of all, therefore he is the controller of all. Furthermore, this person consisting of consciousness, who is such as described and is the light within the heart, does not become greater—nor does he increase—in any respect from his prior state through good action performed according to the injunctions of the scriptures.

He does not become inferior—that is, smaller or less than his previous state—by means of an improper act forbidden by the scriptures; the meaning is that he does not diminish. Furthermore, everyone who performs acts such as protecting a subject becomes connected with what is called merit (*dharma*) or demerit (*adharma*), produced by the benefit or injury done to others; how then can this [Lord] be devoid of that? It is said: because He is the Lord of all, His very nature is such that He is indeed capable of presiding over even action; therefore, He is not bound by action.
Furthermore, the term "Lord of Beings" (bhūtādhipati) means that he is the sovereign over all beings from Brahmā down to a blade of grass; this has already been explained.
He is the protector and guardian of those very beings. He is the bridge.

To the question "Of what nature is he?", he says: *vidharaṇaḥ*, the upholder; that is, the one who maintains the established order (*vyavasthā*) of the castes (*varṇa*), stages of life (*āśrama*), and so forth.

He says this for the sake of the non-confusion (*asaṃbheda*)—that is, for the preservation of unmixed boundaries—of these worlds beginning with the earth and ending with the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*).
If they were not upheld by the Supreme Lord like a dam (*setu*), the worlds would have their boundaries confused.
Therefore, for the sake of the non-confusion of the worlds, this Supreme Lord—who is himself the Self that is self-luminous—is the bridge.
Thus, we have pointed out this fruit of the knowledge of Brahman, beginning with "He who knows thus is the controller of all," and so forth.

In this very knowledge of Brahman, which possesses such a fruit and is established in the sixth chapter starting with "What is the source of this person?", the entire section on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*), excluding only those parts pertaining to optional rites (*kāmya*), exists for the purpose of that [knowledge].
It is enjoined for the sake of [attaining] that.

How so? It is said: they desire to know—that very Puruṣa of such a nature who is described in the Upaniṣads—by means of "Vedānuvacana," which is characterized by the constant study of one's own Veda through the recitation of Mantras and Brāhmaṇas. Who are they?
"Brahmins.
The mention of "Brahmins" is for the purpose of illustration;
for the qualification applies without distinction to all three castes.

Alternatively, they desire to know [Brahman] through the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*), consisting of the *mantras* and *brāhmaṇas*, and through the recitation of the Vedas (*vedānuvacana*). To explain how they desire to know it, the text says "by sacrifice" (*yajñena*) and so forth.

As for those who explain that they desire to know that which is revealed by the recitation of the Vedas characterized by the *mantras* and *brāhmaṇas*, for them, the recitation of the Vedas would consist of the *Āraṇyakas* alone.
For the Supreme Self is not revealed by the ritual portion [of the Veda],
because of the specific scriptural statement, "But that which is based on the Upanishads" (*tad vai tad upaniṣadam*);
and since the phrase "by the recitation of the Vedas" (*vedānuvacanena*) is not qualified, it is a statement intended to include the entirety [of the Veda].
Nor is it logical to exclude only a portion of that [Veda].
[Objection: But even in your position, there would be the status of being "only a portion" because of the exclusion of the Upaniṣads.
[Reply: This fault does not apply to our position, because in the first interpretation there is no contradiction.

When the obligatory daily study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) is enjoined by the term "recitation of the Vedas" (*vedānuvacana*), then the Upanishads are necessarily included; thus, a portion of the meaning of the term *vedānuvacana* is not abandoned.
Furthermore, because it is recited in conjunction with sacrifices and other rites, the author employs the term *vedānuvacana* while intending to enumerate sacrificial acts such as the *yajña*.
Therefore, it is understood that the word *vedānuvacana* refers precisely to the sequence [of study].
For constant Vedic study (*nityasvādhyāya*) is indeed a ritual action (*karman*).
But how, then, do they desire to know the Self through ritual actions such as constant Vedic study?
Indeed, those [scriptures] do not reveal the Self in the same manner as the Upaniṣads.
This is not a fault, because ritual actions are the cause of purification.
For when the selves have been purified by ritual actions, they are able to know the Self revealed by the Upaniṣads without obstruction.

For thus it is said in the *Atharvaṇa*: “Then one of purified being, meditating, beholds Him who is partless”; and there is also the *Smṛti*: “Knowledge arises in men through the destruction of sinful karma,” and so forth.

But how is it understood that obligatory rites (*nitya-karmāṇi*) are for the purpose of purification (*saṃskāra*)? [It is understood] from such scriptural passages as: “He indeed is a self-sacrificer (*ātmayājī*) who knows: ‘By this [rite] this limb of mine is purified; by this my limb is established’”; and because in all the *Smṛti* scriptures they declare that rites are solely for the purpose of purification, in such passages as “the forty-eight purificatory rites” (*aṣṭācatvāriṃśat-saṃskārāḥ*).
And in the Gītā: “Sacrifice, austerity, and likewise charity are the purifiers of the wise;
all these are knowers of sacrifice, whose taints have been destroyed by sacrifice.”
Thus:
"by sacrifice" refers to material sacrifices (*dravyayajña*) and sacrifices of knowledge (*jñānayajña*), which serve for the purpose of purification (*saṃskāra*).
For one who has been purified and whose being (*sattva*) is cleansed, the arising of knowledge will occur without obstruction; therefore, "one desires to know by means of sacrifice."

By means of *dāna*, even [ordinary] giving [is included], because it is a cause for the destruction of evil and a cause for the increase of merit (*dharma*). By means of *tapas*, austerity is [meant]; although this applies generally to practices such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances, the specific qualification here is "by fasting" (*anāśakena*). Fasting (*anāśaka*) is the non-consumption of desired objects, but not the total cessation of eating; for if there were a total cessation of eating, one would simply die, and there would be no realization of the Self (*ātma-vedana*).
By the terms "recitation of the Vedas," "sacrifice," "charity," and "austerity," all obligatory (*nitya*) action is indicated.

Thus, the entire collection of obligatory actions, excluding those performed for specific desires (*kāmya*), attains the status of being a means to liberation by way of generating self-knowledge (*ātmajñāna*).
In this manner, the understanding arises that this [text] forms a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with the section on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*).

Thus, having known this very Self according to the method described and as it has been revealed, one becomes a *muni*; the meaning is that through reflection (*manana*), one becomes a sage, that is, a yogi.

It is only by knowing this very [Self] that one becomes a sage, not by knowing anything else. Now, one might ask: "Even upon knowing something else, could one not attain the state of a sage? How is it determined that it is only this [Self]?"
"Certainly, even if there were knowledge of another [self], one might be a sage;
however, upon knowing another, one would not be a sage alone—rather, he would also be a performer of action (karmī).
But by knowing this Puruṣa taught in the Upaniṣads, one becomes a sage indeed, and not a performer of action."
Therefore, one determines that his intention is to express the unique state of a Sage (munitva) by saying "this very [Self]";
for when this is known, since actions such as "who would see whom" are no longer possible, there remains only the state of a sage (manana).

Furthermore, desiring—that is, longing for—this very Self as their own world, those who have gone forth (pravrājinaḥ), whose nature is renunciation, go forth; the meaning is that they depart completely, having renounced all ritual actions.
From the restrictive statement, "Desiring this world alone," it is understood that those who desire the three external worlds have no entitlement to the life of renunciation (*pārivrājya*).
Indeed, one who wishes to reach Gaṅgādvāra while residing in the region of Kāśī does not set out facing the east.
Therefore, for those seeking the three external worlds, the means of attainment are sons, ritual actions, and the knowledge of the lower Brahman.
“By a son this world is to be conquered, not by any other action,” according to such scriptural statements.
Therefore, it is not proper for those seeking that [world] to renounce the means such as sons and instead adopt the life of a wandering mendicant (pārivrājya),
because the life of a wandering mendicant is not a means for attaining that [world].

Therefore, it is appropriate to maintain the restriction that "those who desire this very world go forth [into the homeless life]," for the attainment of the world of the Self is simply abiding in one's own Self once ignorance has been removed. Consequently, for one who desires the Self as their world, the cessation of all activity is the primary and most intimate means for realizing the vision of the Self.
Just as sons and so forth are [the means] for the three external worlds,
since the act of having sons and so forth is not a means toward the world of the self (ātmaloka),
we have stated that there is a contradiction due to impossibility.
Therefore, those who desire the Self as their world must indeed go forth [into the life of a wandering mendicant]; the meaning is that they must simply desist from all ritual actions.

And just as for those seeking the three external worlds, specific means such as sons and so forth are prescribed, so too for one who desires the world of the Self, the renunciation of all longings—wandering mendicancy—is ordained for the knower of Brahman.
But why, then, do those who seek the self and the world renounce the world?
To this it is said: let it be shown there by way of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
"This, indeed, they have [said]."

This very reason for wandering mendicancy (pārivrājya) is stated: "Indeed, it is said that in times long past, the wise who knew the Self did not desire offspring, ritual action, or the knowledge of the lower Brahman.
For these three—offspring and so forth—are designated as the means for attaining the three external worlds; thus, "offspring" is mentioned.
What [did they not desire]? They did not desire offspring, meaning they did not perform the means for attaining the three worlds, such as sons and the like.
But do they not indeed practice the contemplation of the lower Brahman?
For it is by its power that there is emergence from samādhi.
No, because of the exception.

"Brahman would desert him who knows Brahman as other than the Self; everything would desert him who knows everything as other than the Self"—this [text] indeed rejects even the vision of the lower Brahman (*apara-brahman*), because even the lower Brahman is included within "everything," and because of the passage: "where one sees nothing else."

Furthermore, because of the negation of seeing what is prior or posterior, external or internal— expressed as "without prior, without posterior, without interior, without exterior"— and because of the statement, "By what could one see whom? By what could one know whom?"— therefore,
it does not depend on any cause for emergence other than the perception of the Self.
What, then, is their intention? It is said: "What purpose, what fruit, what goal shall we accomplish by means of progeny? For progeny is known to be the means for the external world;
yet that external world does not exist for us apart from the Self.

For everything is indeed our very self, and we are the self of everything. And the Self, by virtue of being the Self, cannot be produced, attained, modified, or refined by any means whatsoever. As for the claim that ritual action is for the sake of refining the self for one who sacrifices to the self—that too falls within the sphere of viewing the self as consisting of the body and its instruments, since there are scriptural statements regarding the relationship between limbs and the possessor of limbs, such as: "By this [act], this limb of mine is refined."

For one who perceives the uninterrupted continuity of the single flavor of the mass of consciousness (*vijñānaghana*), the perception of the relationship between parts and the whole through the conditioning of the limbs is impossible.

Therefore, we shall achieve nothing by means of such exertions as those involving the *pradāji*. Indeed, it is for the ignorant that the fruit is to be accomplished by means of such exertions as the *pradāji*.

For it is not the case that because one who sees water in a mirage has acted upon it, it is therefore appropriate for one who perceives only the saline soil and the absence of water there to act as well.

Likewise, our intention is this: for us who perceive the Self as the ultimate reality, activity toward the objects of perception of the ignorant—which are like a mirage and consist of the means and ends such as progeny—is not appropriate.

This is what is said: "For us, who perceive the ultimate reality, this Self is free from hunger and other such needs; this world, which is not subject to change by the good or the bad, is the fruit intended."

Furthermore, no means of accomplishment (sādhana) whatsoever is to be sought for this Self, which is entirely free from all the phenomena of saṃsāra such as the goal to be accomplished (sādhya) and the means of accomplishment;
for the search for a means is undertaken for that which is to be accomplished.
Indeed, to search for a means for that which is not to be accomplished would be like attempting to cross dry land with the notion that it is water.
Or it is like searching for the tracks of a bird in the sky.
Therefore, having known this Self, Brahmins should indeed become renunciants; the meaning is that they should not undertake ritual actions.
For the ancient Brahmins, knowing thus and desiring no offspring, [did so].
Having thus censured the conventional practice of the relationship between the goal and its means, and considering that this [practice] pertains only to the ignorant, what did they do?
It is said: "They, indeed, having risen above the desire for sons, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worlds, then wandered about as mendicants," and so forth, as has already been explained.

Therefore, for those desiring the self and the world, the injunction "they should go forth" is consistent with this explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). Indeed, the purposefulness of this *arthavāda* is established through its orientation toward praising the world; for the subsequent text beginning with "For it is said... (*etaddha sma*) is of the nature of an explanatory passage for the statement "they go forth."
If it were a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), it would not require another explanatory praise;
however, this [injunction] "they go forth" does indeed require the explanatory praise beginning with "for so, indeed.

Because the wise men of old desisted from activities such as procreation and went forth, therefore even those of the present day go forth and ought to go forth—when connected in this way, it does not turn its face away from the world.
It must be so;
for we have already stated that it is taught to have the same agent as cognition (*vijñāna*),
and because it is mentioned in conjunction with the recitation of the Vedas and other such acts.

Just as the study of the Vedas and other such acts, which are enjoined as means for the realization of the Self, possess literal truth and are not mere explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), so too it is improper to regard renunciation (*pārivrājya*)—which is mentioned alongside those very acts—as a mere *arthavāda* simply because it is a means for attaining the world of the Self (*ātmaloka*).
This is further supported by the teaching on the distinction between the results:
in the passage, "Having known this very Self as the world," the Self is distinguished from any external world as a distinct result.
Just as this world is to be won by sons alone and not by other action— whereas the world of the ancestors is won by action—
the statement "and they do not go forth" is intended primarily as praise for the world of the ancestors.
Furthermore, like a primary injunction, it would have to be understood as heard only once in dependence upon the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
Therefore, this is merely a non-delusion regarding the ultimate state of the world;
nor is it appropriate for the praise to be based on the practice of wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājya*).

If wandering mendicancy, even while being something to be practiced, were intended for the sake of praising another, then even the performance of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) and other such rites would have to serve as praise.
Nor can the duty to act be known apart from this [context of] objects, such that it would serve as a basis for praise here.

If, however, an injunction were to be postulated for renunciation (*pārivrājya*) somewhere, that [injunction] is possible only here and not elsewhere. Furthermore, if renunciation were to be postulated for one who is not qualified [for Vedic study], then one might as well postulate renunciation for climbing trees and the like.
Because there is no difference in the fact that [the means] are not known as something to be performed;
therefore, not even a scent of being a praise can be imagined here.
If the Self is accepted as the world, for what purpose would ritual actions themselves not be the means for attaining it—why [resort] to wandering mendicancy?
To this it is replied: because this Self, which is the world, has no connection with actions (*karma*).

That Self which they desire and for whose sake they would go forth as renunciants (*pravrajeyuḥ*)—that Self is not connected with actions, whether as a means (*sādhana*) or as an end (*phala*), nor in any other way such as being something to be produced (*utpādya*) and so forth.
Therefore, this very Self is characterized by "not this, not this" (*neti neti*), and it is ungraspable, for it is indeed not grasped, and so on.

Because, according to both scripture and reasoning, the Self possesses such characteristics: it is unrelated to the means for attaining the fruits of action; it is distinct from all the attributes of transmigratory existence; it transcends hunger and other such states;

it possesses attributes such as being "not gross" (asthūla) and so forth; it is unborn, undecaying, immortal, deathless, and fearless; its essential nature is a single flavor of consciousness, like a mass of salt;
it is self-luminous, one alone without a second, without prior or posterior, without interior or exterior.

This has been established particularly here in this dialogue between Janaka and Yājñavalkya; therefore, when the Self is known as such in its true nature, the undertaking of ritual action is no longer possible.
Consequently, the Self is without distinctions.
For one who possesses sight does not fall into a snake, a well, or a pit while walking on a path;
and since the fruit of all karma is included within the fruit of knowledge,
a wise person does not exert effort toward an object that is attained without effort.
“If one should find honey in one’s own lap, why would one go to the mountain?
When a desired object has been attained, what wise person would exert further effort?”
“O Pārtha, all action in its entirety culminates in knowledge,” as it is said in the Gītā;
and here too, it is stated that other beings subsist only on a fraction of this very supreme bliss which is attained by the knower of Brahman.
Therefore, the knower of Brahman does not undertake ritual action.

Because he has desisted from all desires and, having realized the Self as "not this, not this" (neti neti), abides in that very form, these two things about to be mentioned do not overcome— that is, they do not affect— this very knower who has become the Self characterized as "not this, not this."
The ellipsis of the sentence is "this is indeed appropriate.
To the question "What is that?", it is said: "Therefore," meaning for this reason—namely, because of the necessity of maintaining the body and so forth—I have performed a sinful, non-meritorious act.
"Alas! My conduct has been wretched; by this sinful deed, I shall fall into hell"—this is the remorse for sin that occurs later.
One who has performed actions does not cross beyond that which is his very self—consisting of "not this, not this"—which is free from all affliction.
Likewise, even the joy one feels thinking, "I have performed auspicious, meritorious deeds characterized by sacrifice, charity, and so forth, prompted by desires for objects and fruits;
therefore, I shall enjoy the resulting happiness in another body," he does not cross beyond that.
Indeed, one who knows Brahman transcends both these types of action characterized as merit and demerit.

Thus, for the renunciant who knows Brahman, both kinds of action—those performed in previous births and those performed in this life—are destroyed; furthermore, no new actions are commenced. Moreover, neither "the done" nor "the undone" afflict him: "the done" refers to the performance of obligatory rites, and "the undone" refers to the non-performance thereof; yet even these two, the done and the undone, do not torment him.
For one who does not know the Self is tormented by the giving of results for what has been done and by the production of demerit for what has not been done;
but this knower of Brahman reduces all actions to ashes by the fire of the knowledge of the Self, according to the Smṛti: "As fire consumes fuel," and so forth.
However, the exhaustion of those two [karmas] that have initiated the present body occurs only through experience.
Therefore, the knower of Brahman is not connected with action. 4.4.22.
This very thing is expressed by a verse: "This is the eternal greatness of a Brahmin; he does not increase by action, nor does he become less."
"Only he would know its track; having known it, one is not smeared by evil action.
Therefore, one who knows thus—having become calm, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, and concentrated—sees the Self in the very Self;
he sees the All as the Self.
Evil does not overcome him;
he overcomes all evil;
evil does not afflict him.
It burns away all evil;
one becomes free from evil, free from dust, and free from doubt—a Brāhmaṇa.
This, O Emperor, is the world of Brahman.
"You have reached this," said Yājñavalkya.
"Therefore, I give the Videhas to you, my lord, and myself along with my servants."
This very matter has been stated by the Brāhmaṇa and further elucidated by the Ṛk verse;
this eternal glory is characterized as "not this, not this" (neti neti).
Other glories, however, are produced by karma and are therefore impermanent.
But this majesty of the knower of Brahman, the Brāhmaṇa who has renounced all desires, is distinct from that [human condition] and is eternal because it is innate.
He states the reason for its eternity: "He does not increase by good action performed"—that is, he does not undergo modification characterized by growth;
nor is he "diminished by evil action"—nor does he undergo modification characterized by decay.
For all modifications are indeed caused by increase and decrease; these are what are negated by these two [terms].
Therefore, because it is changeless, this greatness is eternal.

Consequently, he is the knower of that very greatness; he is the "knower of the word" (*padavit*), for the word (*pada*) is that which is reached, understood, and known—the very nature of greatness itself—and he is the one who knows that word.

What would be gained by knowing that state? It is said: having known that majesty, one is not smeared—that is, one is not bound—by evil action, characterized as either merit (*dharma*) or demerit (*adharma*); for the knower, both are indeed equally evil.
Therefore, this majesty of the Brāhmaṇa is such that he is no longer connected with action, characterized by "not this, not this" (*neti neti*). Consequently, one who knows thus is peaceful.

One who is tranquil through the cessation of the activity of the external senses, likewise self-controlled by turning away from the thirst of the internal organ, dispassionate being freed from all desires,

a renunciant, patient enduring the pairs of opposites, and concentrated— having become concentrated in the form of one-pointedness by withdrawing from the movement of the senses and the internal organ—
all this has been stated previously: "Having become indifferent to both childhood and panditya."
One perceives the Self—the inward conscious perceiver—within one's own self, that is, within the aggregate of the body and the instruments of perception.

In this regard, it is said that it is not merely a limited portion that is perceived; rather, one perceives the entire whole as the Self alone. One perceives thus: "There is nothing else whatsoever apart from the Self, not even as much as the tip of a hair.
By such contemplation (*manana*), one becomes a sage (*muni*), having abandoned the three states known as waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.
Evil, characterized by merit and demerit, does not overcome—that is, does not reach—the Brahmin who sees in this way;

rather, this knower of Brahman overcomes all evil, pervading and transcending it through his very self-nature. Evil, characterized by what has been done and what has not been done, does not afflict him by producing either desired fruits or the consequences of transgression.

This knower of Brahman burns away all evil, reducing it to ashes by means of the fire of the vision of the Self in all things. Such a one, possessing this knowledge, is free from merit and demerit, stainless and devoid of passion, free from desire and free from doubt; with the conviction that "I am the Self of all, the Supreme Brahman," he becomes a true Brāhmaṇa.
But one who has become such as this in that state is a *brāhmaṇa* in the primary sense; prior to this abiding in the nature of Brahman, his status as a *brāhmaṇa* was only figurative.
"This is the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*)"—that is, Brahman itself is the world, the world of Brahman—in its primary, non-figurative sense, characterized by being the Self of all, O Smārta.
"I have led you to this world of Brahman, which is characterized by 'not this, not this' (*neti neti*) and so forth," Yājñavalkya said.

Thus, having been made one with Brahman by Yājñavalkya, Janaka, who had attained the state of Brahman, replied: "Being thus made one with Brahman by you, I give to your holiness all my kingdom, the Videha lands, as well as myself, along with whatever duties remain to be performed."
The supreme goal of human endeavor is fully accomplished.

This much is to be done by a person; this is the culmination, this is the highest state, this is the ultimate good. Having attained this, a Brahmin has fulfilled his duty; this is the instruction of all the Vedas. //4.4.23//
This indeed is that great unborn Self, the eater of food, the giver of wealth.
He who knows this finds wealth. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.24)

This very Self, which was explained in the narrative of Janaka and Yājñavalkya, is indeed that great, unborn Self, the eater of food, residing in all beings, the consumer of all kinds of food. It is the "giver of wealth" (*vasudāna*);
"wealth" (*vasu*) means the fruit of the actions of all living beings, and its "giver" means the one who joins living beings with the fruit according to their respective karma.

He who knows that one unborn eater of food—the Self—endowed with the qualities of being the eater of food and the giver of wealth, he, having become the Self of all beings, eats food and finds wealth; that is, he obtains the entire collection of fruits of action, because he is the Self of all, he who knows as described.
Alternatively, even by those seeking visible results, the Self endowed with such qualities should be worshipped.

The meaning is that by this very visible fruit—namely, being an eater of food—he obtains wealth, and he becomes possessed of cattle and other such things through his state as an eater of food. //4.4.24//
This indeed is that great unborn Self— undecaying, undying, immortal, fearless Brahman.
Verily, Brahman is fearless.
For indeed, Brahman becomes fearless for him who knows this. *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 4.4.25.
Now, the entire meaning of the Āraṇyaka that has been stated is summarized and pointed out in this section as follows:
"This indeed is the great, unborn Self (ātman), ageless"—meaning it does not decay, nor does it undergo transformation—"immortal.
Because it is ageless, it is therefore immortal; it does not die, thus it is immortal.
For that which is born and decays perishes or dies;
but this [Self], because it is unborn and undecaying, is indestructible, and for that very reason it is immortal.

Since it is devoid of these three states of being—birth and the rest—it is therefore also devoid of the other three modifications of being produced by them, as well as of death in the form of desire, action, delusion, and so forth.
For this very reason, he is fearless;

and because he possesses the aforementioned qualifications, he is devoid of fear. Indeed, fear is the effect of ignorance (avidyā); therefore, by the negation of its effects and by the negation of the modifications of existence (bhāvavikāra), the negation of ignorance itself should be understood as established.
Is this fearless Self, distinguished by such qualities, Brahman—the sovereign, unsurpassed, and great—this being the meaning?
Indeed, Brahman is fearless;
it is well known in the world that "Brahman is fearless."
Therefore, it is indeed logical that the Self, characterized by such qualities, is Brahman.
He who thus knows the aforementioned Self as the fearless Brahman becomes, verily, the fearless Brahman. This is the summary of the meaning of this entire Upanishad that has been stated.

For the sake of the perfect awakening to this very reality, the imagination of origination, subsistence, dissolution, and so forth, as well as the superimposition of action, agent, and fruit, have been attributed to the Self. Then, by means of negating those through the formula "not this, not this" (*neti neti*), which removes all superimposed distinctions, the true nature is once again made known.

This is just as, for the purpose of fully understanding the nature of numbers from one up to the highest possible number (*aparārdha*), one employs the superimposition of lines; having done so, one causes [the student] to grasp and understand the nature of the number itself—saying "this line is one," "this is ten," "this is a hundred," "this is a thousand"—but [the lines] do not constitute the number itself.

Just as numbers, which are essentially lines, convey the forms of letters such as 'a' and so forth, so too here, by employing various means such as origination and the like, the single reality of Brahman has been made known. Furthermore, for the sake of purifying the specific distinctions produced by those imagined means, the summary of the reality was made through the words "not this, not this" (*neti neti*).
That [knowledge], having been withdrawn, is again completely pure and exclusively fruitful; this occurs at the end of this section (kaṇḍikā). //4.4.25//
Thus ends the fourth Brāhmaṇa.
Now, Yājñavalkya had two wives, Maitreyī and Kātyāyanī.
Of these two, Maitreyī was a seeker of Brahman.
"Then Kātyāyanī is indeed possessed of feminine wisdom.
Then Yājñavalkya, wishing to undertake another topic of discourse, said: "Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.1"
In the Madhu-kāṇḍa, which emphasizes traditional scripture (āgama), the reality of Brahman has been determined.
Furthermore, in the Yājñavalkya-kāṇḍa, which emphasizes reasoning (upapatti), it has been investigated through dialectical debate by adopting opposing positions and counter-positions.
And in the sixth [section], having investigated it in detail through the method of questions and answers in the relationship between disciple and teacher, it has been concluded.
Now begins the Maitreyī Brāhmaṇa, which serves as the conclusion.

This is the method adopted by those skilled in the science of sentences: "The restatement of the proposition after the presentation of the reason is the conclusion. Alternatively, that very knowledge of the Self, accompanied by renunciation, which was declared in the Madhu-kāṇḍa—which is primarily based on scripture—as the means to immortality, is here likewise established through reasoning as the means to immortality, accompanied by renunciation.
For the section [of the Veda] belonging to Yājñavalkya is preeminent in reasoning;
therefore, it has been ascertained through both scripture and reasoning that this knowledge of the Self, accompanied by renunciation, is the means to immortality.
Consequently, those who have faith in the scriptures and desire to attain immortality should practice this.
For an object that has been ascertained through both scripture (*āgama*) and reasoning (*upapatti*) is to be trusted because it is non-erroneous.
The meaning of the syllables here should be understood in the same way as their meaning was explained in the fourth [chapter].
We shall now explain those syllables which have not yet been explained.
The word "atha" (now/then) is intended to show the immediate succession following the instruction on causes.

For the preceding statements were primarily concerned with causes; immediately after them, the matter proposed is concluded by means of the Maitreyī Brāhmaṇa, which is primarily concerned with scriptural tradition (āgama).
The particle "ha" indicates the occurrence [of the narrative].

It is said that the sage Yājñavalkya had two wives: one was named Maitreyī and the other was named Kātyāyanī. Of these two wives, Maitreyī was indeed a seeker of Brahman (*brahmavādinī*), meaning she was habituated to discoursing upon Brahman;
whereas Kātyāyanī at that time possessed only "womanly wisdom" (*strīprajñā*)—that is, her wisdom was characterized solely by the pursuit of domestic affairs appropriate for a woman.

Now, this being the case, it is said that Yājñavalkya, desiring to undertake—that is, wishing to perform—the mode of life characterized by wandering mendicancy (pārivrājya), which is different from his previous mode of life characterized by the householder's state (gārhasthya). 4.5.1.
"O Maitreyī," Yājñavalkya said,
"I am indeed about to depart from this state, intending to go forth into the life of a wandering mendicant."
"Come, let me bring this Kātyāyanī to an end for you."

"O Maitreyī," he addressed his eldest wife; having addressed her, he said, "Indeed, O Maitreyī, I am about to depart from this state, that is, I am about to enter the life of a wandering mendicant (pārivrajya). O Maitreyī, give me your leave. "Well then, if you wish, let me make an end with this Kātyāyanī," and so forth—this has already been explained. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad Bhāṣya 4.5.2)
Maitreyī said: "If,
O Venerable Sir, this entire earth were filled with wealth for me, would I thereby become immortal, or not?"
"No," said Yājñavalkya,
"your life would be just like the life of those who possess material possessions."
"But there is no hope for immortality through wealth. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.3)
Maitreyī said:
"What should I do with that by which I would not become immortal?
Tell me only that which you know, O Venerable One."

Thus addressed, Maitreyī said: "If this entire earth were filled with wealth, would I become immortal through that wealth—through the rites accomplished by wealth—or would I not? "No," said Yājñavalkya; the rest is the same as before. (BrhUpBh 4.5.3–4)
Yājñavalkya said:
"Indeed, you, being dear to us, have increased what is dear."
"Well then, this shall be; I will explain it to you.
But while I am explaining, you must reflect upon it. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.5)
He said: "Indeed, previously you were dear to us; you have increased what is dear to us, you have determined it.
Therefore, being pleased, if you wish to know this means of immortality, O lady, I shall explain that means of immortality to you. 4.5.5.
He said:
"Verily, it is not out of love for the husband that the husband is dear; rather, it is out of love for the Self that the husband is dear."

"Verily, it is not out of love for the wife that the wife is dear, but it is out of love for the Self that the wife is dear. Verily, it is not out of love for the sons that the sons are dear, but it is out of love for the Self that the sons are dear.
Verily, it is not out of love for wealth that wealth is dear, but it is out of love for the Self that wealth is dear."

"Verily, it is not for the sake of cattle that cattle are dear; rather, it is for the sake of the Self that cattle are dear. Verily, it is not for the sake of the priesthood (brahman) that the priesthood is dear; rather, it is for the sake of the Self that the priesthood is dear.
Verily, it is not for the sake of the nobility (kṣatra) that the nobility is dear; rather, it is for the sake of the Self that the nobility is dear."
Verily, it is not for the sake of the worlds that the worlds are dear, but for the sake of the Self that the worlds are dear.

Verily, it is not for the sake of the gods that the gods are dear, but for the sake of the Self that the gods are dear. Verily, it is not for the sake of the Vedas that the Vedas are dear, but for the sake of the Self that the Vedas are dear.
"Verily, it is not for the sake of beings that beings are dear, but for the sake of the Self that beings are dear.
Verily, it is not for the sake of everything that everything is dear, but for the sake of the Self that everything is dear.
Therefore, O Maitreyī, the Self indeed should be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon."
Verily, my dear, when the Self is seen, heard, thought upon, and realized, all this is known.
"Verily, Maitreyī, when the Self is seen"—how is the Self seen? It is said:

first it is heard through the teacher and the traditional scripture (*āgama*), and then it is reflected upon through reasoning (*tarkeṇa*) and understood through logical justification (*upapatti*). It is thus investigated.
Hearing (*śravaṇa*) occurs through mere scripture; reflection (*mata*) occurs through reasoning; and subsequently, through wisdom (*vijñāna*), it is determined that "this is so and not otherwise.
What happens then? It is said: this becomes known.
"This all" refers to everything other than the self (*ātman*).
Because of its non-existence apart from the self. //4.5.6//
Brahman deserts him who knows Brahman as other than the Self;
the Kṣatra deserts him who knows the Kṣatra as other than the Self.
The worlds reject him who knows the worlds as other than the Self; the gods reject him who knows the gods as other than the Self;
the Vedas reject him who knows the Vedas as other than the Self.
The elements desert him who knows the elements as other than the Self;
everything deserts him who knows everything as other than the Self.
This is Brahman, this is the Kṣatra, these worlds, these gods, these Vedas, these beings—this whole world is what this Self is. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.7)
Just as, when a drum is being beaten, one would not be able to grasp the external sounds; but by grasping the drum, or the striking of the drum, the sound is grasped. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.8)
Just as when a conch shell is being blown, one would not be able to grasp the external sounds;
yet by grasping the conch shell, or the blower of the conch, the sound is grasped.
Just as when a lute is being played, one would not be able to grasp the external sounds;
but by grasping the lute, or the lute-player, the sound is grasped.

"He would cast him aside"—that is, he would exclude him from the state of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*)—on account of his offense, thinking: "This one perceives me through a nature that is not the Self. This is the intended meaning.
Just as from a fire of wet fuel that has been kindled, various clouds of smoke issue forth, even so, O dear one, from this Great Being...

This is the breath of the Existent: the Rigveda, the Yajurveda, the Samaveda, the Atharva-Angirasa, history, the Puranas, the sciences, the Upanishads, the verses, the aphorisms, the explanations, the commentaries; the sacrificed, the offered, the eaten, the drunk; and this world, the next world, and all beings.
All these are but His breaths.
Just as the ocean is the single point of convergence for all waters,
so the skin is the single point of convergence for all tactile sensations; so the two nostrils are the single point of convergence for all odors.
In this way, the tongue is the single point of convergence for all tastes; in this way, the eye is the single point of convergence for all forms;
in this way, the ear is the single point of convergence for all sounds.
Thus, the mind is the single point of convergence for all volitions;
thus, the heart is the single point of convergence for all branches of knowledge;
thus, the two hands are the single point of convergence for all actions.
In this way, the organ of generation is the single point of convergence for all joys;
in this way, the anus is the single point of convergence for all excretions;
in this way, the feet are the single point of convergence for all paths.
In this way, speech is the single point of convergence for all the Vedas.
In the fourth [chapter], the emission of the worlds and other objects was not mentioned separately because it follows by implication from the emission of the word itself.
However, here, since this constitutes the conclusion of the entire treatise, even though the meaning is already established, it must be made explicit; therefore, it is stated separately. (4.5.11–12)
Just as a mass of salt has no interior and no exterior, but is entirely a solid mass of flavor,
even so, my dear, this Self has no interior and no exterior, but is entirely a solid mass of consciousness.
"Arising from these very elements, one returns and dissolves into them.
After death, there is no consciousness," so I say, O Maitreyī.
Thus spoke Yājñavalkya.

In the dissolution of all effects caused by knowledge, the Self remains as a single mass of consciousness, without interior or exterior, like a lump of salt—entire and undivided. Previously, however, it possessed specific cognition acquired through contact with the elements and objects of experience.

When that specific cognition and its cause, the contact with the elements, have been dissolved by knowledge, Yājñavalkya stated: "After departing [from this world], there is no consciousness. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.13)
Maitreyī said:
"Right here, sir, you have landed me in the depths of confusion."
"Or rather, I do not know this.
He said: "Truly, I am not speaking a falsehood;
for truly, O Maitreyī, this Self is indestructible and its nature is such that it does not perish. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.14)

She said: "In this very matter, O Venerable One, you have pressed me down, as it were, from the edge of delusion to the very center of delusion—meaning you have confounded me—by saying that there is only a mass of consciousness and that there is no consciousness after death.
Therefore, I do not understand this Self as described by you through discrimination."

He said: "I do not speak out of delusion; for indeed, O Maitreyī, this Self is indestructible (*avināśī*). That which has the nature of perishing is 'destructible' (*vināśī*); it is not destructible, hence 'indestructible. By the word 'destructible,' the meaning is that the Self is changeless (*avikriya*), being free from destruction through modification. O Maitreyī, this Self under discussion possesses the quality of non-annihilation (*anucchittidharmā*)."

*Ucchitti* means cutting off; *uccheda* means annihilation, an end, or destruction. That which has *ucchitti* as its nature is *ucchittidharman*. One who does not have that nature is *anucchittidharman*. The meaning is that for him there exists neither destruction characterized by transformation nor destruction characterized by disintegration. // 4.5.14 //
For where there is duality, as it were, there one sees another;
there one smells another.
Then one tastes the other;
then one speaks to the other;
then one hears the other.
Therefore, one perceives another; therefore, one touches another;
therefore, one cognizes another.
But where for him everything has become the Self alone—then by what and whom should he see? Then by what and whom should he smell? Then by what...?
What would one relish, and by what means? What would one speak, and by what means? What would one hear, and by what means? What would one think, and by what means?
What would one touch, and by what means? What would one perceive, and by what means? By what could one perceive that by which all this is perceived?
This very Self is "not this, not this.
It is ungraspable, for it is not grasped; it is indestructible, for it is not destroyed.
Unattached, for he is not attached; unbound, he is neither shaken nor injured.
"By what, my dear Maitreyī, could one know the knower?"—thus has the instruction been imparted to you.
"Verily, my dear, this much is immortality," having said this, Yājñavalkya departed.
In all four chapters, one and the same Self—the supreme Brahman—is determined to be identical.
However, the specific means for its realization differ from one to another.
The goal, however, is that very same Self which was pointed out in the fourth chapter as "Now, therefore, the instruction is: not this, not this."
That very [Self] was determined in the fifth [book], through the presentation of the wagering of one's life in the dialogue between Śākalya and Yājñavalkya;
again at the conclusion of the fifth [book];
and again in the dialogue between Janaka and Yājñavalkya.
Furthermore, here at the conclusion of the Upaniṣad,

this final summary beginning with "That is this— 'Not this, not this'" is intended to demonstrate that all four chapters culminate in the Self alone, and that there is no other intended meaning in between.
For when the Reality is examined even by a hundred methods, the culmination is found to be only the Self as "Not this, not this," and nothing else is perceived.

Whether by reasoning or by scripture, therefore, this alone is the means to immortality: the thorough knowledge of the Self as "not this, not this," together with the renunciation of everything. Desiring to conclude this point, he says: "This much"—that is, only this much—namely, the vision of the non-dual Self as "not this, not this";
and this, O Maitreyī, is the means to immortality, independent of any other auxiliary cause.

"Whatever you know, O Blessed One, tell that very thing to me—the means to immortality. "This alone is what must be known by you," he said; thus indeed, having explained to his beloved wife the knowledge of the Self as the means to immortality—culminating in renunciation—this much is the instruction, this is the teaching of the Vedas, this is the supreme goal, and this is the finality of the duties to be performed for the sake of the human purpose.

Now, for the sake of discerning and understanding the meaning of the scriptures, this is investigated; for indeed, conflicting statements are observed, such as: "One should perform the *agnihotra* as long as one lives," "One should sacrifice with the *darśapūrṇamāsa* as long as one lives," "Performing actions here in this world, one should desire to live a hundred years," and "This *agnihotra*, indeed, lasts until old age"—these and others are indicators of the single stage of life (*aikāśramya*).

Furthermore, there are statements that prescribe the transition to other stages of life (*āśrama*), such as: "Having known [the Self], they depart from home and go forth into the wandering life" (*viditvā vyutthāya pravrajanti*); "Having completed the stage of the student, one should become a householder; having been a householder, one should become a forest-dweller and then go forth"; and "Or otherwise, one may go forth directly from the stage of the student, or from the household, or from the forest"; as well as:
"Neither by ritual action, nor by progeny, nor by wealth, but by renunciation alone did some attain immortality," and so forth.

Likewise, there are Smṛti texts: "One who has practiced celibacy goes forth [into the forest]"; "He whose celibacy is unbroken may dwell in whichever [stage] he desires"; and some declare that his stage of life is non-distinct [from the preceding]; likewise: "Having studied the Vedas according to the rule of celibacy, one should desire sons and grandsons for the sake of purifying the ancestors; having established the sacred fires and performed sacrifices according to the injunctions, one should then enter the forest and desire to become a sage."
“Having performed the Prājāpatya sacrifice, in which all one's possessions are given as the sacrificial fee,
and having internalized the sacred fires within oneself, a Brāhmaṇa should go forth from his home.”
These and other such statements exist;

indeed, hundreds of Vedic and Smṛti passages are found that are mutually contradictory, which prescribe the sequence of emerging from meditative absorption (*vyutthāna*), the stages of mental modification (*vikalpa*), and the undertaking of desired stages of life (*āśrama*).
Furthermore, there is the conduct of those who know these matters.
Furthermore, there is a divergence of opinion even among the learned who understand the meaning of the treatise;
therefore, it is not possible for those of dull intellect to discern and comprehend the meaning of the treatise.
Indeed, only those whose intellects are perfected in the logic of the treatise are able to determine the specific scope of these statements.
Therefore, in order to make known the distinction between their respective domains, we shall investigate them according to the capacity of our intellect.
Since it is impossible for statements such as "as long as one lives" (*yāvaj-jīva*) to have any other meaning, the purpose of the Veda culminates in action.

This is because of the scriptural injunction regarding funeral rites—namely, "they burn him with the sacrificial vessels"—and because of the indicative mark found in the text "one dies with old age" (*jarā-marya*), as well as the traditional saying, "the body ends in ashes."
For, according to the path of wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājya*), the body would not end in ashes;

and there is a Smṛti text: "He for whom the ritual procedure—from the impregnation rite (*niṣeka*) until the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*)—is prescribed by means of mantras, it should be known that he alone has the qualification (*adhikāra*) for this scripture, and no one else."
For the Smṛti shows that whatever action is prescribed here by the Veda along with its ritual formulas (mantras) has the cremation ground as its final end.
Furthermore, by demonstrating the absence of qualification [for rites], it is understood that one who is without action is absolutely excluded from the qualification for the Śruti.
This is also because of the exception regarding the removal of the sacred fires: "He who removes the fire is indeed a slayer of the heroes of the gods."
[Objection: Is it not the case that the completion of the Vedic ritual act is optional, depending on whether one has renounced worldly life (*vyutthāna*) or not?
[Reply: No, because the scriptural texts concerning renunciation and so forth have a different purpose.
This refers to such scriptural injunctions as, "One should perform the *agnihotra* as long as one lives," and "One should sacrifice with the *darśapūrṇamāsa* as long as one lives."

Since it is impossible to assume any other purpose because [the injunction] has as its sole motive the mere fact of living, and since the passages concerning renunciation (*vyutthāna*) and so forth can thus be understood as referring to those who are not qualified for ritual action,
[this is supported by] the Vedic mantra: "One should indeed live here performing rituals for a hundred years," and [by the fact that] one is released from them either by old age.

Nor does the phrase "or by death" imply that for those engaged in ritual action (*karmiṇ*), the state of ending at the cremation ground is optional—given that apart from old age and death there is no possibility of an interval due to the non-separation from karma.

Furthermore, even those such as the one-eyed or the humpbacked, who are not qualified for ritual action, are indeed to be favored by the Śruti; thus, the injunction of other stages of life (*āśrama*) such as renunciation (*vyutthāna*) is not untenable.
If it is argued that there would be no room for the sequential injunction of wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājya*), we say no.

Because the *viśvajit* and *sarvamedha* sacrifices constitute exceptions to the injunction of lifelong performance (*yāvajjīvavidhi*), the exception applies specifically to the lifelong *agnihotra* and other such rites; and in those two cases, it is possible to determine a sequence [of stages], as there is no contradiction in the statement: “Having completed the period of studentship (*brahmacarya*), one should become a householder; having been a householder, one should become a forest-dweller (*vanī*), and then renounce. (Note: The term *vanī* is a Vedic form of *vānaprastha*.)

For if it has such a scope, there is no contradiction whatsoever with the scriptural injunction regarding the life of a wandering mendicant (pārivrājya), since that is understood as a sequential stage. There is no sublation in assuming another scope either,
because the self-knowledge is accepted as the cause of immortality.

You have accepted that the knowledge of the Self—which begins with the passage, "One should meditate upon [the Self] as 'This indeed is the Self,'" and concludes with the section ending, "He is 'not this, not this'"—is the means to immortality.
However, you do not tolerate the idea that this alone is the means to immortality, independent of anything else.
Regarding this, I ask you: for what reason do you accept the knowledge of the Self?

Listen to the reason for this: just as one who desires heaven, not knowing the means to attain it, accepts that the Agnihotra and other rites are the instruments for achieving heaven, so too here [the scriptures] accept that the knowledge of the Self is the means [to immortality].
Since the authority is equal in both cases, it is proper to accept that the knowledge of the Self, as it is made known, is indeed the instrument for attaining immortality.
If this were so, what would follow?

Because the knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna*) sublates the causes of all actions, the cessation of karma occurs upon the arising of that wisdom (*vidyā*). As for the Agnihotra and other rites connected with wife and fire, they are accomplished by means of an instrumental factor (*kāraka*) consisting of a recipient (*saṃpradāna*) which is the object of the notion of duality. For indeed, that rite cannot be completed by means of a mantra unless one perceives the deity, such as Agni, as an instrumental factor in the form of a recipient, which is to be distinguished from [the knower's] own cognition.

For that notion of the recipient (*saṃpradāna-kāraka*) by which the recipient is taught as being an instrument for the action is here sublated by knowledge, [as shown in such passages as]: "He who thinks, 'He is one and I am another,' does not know"; "The gods abandon him who knows the gods as other than the Self";
"From death to death he goes who perceives here as if there were multiplicity"; and "The Self alone is to be beheld as one."
This is known from such scriptural passages as, "He sees," and so forth.
Furthermore, the knowledge of the Self does not depend on place, time, or instrumental causes, because its object is the established reality that is the Self;
whereas ritual action, being dependent on the person performing it, may indeed depend on place, time, and instrumental causes.
Knowledge, however, because it depends on the nature of the object (*vastutantratvāt*), does not depend on place, time, causal conditions, and so forth;
just as fire is hot and space is formless, so too is the realization of the Self (*ātmavijñāna*). [Objection:
If this were so, would there not be a subversion of the injunctions that constitute the means of valid knowledge?
Nor is it logical for two things of equal authority to mutually negate one another;
no, because [the knowledge of the Self] merely negates the cognition of inherent difference.
For the knowledge of the Self, which negates other injunctions, does not merely negate the cognition of inherent difference.
If it is argued that, nevertheless, because the cause has been removed, the action cannot occur and thus there would be a cessation of the injunction itself—this is not so;
for there is no fault here, as it is like the cessation of engagement in a desired act due to the prohibition of the desire.

Just as in the case of the injunction "One desiring heaven should sacrifice," when a person engaged in the sacrifice as a means to attain heaven has their desire thwarted by a prohibition of that desire, their engagement in the performance of the desired sacrifice comes to a halt.
Nor does the injunction for optional rites (kāmya-vidhi) become nullified by this much.
If it is argued that because the injunction prohibiting desire makes one know the undesirable nature of the optional rite, its performance becomes impossible;

and if it is further argued that since there would be no performer if the rite were not to be performed, the injunctions for performance would be purposeless, and thus the ritual injunctions (karma-vidhi) would lack authority—[we reply]: No.

Since activity is possible prior to the knowledge of the Self, it is indeed logical that the innate cognition of the distinction between action, its factors, and its results serves as the cause for ritual action before the knowledge of the Self.

Just as, regarding objects of desire, the innate longing for heaven and so forth serves as the cause for engaging in optional rites prior to the arising of the cognition of their defects, so it is here.
If it is argued that this being the case, the Veda would have no purpose, we say: no.
Because benefit and harm depend upon the intention [of the agent];
for, with the single exception of liberation, everything else falls within the domain of ignorance,
since benefit and harm are dependent upon the intention of the person.

Because one desires to see the desired [result] even at the time of death and so forth, therefore, ritual injunctions (karma-vidhi) remain in force only as long as there is no orientation toward the injunction for self-knowledge (ātmajñāna).

Consequently, it is established that rituals do not coexist with self-knowledge; thus, self-knowledge alone is the means to immortality, as expressed in the words: "Verily, this much, my dear, is immortality."

Because knowledge is independent of action, renunciation is established for the wise man by the mere firm realization of the Self as Brahman—which is immutable and devoid of categories such as the agent of action (e.g., the recipient of a gift), action itself, and genus—even without an explicit scriptural statement, according to the reasoning already stated. This has been explained by the Hotṛ’s words: “For us, this Self is the world.”
"Former wise men, desiring no offspring, renounced the world"—thus the state of wandering mendicancy (pārivrājya) was known by the wise solely through the awakening to the Self as the world.

And so, the state of wandering mendicancy is established even for one who merely desires to know (vividiṣu), according to the scriptural statement: "Desiring this very Self as their world, they go forth into homelessness."
We have already stated that ritual actions (karmas) pertain to the domain of the ignorant;

and since actions consist of production, acquisition, modification, and refinement within the domain of ignorance, we have also stated that actions serve as means for attaining self-knowledge by way of purifying the self—based on the scriptural statement, "Those who desire to know [Brahman] through sacrifice and other rites. Now, in considering the relative strength and weakness of the duties belonging to the stages of life (āśramas), which fall within the domain of the ignorant, with respect to the production of self-knowledge, there are the mental qualities such as humility (amānitva) and others where self-restraint (yama) is predominant, as well as meditation, knowledge, dispassion, and so forth.
[The former] consists of cooperative assistance (*sannipatyopakāratva*).

Because of the abundance of violence, passion, hatred, and so forth, the other [type of person] is mixed with many afflicted actions (*kliṣṭakarman*); for this reason, they praise the wandering life (*pārivrājya*) for those seeking liberation: "Indeed, the renunciation of all actions—even those previously performed—is detachment; furthermore, this is the supreme limit of liberation."
“O Brahmin, what use have you for wealth, what use for kinsmen, or what use for a wife, since you must die?
Seek the Self that has entered the cave; where have your grandfathers and your father gone?”
"Thus, in the Sāṃkhya and Yoga treatises as well, renunciation is said to be proximate to knowledge;
for the absence of the impulse toward desire is [the means].
Indeed, the fact that the impulse toward desire is antagonistic to knowledge is well-established in all the scriptures."

Therefore, it is logically consistent that one who is dispassionate and seeks liberation should renounce the world from the stage of studentship (*brahmacarya*) itself, even without [prior] knowledge; for this is supported by such scriptural passages as "one should renounce from studentship alone. Now, it might be argued that because this statement leaves room for interpretation, it refers only to those who are not yet qualified [for renunciation], since it would otherwise contradict the scriptural injunction to live the life of a householder "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīva*).
This is not a valid objection.
Because the scriptural injunctions regarding lifelong duties possess ample scope,
we have indeed stated that all ritual actions must be performed by one who desires to avoid blame;
however, it does not follow that an action must be performed solely for the sake of life itself, independent of other considerations.
For generally, human beings abound in desire,
and desire has manifold objects and is to be accomplished through manifold ritual means.
Furthermore, Vedic rituals— which have manifold fruits and require the performance of acts involving wives, fire, and personal agency— are to be performed again and again.

Just as agriculture and other such activities yield abundant fruits only upon completion over a period of hundreds of years, so too do the stages of life in the household or the forest; therefore, with reference to those, there are scriptural injunctions for "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīva*).
Furthermore, there is the mantra-text: "Performing indeed here [in this world] actions...
And according to that view, there is the abandonment of ritual action only in the cases of the Viśvajit and Sarvamedha sacrifices.
Furthermore, in that view where the practice lasts for as long as one lives, the body ends at the cremation ground and its finality is in ashes;
or else, the scriptural injunction regarding lifelong practice is with respect to other castes,
for there is no undertaking of wandering mendicancy for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas.

Likewise, statements such as "for whom the rule is declared by means of mantras" and "the teachers [maintain] the single stage of life," and so forth, refer specifically to Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas. Therefore, depending on the individual's capacity, knowledge of sacrifice, dispassion, desire, and other factors, the various methods for renouncing worldly life, the options for withdrawal, the sequence of stages, and the attainment of the state of a wandering mendicant (pārivrājya) are not contradictory.

Furthermore, because various [other] types of renunciation are prescribed for those who are not qualified [for the householder stage], such as "whether he be one who has completed his studies or one who has not, whether he be one whose sacred fires have been extinguished or one who is without fires," and so forth;
therefore, the other stages of life (āśramas) are established as being intended only for those who are qualified.
Thus ends the fifth Brāhmaṇa.
